title: Quantifying and Mitigating Consensus Disparity in Social and Information Networks
affiliations: and Cornell University - Department of Computer Science

detail.title: Quantifying and Mitigating Consensus Disparity in Social and Information Networks
detail.abstract: We introduce a computational framework to measure and optimize disparity, which corresponds to the difference in consensus outcomes attributable to distinct social groups, under classical models of opinion dynamics. We study this problem in the Friedkin-Johnsen setting under uncertainty about group structure and characterize its algorithmic complexity. For the structural analysis, we demonstrate that disparity can be arbitrarily larger than polarization in well-connected networks that nonetheless carry an identifiable group structure. For the mitigation problem, we derive robust formulations and active set optimization procedures to minimize worst-case disparity via recommendation reweighing and opinion seeding. Our methods provide provable guarantees and are validated on multiple real-world social networks. The results bridge opinion dynamics and network optimization, offering computational tools for analyzing and reducing polarization in social networks.

title: Infodynamics of Corruption and Parasitism, a Review
affiliations: Universidad Simon Bolivar

detail.title: Infodynamics of Corruption and Parasitism, a Review
detail.abstract: Infodynamics studies how energy and information interact and change over time. In social behaviour this interaction is especially visible: relationships involving asymmetric energy exchange, often take the form of parasitism or corruption. Corruption denotes behaviour that is unlawful, whereas social parasitism describes exploitative relationships that are socially damaging but legal. In contemporary societies a primary form of energy is money, and many instances of parasitic or corrupt behaviour revolve around its distribution and use. Social parasitic behaviour predate human society: primate studies document bribery-like exchanges for favours, status, food, shelter, transport, or priority in scarce resources, showing that moneyless systems are not immune to corruption. Corruption can cause incalculable harm to society as victims of earthquakes in Haiti, Tukey and Venezuela can attest. This essay reviews essential aspects of corruption and social parasitism among humans. Both phenomena are sustained when information is distorted and transparency is suppressed, preventing antagonistic or corrective forces from acting.

title: The Two Wings AI Framework

detail.title: The Two Wings AI Framework

detail.abstract: Enterprises are investing heavily in artificial intelligence, yet a large share of initiatives are reported either to stall before production or to reach it without delivering measurable value. This paper argues that the gap is structural: an initiative is assessed for whether AI is done right (trust, safety, compliance) and for whether it is worth doing (value, return), but seldom for both on one structure. In response it develops the Two Wings AI Framework (TWAF), a conceptual governance framework that scores an initiative on two co-equal axes, Value and Trust. Each axis is a six-altitude, bottom-up dependency stack mapped to recognised standards, the two stacks paired altitude by altitude into twelve boxes, and the decision to enter production is taken where the two axes meet, not along either one alone. TWAF is positioned against its nearest neighbours: strategic portfolio matrices, the balanced scorecard, stage-gate innovation control, and IT- and AI-governance frameworks. Pairing value with risk is not itself new, as COBIT and Val IT attest; the contribution claimed here is narrower: rendering each axis as an AI-specific, standards-anchored dependency stack and fusing the two into a single, layered production decision. The paper also weighs the failure-rate evidence that motivates it, finding a consistent direction but underlying rates that are not commensurable. TWAF is presented as a design-science and conceptual-framework artifact: a structured lens that yields testable propositions. Those propositions are stated explicitly, each holding that the two-sided pairing, the interaction between the axes, and the foundational altitudes carry distinct, disconfirmable consequences, alongside the observations that would disconfirm them and a staged programme for their evaluation. Its strongest empirical anchor, that governed data, or more precisely the quality and structure of that data, is a precondition for trustworthy AI, rests on independent peer-reviewed evidence; its central pairing claim is stated plainly as not yet empirically validated.

title: When the Metric Sets the Standard: Experienced Technological Shaping, Perceived Autonomy, and Continuance Intention in AI Wearables

detail.title: When the Metric Sets the Standard: Experienced Technological Shaping, Perceived Autonomy, and Continuance Intention in AI Wearables

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) wearables continuously monitor behaviour and generate feedback, goals, and metrics that may influence both behaviour and the standards through which that behaviour is evaluated. Research on continuance intention typically explains continued technology use through instrumental evaluations and habit, yet these models may not fully capture this shaping dimension. This study introduces experienced technological shaping (ETS), defined as the reflective awareness that wearable feedback has influenced users’ evaluative standards, and examines whether it explains continuance intention beyond perceived usefulness, privacy concerns, and habit, and whether perceived autonomy (PA) mediates this relationship. A cross-sectional survey of 201 current AI wearable users was analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). Contrary to the hypothesised positive direction, ETS showed a small but statistically significant negative association with continuance intention once the established predictors were controlled, interpreted through Self-Determination Theory (SDT) as a form of metric-driven pressure associated with reduced continued engagement. PA emerged as both the strongest predictor of continuance intention and the mediating mechanism through which ETS generated a positive indirect effect on continued use, producing a pattern of competitive mediation in which the two pathways largely cancel each other out. These findings suggest that the conscious experience of being shaped by a wearable device carries two simultaneous consequences for continued use, and that supporting users’ sense of autonomy is consequential both as a direct driver of sustained engagement and as the mechanism through which shaping generates positive continuance effects. The study supplies a new construct to continuance research and points to autonomy-supportive design as a direction for improving wearable retention.

title: AI-Powered Personalized Marketing and Consumer Purchase Decisions: Evidence from Pakistan's E-Commerce Sector
affiliations: Bahauddin Zakariya University

detail.title: AI-Powered Personalized Marketing and Consumer Purchase Decisions: Evidence from Pakistan's E-Commerce Sector

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved human participants and was conducted in accordance with accepted ethical standards for social science research. Participation was voluntary, and informed consent was obtained from all respondents prior to data collection. Participants were assured of anonymity and confidentiality, and no personally identifiable information was collected. The study posed minimal risk to participants and was conducted solely for academic research purposes.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming e-commerce environments by enabling firms to deliver AI-powered personalized marketing that enhances consumer engagement and decision efficiency. Despite growing global interest, limited empirical evidence exists in emerging markets regarding how AI-driven personalization influences consumer purchase decisions through psychological mechanisms such as trust and familiarity. This study examines the impact of AI-powered personalized marketing on consumer purchase decisions in Pakistan's e-commerce sector, integrating consumer trust in AI as a mediating variable and consumer familiarity with AI as a moderating variable. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the study extends traditional TAM by incorporating trust and familiarity as key behavioral determinants in AI-mediated decision environments. A quantitative research design was employed, and data were collected from 300 online consumers using a structured questionnaire. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to analyze the data due to its suitability for complex models involving mediation and moderation, as well as its predictive orientation. The results reveal that AI-powered personalized marketing significantly influences consumer purchase decisions both directly and indirectly through consumer trust in AI. Furthermore, consumer familiarity with AI strengthens the relationship between trust and purchase decisions, indicating that prior exposure to AI technologies enhances behavioral responsiveness. The study contributes to AI marketing literature by extending TAM and providing empirical evidence from an emerging economy context. Practically, the findings highlight the importance of building transparent, trustworthy, and user-friendly AI systems to improve consumer adoption and purchase behavior.

title: Building Epistemic Coalitions: How Cross-Sector Alliances Between Academia, Industry, and Civil Society Shape AI Governance Norms

detail.title: Building Epistemic Coalitions: How Cross-Sector Alliances Between Academia, Industry, and Civil Society Shape AI Governance Norms
detail.abstract: AI governance norms do not emerge through top-down regulation alone. Before formal legislation arrives-and often determining what legislation looks like when it doesgovernance norms are shaped by informal coalitions that establish shared language, produce evidence, define problem boundaries, and create policy templates that regulators subsequently adopt, adapt, or contest. This paper maps how these epistemic coalitionscross-sector alliances between academic researchers, industry practitioners, civil society advocates, and policy entrepreneurs-actually function in the AI governance space. Drawing on epistemic community theory from international relations (Haas, 1992) and co-production frameworks from science and technology studies (Jasanoff, 2004), the paper introduces the Epistemic Coalition Architecture Model (ECAM)-a framework identifying four structural features that determine whether cross-sector coalitions produce governance norms that serve broad public interest or are captured by the most resource-rich participants. The model is validated through comparative analysis of four norm-formation episodes: the development of AI fairness metrics and benchmarks (academia-led, industry-adopted), the establishment of AI transparency norms (civil society-led, partially legislated), the construction of AI safety narratives (industry-led, contested by researchers), and the emergence of AI sovereignty discourse (government-led, industry-resisted). Analysis of 31 coalition-level interactions across these episodes reveals that coalition effectiveness depends on four structural features: shared evidentiary standards, credible boundary-spanning individuals, institutional platforms for sustained interaction, and governance of resource asymmetry between coalition members. The paper argues that epistemic coalitions are the invisible infrastructure of AI governance and that understanding their dynamics is essential for anyone seeking to shape-or resist-the norms that will govern algorithmic systems.

detail.abstract:
Software teams now face a familiar problem in a new form. Many enterprises adopted Agile methods as a process system, treated psychological safety as a culture slogan, and are now adding artificial intelligence to teams whose operating models were already strained. The result is predictable: more tools, faster outputs, better-looking reports, and uneven improvement in actual team performance. 
This paper proposes that sustainable high performance in software teams requires the alignment of three mutually reinforcing conditions: Agile mindedness, the disciplined orientation toward learning, adaptation, feedback, and evidence; psychological safety, the interpersonal condition that allows teams to surface risk, admit uncertainty, challenge assumptions, and learn without social punishment; and AI integration, the deliberate embedding of AI capabilities into team knowledge flow, decision support, and workflow automation in ways that amplify human judgment rather than displace it. 
Drawing on research in psychological safety, Agile software development, software delivery performance, and human-AI collaboration, this paper develops the Learning-Trust-Amplification (LTA) Framework. The framework argues that AI does not independently make software teams high performing. AI amplifies the operating model into which it is introduced. Teams with strong learning loops and trust conditions can use AI to improve adaptability, decision quality, delivery flow, and organizational learning. Teams without those foundations often use AI to accelerate confusion, obscure risk, and automate flawed assumptions.

title:
Statement of Cash Flows and Related Matters:

A Critical Review of Reporting Practice, Regulation, and Decision-Usefulness in Emerging Economies

detail.title:
Statement of Cash Flows and Related Matters:

A Critical Review of Reporting Practice, Regulation, and Decision-Usefulness in Emerging Economies
detail.abstract: The statement of cash flows (SCF) is, in principle, the least judgmental of the primary financial statements. In practice, however, its preparation, presentation, and interpretation are shaped by deep institutional, regulatory, linguistic, and economic forces that operate with particular intensity in emerging economies. This paper develops a critical synthesis of how the SCF is prepared, audited, and used in emerging-market settings, with explicit attention to International Accounting Standard 7 (IAS 7), the indirect-method bias inherited from common reporting practice, the classification of interest, dividends, and taxation, non-cash transaction disclosure, the treatment of foreign currency translation and hyperinflation, supplier finance and reverse factoring arrangements, restricted cash, and the role of the SCF in earnings-quality assessment. The paper is structured around a transparent, replicable, and reflexive methodology: a structured narrative review combined with a thematic synthesis of 124 sources identified through a systematic search of Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO Business Source Complete, ScienceDirect, JSTOR, SSRN, and Google Scholar, supplemented by hand searches of leading journals, snowballing of citations, and targeted retrieval of regulator and standard-setter pronouncements. The review documents pervasive evidence of classification shifting between operating and non-operating sections of the SCF in jurisdictions with weak enforcement and concentrated ownership, persistent under-disclosure of non-cash items, inconsistent treatment of foreign currency cash flows and the effects of restating hyperinflationary economies, and growing concern over supplier finance arrangements that obscure operating cash-flow dynamics. The paper also surfaces a methodological lesson for emerging-economy scholarship: the SCF is best studied as a socio-technical artefact whose information content depends jointly on standards, enforcement, audit quality, governance, and macroeconomic volatility. The implications for standard-setters, securities regulators, auditors, preparers, and accounting educators are discussed, and an agenda for future empirical and qualitative research is proposed.

title: The AI Lobbyist's Dilemma: Navigating Credibility, Commercial Interest, and Genuine Public Benefit in Technology Policy

detail.title: The AI Lobbyist's Dilemma: Navigating Credibility, Commercial Interest, and Genuine Public Benefit in Technology Policy
detail.abstract: AI companies face a structural credibility paradox in policy advocacy: they are simultaneously the most technically informed participants in AI policy debates and the most commercially conflicted. A company that advocates for responsible AI regulation while lobbying against specific provisions affecting its business model faces growing skepticism from policymakers, civil society, and the public-yet the same company possesses technical expertise that governance processes genuinely need. This paper investigates the structural tensions in corporate AI policy engagement through the lens of credibility economics, analyzing when and why corporate AI advocacy is perceived as legitimate versus self-serving. Drawing on signaling theory (Spence, 1973), cheap talk models in game theory (Crawford & Sobel, 1982), and empirical analysis of corporate advocacy strategies across the EU AI Act, US state-level AI legislation, and India's data protection and AI governance debates, the paper introduces the AI Advocacy Credibility Model (AACM)-a framework identifying three corporate advocacy archetypes (the Aligned Advocate, the Strategic Compromiser, and the Transparent Opponent) and mapping the conditions under which each archetype builds or destroys policy credibility. Analysis of 67 documented corporate advocacy episodes across the three jurisdictions reveals that credibility is not primarily a function of policy position-companies can credibly oppose regulation-but of positional consistency, cost-bearing signals, and transparency about commercial interest. The paper argues that long-term commercial success in AI depends on building durable policy credibility rather than winning short-term lobbying battles, and proposes a credibility investment framework for corporate AI policy teams.

title: Evaluative Ambiguity in LLM-Based Judgment Systems: Evidence from Platform
affiliations: and

detail.title: Evaluative Ambiguity in LLM-Based Judgment Systems: Evidence from Platform
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to transform unstructured textual feedback into structured evaluative signals. We examine when LLM-based evaluators can reliably infer platform ratings from review narratives and when this evaluative translation breaks down. We conceptualize LLM-based evaluative translation as the process of converting unstructured evaluative narratives into structured platform-rating inferences. Using 20,000 Yelp reviews scored by GPT, Claude, and Gemini, we find that LLM-platform rating divergence increases when review text contains evaluative ambiguity, especially high transformer-based sentiment entropy. Divergence is lowest when textual signals and platform ratings are evaluatively congruent, but rises sharply when they are ambiguous, mixed, or incongruent. Multi-LLM analyses further show that the main patterns are stable across GPT, Claude, and Gemini, suggesting that evaluative ambiguity and text-rating incongruence affect LLM-based rating inference beyond any single model provider. The findings are robust across alternative sentiment measures, congruence thresholds, and leave-one-LLM-out consensus constructions. This study theorizes LLM-based evaluative translation as a key mechanism through which generative AI converts qualitative user-generated content into structured decision inputs.

title: Public Knowledge Is Made: Information Production in a Networked Society

detail.title: Public Knowledge Is Made: Information Production in a Networked Society
detail.abstract: Public knowledge is not simply found; it is produced, filtered, circulated, and contested across institutions, platforms, algorithms, and everyday acts of participation. Bringing together contributions on journalism, education, marketing, archives, health communication, cultural representation, and artificial intelligence, this special issue examines how information gains visibility, credibility, meaning, and public consequence in a networked society.

title:
The Cybersecurity Consequences of AI Strategy: 
How Automation-orientation and Augmentation-orientation Shape Data Breach Risk
affiliations: Virginia Tech, University of Delaware - Accounting & MIS and University of Miami Herbert Business School

detail.title:
The Cybersecurity Consequences of AI Strategy: 
How Automation-orientation and Augmentation-orientation Shape Data Breach Risk
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a strategic cornerstone of organizational transformation, offering the potential to enhance cybersecurity while introducing new risks. Yet the cybersecurity implications of AI adoption remain poorly understood empirically. We argue that security outcomes depend not only on whether firms use AI, but also on the strategic orientation firms take toward AI deployment. Drawing on organizational control theory, we develop a framework theorizing how AI Automation Strategy and AI Augmentation Strategy shape two organizational control capabilities, visibility and intervenability, with consequences for breach risk. Using LLM-assisted classification of large-scale job-posting data linked to data breach records for 3,006 U.S. public firms from 2018 to 2024, we find that AI Automation Strategy is associated with higher breach risk while AI Augmentation Strategy is associated with lower breach risk. These findings remain consistent across panel fixed-effects models, difference-indifferences analyses, Oster bounds, falsification tests, and alternative model specifications. Mechanism evidence shows that automation operates by eroding visibility of AI-mediated workflows and downstream operations, reflected in longer breach detection latency, while augmentation operates by improving both visibility and intervenability, reflected in shorter breach detection and containment latency. We further find that these associations respond to different organizational levers: AI Integration Depth attenuates automation's riskamplifying association, whereas AI Governance strengthens augmentation's protective association, an asymmetry suggesting that the effectiveness of organizational safeguards depends on the AI strategy in play. The cybersecurity consequences of AI thus depend critically on how AI is assigned to organizational work, embedded in firm operations, and governed through organizational oversight.

title: Climbing Down the Ladder: Regressive Integration in Global Value Chains across Middle-Income Economies (2000-2024)

detail.title: Climbing Down the Ladder: Regressive Integration in Global Value Chains across Middle-Income Economies (2000-2024)

detail.abstract: How has the integration of middle-income economies into global value chains (GVCs) evolved as hyperglobalization gave way to slowbalization and as China and the United States diverged? This article addresses that question with an original empirical base computed directly from the Asian Development Bank multi-region input-output tables. Regressive integration was first formulated as declining industrial competitiveness and reprimarization in trade. This article relocates it within the structure of global value chains and value-added accounting, and redefines it as a single structural repositioning with four simultaneous faces-export composition, foreign value added, structural sophistication, and embodied carbon-of which the value-added and environmental dimensions are new. Rather than a list of symptoms, the four are co-moving readings of one movement: a retreat toward upstream, resourcebased links that are at once lower in value added, thinner in technology, and higher in carbon. We turn this from a single-country diagnosis into a measurable, falsifiable, and comparable category, and use it to distinguish alternative routes of subordinate integration rather than to describe any single country. The analysis proceeds at three levels: global, regional, and a set of salient economies, with Brazil as the central case. Regressive integration turns out to be selective, not a function of income. Across a panel of twenty-six middle-income economies, exposure to Chinese demand is associated with reprimarization but not with import dependence, and a principal component analysis shows that subordinate integration is two-dimensional: a commodity route (Brazil, Indonesia, the Andean economies) is distinct from an assembly route (Mexico, Vietnam, Thailand) and from upgrading (China, India, Turkey). Brazil is the most illustrative case of the commodity route, regressing toward the primary-export pattern of its own region from a historically more industrialized position. By rendering this position measurable and comparable, the framework offers an empirical basis for the current revival of strategic-technology and industrial policy, in which critical-mineral value chains are becoming decisive.

title: Inclusive governance, innovative services and reach: trade unions adapting to a diverse workforce

detail.title: Inclusive governance, innovative services and reach: trade unions adapting to a diverse workforce

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Inclusive governance is about who participates in trade union decision-making and how. It is critical to the effectiveness of unions, as member-driven organisations, and their inclusiveness in engaging with diverse worker groups. This means that inclusive governance is strongly connected to measures to enhance member services and reach. All three are vital responses to the important challenges of key transformations in the world of work and broader society, spanning socio-economic and political shifts, environmental, demographic and technological disruptions, and widespread violation of core labour rights worldwide.

In seeking to navigate this rapidly changing world of work, unions are no strangers to innovation. This report explores current trade union actions, challenges and opportunities around inclusive governance, servicing and reach in response to key transitions. It draws on a mapping exercise of documented practices worldwide, focusing on results from an international survey and interviews with global union leaders.

title: When a Foreigner Shows Us Home: Filipino Provincial Culture as Public Knowledge on YouTube

detail.title: When a Foreigner Shows Us Home: Filipino Provincial Culture as Public Knowledge on YouTube
detail.abstract: This article explores how Jessica Lee’s Probinsya series transforms YouTube travel vlogging into a form of public knowledge production. Viewed through a foreigner’s perspective, familiar places are reintroduced with renewed curiosity and appreciation, encouraging Filipinos to see their own communities in a different light. By documenting provincial life and circulating it through digital media, Probinsya functions as a cultural archive that preserves, shares, and reactivates knowledge about Filipino culture. The series demonstrates how travel content can become a meaningful space for producing, remembering, and making cultural knowledge accessible to the public.

title: Distorted Memory In The Digital World: The Vulnerability of Online Public Memory in The Philippines
affiliations: University of Philippines

detail.title: Distorted Memory In The Digital World: The Vulnerability of Online Public Memory in The Philippines
detail.abstract: Journalism is, by design, factual yet subjective to its meaning. Individuals favor the truth when it speaks for their personal interests—a quiet authority influencing what the public comes to accept as the truth. Set against the backdrop of political media in the Philippines, the public themselves maneuvers the normalities within the ideology of what is socially accepted and ethically right. Media were the vehicle to arrive at the concept of truth in power within a public discourse. And the newsroom is not by choice, flooded by information offering different perspectives contrastingly, forcing journalists to navigate a constant stream of competing narratives, biases, and interpretations in pursuit of engaging yet accurate reporting. The challenges of journalism were not limited to the premises of the newsroom, instead, it extended beyond and into broader political and institutional structures that influence how information is produced and circulated.

title: Multistage Assessment of Construction Delay Factors using Expert Evaluation and Real Project Data
affiliations: Military Technical College - Egypt, Port Said University, Military Technical College - Egypt and Military Technical College - Egypt

detail.title: Multistage Assessment of Construction Delay Factors using Expert Evaluation and Real Project Data
detail.abstract: Construction delays remain a major challenge, especially in developing countries where financial, administrative, and resource constraints intensify schedule disruptions. This study identifies and prioritizes construction delay factors through a three-phase research framework consisting of a literature review, an expert survey evaluation, and validation using real-life construction projects in Egypt. First, a comprehensive review of global literature led to the identification of 98 delay factors, which were classified into four main categories: owner-related factors (25 factors, 26%), contractorrelated factors (34 factors, 35%), consultant/design-related factors (14 factors, 14%), and external factors (25 factors, 26%). Second, an expert survey was conducted to evaluate the previously identified delay factors. This phase employed a composite scoring approach that integrates both the frequency of occurrence and the impact of each factor to rank the most critical delay drivers. The findings indicate that owner-related factors constitute the most significant sources of delay, accounting for approximately 50% of the top 22 critical factors. Finally, the reliability of these findings was validated using the top 22 factors and a dataset of 141 real construction projects, showing strong alignment between the survey-based rankings and actual outcomes. Key factors, such as frequent change orders and design modifications, remained top-ranked, while some factors ranked higher or lower in practice, indicating minor variations in their relative importance under real project conditions. The study contributes a validated dataset of delay factors derived from both expert evaluation and real project evidence, providing a strong foundation for future predictive modeling applications using artificial intelligence and machine learning.

title: The Dual-Track for Multipotential Youth Talent (DTMYT) Framework: Conceptual Foundations for Developing Talent Managers and Entrepreneurs

detail.title: The Dual-Track for Multipotential Youth Talent (DTMYT) Framework: Conceptual Foundations for Developing Talent Managers and Entrepreneurs
detail.abstract: Contemporary organizations require individuals who can both create value through entrepreneurial initiative and develop the capabilities of others within complex human systems. Yet many education systems, including Korea's, provide limited structured opportunity for young people to develop either set of capacities in a deliberate and integrated way. This paper proposes the Dual-Track for Multipotential Youth Talent (DTMYT) framework as a response. The framework distinguishes two interconnected developmental pathways that begin in secondary school: a Talent Manager track focused on recognizing potential, designing developmental experiences, facilitating collaboration, and building enabling conditions for others; and a Talent Entrepreneur track centered on opportunity identification, resource mobilization, iterative value creation, and resilient adaptation. Drawing on strategic talent management scholarship, practice-based entrepreneurship education research, the European EntreComp framework, and work on multipotentiality, the paper argues that these two pathways are complementary rather than competing and that their parallel cultivation from adolescence onward addresses structural gaps in current provision. The framework is offered as a conceptual resource for program design, policy discussion, and further empirical investigation rather than as a finished blueprint.

title: Foreign Aid and Conflict: Evidence from the Chinese Belt and Road Initiative in Pakistan

detail.title: Foreign Aid and Conflict: Evidence from the Chinese Belt and Road Initiative in Pakistan
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of large-scale infrastructure aid on political violence, focusing on Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) projects in Pakistan. While the relationship between aid and armed conflict has been widely studied, the effects of Chinese aid to developing countries remain less understood. Using an event study design on district-level violent conflict data in Pakistan from 2010 to 2020, I find that violent incidents decreased in districts along the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) during the month of construction and shortly after. However, when examining patterns on an annual scale, there is increased volatility of violence in subsequent years, suggesting that the initial reduction in conflict is temporary. I explore the channels through which aid impacts conflict, showing that large-scale, government-supported transportation projects, carried out under military protection, initially reduce conflict but return to previous levels over time. These findings highlight significant short-term effects of infrastructure aid on local political violence but suggest no enduring decrease. This study also provides the first rigorous evidence on the social impacts of BRI projects, a growing but understudied form of foreign aid, specifically addressing impacts on local violence.

title: The Antagonistic Reflex: How Early Warnings Trigger Runaway Collapse in Competitive Societies

detail.title: The Antagonistic Reflex: How Early Warnings Trigger Runaway Collapse in Competitive Societies

declarations.ethicsApproval: This is a theoretical study based on mathematical modeling and computational simulation. It does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or personal data collection. Therefore, ethical approval is not applicable.

detail.abstract: This is a working paper. Comments welcome. Complex adaptive systems face a fundamental paradox: how can individually rational, self-preserving behaviours catalyse collective ruin? Prevailing theories, focused on internal stress or single-actor adaptation, cannot explain why, in multi-actor competition, a public early-warning signal-such as a decay in systemic resilience (W″<0)-can trigger a fatal, runaway race to the bottom. We introduce the theory of the Antagonistic Phase Transition, revealing its core mechanism: when the system's Conflict Multiplier (Γ)-quantifying how efficiently competitors transform a shared warning into antagonistic acts-exceeds a critical threshold, the system is inevitably drawn into a co-loss Runaway Attractor. Through formal theory, computational experiments, and historical validation-from Sumerian irrigation rivalry to contemporary global climate governance-this work lays a critical foundation for anticipating and governing the destructive dynamics of competitive complex systems.

detail.abstract: The mid-2026 semiconductor correction generated two competing interpretive narratives: a bubble-burst reading grounded in legacy DRAM cycle models, and an infrastructure-repricing reading grounded in bottleneck economics and AI CapEx fundamentals. This paper uses the divergence in analyst and retail commentary around Micron Technology as a case study in regime mis-specification - the application of a prior-cycle statistical model to a structurally transformed market environment. Building on the Class A/B/C taxonomy and Irreplaceability Index (IRI) developed in Huang (2026a), the Equipment-CapEx Divergence Ratio (ECDR) introduced in Huang (2026b), and the Business Model Score valuation framework of Huang (2025), this paper argues that the June 2026 correction is broadly consistent with a macrofinancial repricing event rather than AI infrastructure demand collapse. The paper's primary independent contribution is a three-dimensional analytical framework - value-chain positioning via IRI, cash-flow time structure via ECDR context, and gross margin as a real-time regime indicator - as a replicable instrument for distinguishing durable AI infrastructure premiums from speculative excess under market stress conditions.

title: Implementing Dual-Track Talent Development in Korean Secondary Education: Curriculum, Assessment, and Partnership Guidelines

detail.title: Implementing Dual-Track Talent Development in Korean Secondary Education: Curriculum, Assessment, and Partnership Guidelines
detail.abstract: Translating a dual-track framework for youth talent development into practice requires more than the addition of new program elements to an already crowded secondary education landscape. It requires a coherent architecture that aligns curriculum, assessment, partnership structures, and incentive systems around a shared developmental logic. This paper provides implementation guidance tailored to the Korean context. It outlines recommended sequencing from middle school through early post-secondary transition, presents illustrative curriculum modules for Talent Manager and Talent Entrepreneur pathways, proposes the K-TEC (Korea Talent and Entrepreneur Competency) index as a multi-dimensional assessment tool, and identifies design principles for school-platform-community partnerships. Special attention is given to equity considerations, teacher and facilitator development, and the alignment of incentives across the education-to-work ecosystem. The guidance is intended to support both new program design and the strategic adaptation of existing initiatives.

detail.abstract: Purpose: Business NPDI management models can often separate engineering specifications from user needs, causing misalignment in R&D decisions. This study proposes a consumer model that tests technical specifications against structured utility feedback to improve product development as well as product improvement outcomes, as applicable. Design/methodology/approach: The consumer model integrates functional performance metrics with utility feedback loops across concept, prototype, and pre-launch stages. It was validated through user test case study on 14 modern consumer laptop models powered by modern processor series microchips boasting exceptional battery life with [14] participating users targeting evaluating the battery life across ~ unmatched portability (in terms of work anywhere, fewer cables, and seamless mobile transitions); uninterrupted productivity (in terms of no data loss, focus & flow, and background freedom); and better overall system health (in terms of longer lifespan and thermal management) specifications. Findings: Results show tangible gaps between engineering scores and user-perceived functionality for 2 of 5 specs. Projects re-scoped using the consumer test model reduces development waste and improves alignment with market requirements. Originality/value: Unlike TRL or QFD, this product testing model places consumer feedback at the center of specification evaluation, giving technology business leaders a decision tool to assess if "the tech works" and "users care". Practical implications: R&D managers should apply the consumer model at stage-gate reviews. If user feedback <3/5 despite passing technical specs, the project should be re-scoped or terminated.

title: Human Development as Pure Awareness

detail.title: Human Development as Pure Awareness
detail.abstract: This thesis establishes that the most widely used frameworks for human development today (from the UN Sustainable Development Goals to the capability approaches of Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum, all based on philosophical foundations that relegate the inner life of human beings to a secondary level) can accommodate ‘pure awareness’ conceptually but not at the deeper paradigmatic level, where only Ken Wilber’s Integral Theory proves consistent with it. It examines how can ‘pure awareness’ be accommodated within these frameworks (a heightened, non-conceptual state of alertness to inner and outer reality, distinct from ordinary waking vigilance, which can be cultivated and is associated with cognitive, emotional, ethical and embodied benefits across neuroscientific, phenomenological and contemplative literature). Through analysis and critique, it tests the frameworks against exclusionary criteria (ontological compatibility and measurement methods) and subjects their internal requirements to meticulous scrutiny. The divergence is clear: pure awareness's non-materialist, non-rationalist and non-mechanistic ontology, anthropology and teleology are incompatible with the Aristotelian, Kantian and Lockean traditions that still shape modern Western thought and influence Sen's and Nussbaum's frameworks, while Wilber's Hegel-Sri Aurobindo inheritance aligns with them. The thesis therefore proposes a set of recommendations for the post-2030 development agenda: some measures that can be implemented immediately within the context of the current Western paradigm, and others that are applicable in the long term, with a view to integrating ‘pure awareness’ as a new and future paradigm for global development (SDG 0).

title: High-Growth Institutional Entrepreneurship in Africa: What AI Does and Does Not Tell You
affiliations: , Carnegie Mellon University Africa, Utrecht University - School of Economics, Carnegie Mellon University - College of Engineering and Carnegie Mellon University Africa

detail.title: High-Growth Institutional Entrepreneurship in Africa: What AI Does and Does Not Tell You
detail.abstract: High-growth ventures remain understudied in Africa due to persistent data scarcity. This paper analyses the co-evolution of high-growth ventures and entrepreneurial ecosystems across the African continent. We introduce a scalable methodology that leverages retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and large language models (LLMs) to extract founder-level insights from unstructured online data, producing AI-generated founder narratives. Recent advancements in LLMs and RAG enable the systematic synthesis of qualitative data into structured, comparable narratives at a scale and speed unattainable by traditional qualitative methods. To address the limitations of AI, we supplement these narratives with primary founder interviews, identifying blind spots and defining the boundaries of effective human-AI collaboration. Our analysis reveals that AI-generated narratives, may contain factual errors, framing errors and overlook private considerations that founders do not disclose publicly. We argue that AI-assisted qualitative research in data-sparse contexts still requires primary triangulation. Furthermore, we formalize the distinction between source-faithfulness and ground truth-faithfulness (from the founder's perspective) as a critical evaluative framework for AI-assisted research. Our findings also reveal that African unicorn founders not only scale high-growth ventures but also actively construct institutions: "high-growth institutional entrepreneurship".

title:
Strategic Advantage or Structural Trap? 
Competitiveness in Brazil's Ecological Transformation Plan

detail.title:
Strategic Advantage or Structural Trap? 
Competitiveness in Brazil's Ecological Transformation Plan

detail.abstract: Competitiveness has become a central rationale in green industrial policy, shaping not only the design of policy instruments but also the selection of sectors and economic activities prioritised for socio-ecological transformation. Yet competition unfolds within a structurally unequal world economy, where productive, technological, financial, and ecological asymmetries constrain the development strategies available to peripheral countries. Although the relationship between sustainability and competitiveness has received increasing attention, its implications for green industrial policy in the Global South remain underexplored. The paper examines how competitiveness is mobilised within Brazil’s Ecological Transformation Plan (ETP), an overarching framework that combines ecological transformation, industrial policy, and national development strategy. Drawing on theory-informed qualitative textual analysis, it investigates how competitive and strategic advantage arguments legitimise sectoral priorities, particularly across renewable energy, biofuels, green hydrogen, and fossil-fuel production. The case study identifies the emergence of an ambiguous role for competition in SET contexts in the periphery and semi-periphery, as it can both reinforce global economic subordination and contest dependent development patterns. On the one hand, competitiveness is mobilised as a guiding principle to guarantee national autonomy, industrial and technological densification, and strategic repositioning in emerging markets, dimensions that enable improving production patterns. On the other hand, it legitimises extractive expansion, primary-export specialisation, fossil-fuel continuity, and continued dependence on imported green technologies and transnational capital. The paper conceptualises these competing tendencies through the distinction between strategic advantage and structural trap. The arguments explored in the analysis further illustrate this contradiction.

title: Leadership Communication and Strategic Influence
affiliations: Bellevue University

detail.title: Leadership Communication and Strategic Influence
detail.abstract: Communication is the defining mechanism through which executive leadership transforms strategic vision into organizational action, strengthens stakeholder trust, and sustains institutional performance. This chapter examines leadership communication as a strategic capability that extends beyond the transmission of information to encompass influence, relationship building, organizational alignment, and cultural stewardship. Drawing upon contemporary leadership theory and executive communication research, the chapter explores how effective leaders communicate vision, develop executive presence, foster strategic listening, navigate organizational conflict, lead through crises, and influence stakeholders without relying solely on formal authority. Particular attention is given to the unique communication responsibilities of credit union executives, whose success depends upon balancing governance, member service, regulatory expectations, community engagement, and cooperative values. The discussion emphasizes that communication is not merely an interpersonal competency but a strategic leadership function that shapes organizational culture, enhances decision-making, strengthens employee engagement, and prepares future generations of leaders. Through an examination of executive communication during periods of stability, organizational transformation, and uncertainty, the chapter demonstrates that trust, credibility, and leadership effectiveness are established through consistency between words and actions. It further argues that executive communication serves as the primary vehicle for succession planning by transferring institutional knowledge, reinforcing organizational values, and developing leadership capacity across generations. Ultimately, this chapter positions communication as the practical expression of executive leadership. Leaders who communicate with authenticity, clarity, empathy, strategic intent, and ethical consistency create resilient organizations capable of adapting to change while preserving institutional purpose and stakeholder confidence. For cooperative financial institutions, effective communication not only advances organizational performance but also reinforces the trust, transparency, and member-centered principles that distinguish the credit union movement and ensure its long-term sustainability

title: From Project Proliferation to Portfolio Diversification: Implementation Capability, Carrying Capacity, and the Sectoral and Geographic Reach of CSR

detail.title: From Project Proliferation to Portfolio Diversification: Implementation Capability, Carrying Capacity, and the Sectoral and Geographic Reach of CSR
detail.abstract: Firms may undertake numerous CSR projects while concentrating resources within narrow sectors or proximate territories-proliferating symbolically without diversifying substantively. Prior research, relying on aggregate expenditure and project-count measures, cannot distinguish between the two, leaving the structural determinants and organizational limits of CSR diversification largely unexplored. This study introduces a distinction between project proliferation and genuine CSR portfolio diversification,  and examines whether Project Diversification translates into broader Sectoral Diversification, State-Level and Regional-Level Geographic Diversification, and Physical Geographic Dispersion-the last measured through Mean Pairwise Geographic Distance (MPGD), which captures actual spatial spread rather than administrative geographic categories. Drawing on Instrumental Stakeholder Theory, the Resource-Based View, and Organizational Complexity Theory, the study develops a demand-capability boundary framework and introduces organizational carrying capacity as the threshold beyond which coordination costs erode diversification benefits. Using panel data on 629 Indian firms (4,357 firm-year observations, 2015-2024) with firm-fixed effects, moderation, mediation, and nonlinear specifications, the findings show that Project Diversification significantly enhances all diversification dimensions, confirming that portfolio structure-not project count-determines CSR breadth and spatial reach. Implementation-Mode Diversification mediates the link between project diversity and physical geographic reach, operating as an organizational capability that enables territorial execution. Nonlinear analyses reveal an inverted U-shaped relationship between Project Diversification and Physical Geographic Dispersion, providing evidence of carrying capacity limits. The study contributes a theoretically grounded distinction between proliferation and diversification, identifies Implementation-Mode Diversification as a mediating capability for territorial reach, and validates organizational carrying capacity as a boundary condition governing CSR portfolio expansion.

title: Putting AI to the Test: Evidence from a Large-Scale RCT in Rural China
affiliations: Stanford University, University of Electronic Science and  Technology of China, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Peking University, Stanford University - Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, Stanford University - Freeman Spogli Institute of International Studies and Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology

detail.title: Putting AI to the Test: Evidence from a Large-Scale RCT in Rural China
detail.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has heightened interest in personalizing computer assisted learning (CAL) programs to tailor their instruction to individual students. Despite the proliferation of AI-driven CAL programs, evidence for their effectiveness remains limited. We present findings from a large-scale field experiment in rural China examining whether an AIdriven personalized CAL program improves student achievement. We randomly assign 8,647 students from 315 primary school classes to one of three treatment arms: (i) AI-CAL, (ii) nonpersonalized CAL (active control), and (iii) non-CAL educational activities (pure control). Results indicate that AI-CAL does not significantly improve achievement, with estimates precise enough to rule out non-trivial positive effects. This finding holds across the difficulty of assessment items and across the baseline achievement of students. The finding that R-CAL modestly benefits students in the middle ability tercile while AI-CAL shows no impact on students in any ability tercile suggests caution when projecting the promise of scaling adaptive AI-driven educational technologies in under-resourced settings.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has emerged as foundational national infrastructure, reshaping economic competitiveness, industrial transformation, public administration, and national security simultaneously. Among major economies, China has constructed one of the world's most systematically coordinated national AI ecosystems, an achievement that warrants serious study by any nation building its own AI strategy, regardless of political differences. Over nearly a decade, China has integrated industrial policy, scientific research, education reform, standards development, manufacturing transformation, consumer protection, and international standards diplomacy into a mutually reinforcing national framework. This paper provides a comparative policy analysis of China's AI governance architecture based on primary documents including the State Council AI+ Opinions (2025), the CAC Provisional Measures on Human-like Interactive AI Services (2026), the AI Industry Standardisation Guidelines (2024), the AI+ Manufacturing Opinions (2026), the Beijing Municipal AI+ Plan (2024-2025), and the school GenAI guide (2025). From this empirical base, the paper derives a ten-pillar framework for an Indian Sovereign AI Strategy grounded in India's constitutional values, democratic institutions, linguistic diversity, and existing Digital Public Infrastructure. The paper further argues that BRICS nations and the broader democratic Global South should coordinate on compute access, multilingual AI development, and AI governance norms rather than passively accepting frameworks designed by and for the US-EU technology axis. Specific institutional actors are identified throughout: MeitY, NITI Aayog, C-DAC, BIS, CERT-In, STQC, IITs, NASSCOM, sector ministries, and multilateral bodies. Future work will extend this analysis using computational knowledge graph methods to quantify coordination density across both ecosystems.

title: Correlated Pairwise Stability in Network Formation Games
affiliations: Nanjing University, Nanjing University, Nanjing University, Nanjing University and Independent

detail.title: Correlated Pairwise Stability in Network Formation Games
detail.abstract: We introduce correlated pairwise stability (CPS) for network formation games, which allows a mediator to coordinate agents' linking decisions through correlation plans. CPS generalizes pairwise stability and can strictly improve pairwise stable networks involving substantial randomization. We show that CPS admits an optimization-based characterization, transforming equilibrium computation in network formation games into a disjunctive program. This characterization leads to scalable algorithms for computing welfaremaximizing CPS distributions. Numerical experiments demonstrate substantial welfare gains from correlation and strong computational performance on large-scale instances.

title: Measuring Corporate Governance with Large Language Models
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - School of Law

detail.title: Measuring Corporate Governance with Large Language Models
detail.abstract:
Empirical corporate governance research depends on structured data extracted from legal text, a translation exercise that has traditionally required costly and difficult-to-scale human coding. Using the DECODEM benchmarks developed in companion work, this paper asks what role LLM-based extraction can play in governance data production: whether automated extraction routines perform on par with realistic human coding workflows and whether model-human disagreement can guide audits of human-coded data. The paper's main findings are based on a blind adjudication of observations on which human coding and the automated extraction routines disagree. 

The analysis supports three main findings. First, for many governance variables, LLM-based extraction performs at levels at least comparable to feasible human coding workflows, at less than two percent of the marginal cost of human coding. Second, different extraction routines often make only partially overlapping errors, creating value from ensemble rules that aggregate multiple routines. In the setting studied here, labels generated through ensemble rules agree with the adjudicated labels substantially more often than initial human labels did. Third, substantial variation across variables remains, so LLM-generated governance variables should not be used for downstream research without validation against hand-collected data. The results also carry an implication for settings where fully automated coding is not appropriate: because human and model errors also overlap only weakly, flagging observations on which any of six routines disagrees with the initial human label would surface more than ninety percent of observed human coding errors while requiring review of roughly seven percent of observations. Together, the results point towards a new model of data production in which human judgment defines and validates governance variables, while LLM-based extraction supplies scalable coding and targeted quality control.

title: Business Plan Feedback and New Venture Performance: A Randomized Field Experiment
affiliations: Universidad Adolfo Ibañez and UAI Business School

detail.title: Business Plan Feedback and New Venture Performance: A Randomized Field Experiment
detail.abstract:
Feedback on business plans is common in organizations that evaluate and accelerate new ventures. Yet little is known about what happens to the ventures that receive such feedback. It may improve ventures, or it may accelerate sorting and exit as startups become better informed of their prospects. This paper provides causal evidence on the effects of business plan feedback on venture outcomes,

using a randomized field experiment in Start-Up Chile, a global startup accelerator. Half of 88 admitted ventures were randomly assigned to receive written feedback from independent expert judges. Feedback increased the likelihood of securing external funding by 7 percentage points and helped raise more external funds. It also improved venture survival years after the program. Overall, the results are more consistent with a business improvement effect than with a pure screening mechanism.

title: Sniper Cohorts and Algorithmic Filter Rejections in Solana Memecoin Markets: Two-Window Replication of Lifecycle-Stage Population Separation

detail.title: Sniper Cohorts and Algorithmic Filter Rejections in Solana Memecoin Markets: Two-Window Replication of Lifecycle-Stage Population Separation
detail.abstract: Prior empirical work on Solana memecoin markets has often conflated pre-graduation (bonding-curve) and post-graduation (open-market) token populations. We test the assumption of population overlap between two independent algorithmic detection streams operating on the same underlying market: sniper-cohort detection and algorithmic filter rejection. Using two non-overlapping observation windows (June 11 to June 25, 2026, and June 29 to July 16, 2026) and two independent versions of the cohort-detection pipeline (v1 and v2), we compute set overlap between cohort-detected mints and rejection-stream mints in each window. Overlap remains under 1 percent of the cohort population in both windows despite substantial variation in cohort detector selectivity (v1: 20,162 mints; v2: 623 mints) and rejection-stream coverage (v1 window: 83 mints; v2 window: 1,743 mints). The lifecycle-stage separation is structural rather than statistical: cohort detection operates at the pump.fun bonding-curve stage, while rejection filtering operates on PumpSwap and other post-graduation venues. Cross-window cohort overlap is zero, confirming that different time windows detect distinct token populations. We systematically rule out four alternative explanations: time-window artifact, data-source mismatch, DEX venue asymmetry, and pipeline-version artifact. Implications for filter design, coordinated-behaviour research, and cross-stage token surveillance are discussed. All datasets are released under CC-BY-4.0 for replication.

detail.abstract: Regional economic integration in the East African Community commits partner states to eliminate internal tariffs and ensure the free movement of goods. In practice, however, states depend heavily on domestic taxation, and revenue authorities often adopt fiscal measures that conflict with regional law. This paper examines how courts have become central actors in resolving this tension. Through analysis of recent litigation before the East African Court of Justice and national courts, the study shows that judicial enforcement has translated treaty commitments into concrete economic rights for traders. The judgments reviewed reveal that courts are engaging in forms of judicial reasoning that closely resemble proportionality analysis, even though the doctrine is not expressly articulated when assessing whether national tax measures genuinely pursue public objectives or disguise protectionism. Building on this judicial trend, the paper proposes an explicit proportionality framework that would allow courts to balance fiscal autonomy with the integrity of the common market. The research suggests that proportionality provides a workable doctrinal bridge, offering states regulatory flexibility while protecting the legal certainty necessary for regional integration. The conclusion argues that formalising this standard may strengthen the EAC as a rule-based regional order, reducing reliance on political negotiation and reinforcing the binding nature of supranational law.

detail.abstract: Populism poses a persistent challenge to democratic governance by attacking the normative foundations of the administrative state. This essay diagnoses that challenge across four interconnected levels: populist assaults on bureaucratic institutions, the incentives confronting individual officials, pressures on street-level bureaucrats, and the deliberative deficits that populists exploit. It argues that democracy depends upon an administrative order grounded in the rule of law, accountability, transparency, impartiality, and efficiency. Competing responses including bureaucratic guardianship and expanded public participation offer important insights but risk either empowering unelected officials or displacing legitimately constituted democratic values. The essay advances authorized discretion as a middle path, contending that bureaucratic resilience requires legal, organizational, and professional structures that preserve administrative capacity while ensuring that official action remains firmly aligned with democratically authorized principles.

title: Faith That Thinks: Judaism's Case Against Blind Obedience and the Deadly Cost of Certainty
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business

detail.title: Faith That Thinks: Judaism's Case Against Blind Obedience and the Deadly Cost of Certainty
detail.abstract: The most dangerous words in any language may be "because I said so and I know." History's greatest atrocities were committed not by the ignorant, but by the obedient who surrendered their judgment to forces claiming a monopoly on truth. This paper argues that Judaism, properly understood, is a standing rebuke to that surrender. Drawing on the Hebrew Bible, the Talmud, and the Midrash, this paper demonstrates that Jewish tradition treats independent reasoning as a religious obligation and blind obedience as a spiritual failure. The evidence spans the entire tradition: Scripture deliberately preserves the moral flaws of its greatest heroes. Prophets vindicate those who argue with God. The sages of the Talmud overrule a Heavenly voice, institutionalize the intellectual adversary, and preserve minority opinions. Maimonides links the love of God to a disciplined mind. When this tradition is betrayed from within, as seen in the Shammaites' violence, the Bar Kochba catastrophe, and Maimonidean book burnings, enforced certainty produces destruction. The paper distills this argument into a diagnostic framework for distinguishing an authentic tradition from a counterfeit one, applicable to any religion or belief system. In an age when certainty is mistaken for strength and dissent for betrayal, this Jewish countermodel of sacred argument is urgently needed.

detail.abstract: When emotionally compelling human-interest stories and consequential but undramatic developments compete for attention, the former routinely dominate. Existing research explains how media select, emphasize, and frame content, but says less about why receivers fail to process consequential information that is fully available. This article specifies the throttling effect: a receiver-side process in which empathy-recruiting narratives automatically claim limited cognitive capacity and sustain that claim through narrative absorption and monitoring of unresolved outcomes. Because withdrawing attention from suffering is effortful and morally sanctioned, the displacement resists self-correction, and low-arousal information whose significance must be inferred remains unelaborated. The model is presented as an empathy-specific, temporally extended, politically indexed specification of the limited-capacity tradition. It advances five propositions and four hypotheses, including a novel inner-speech moderation prediction; reports a coverage-level analysis of the February 2026 expiration of the New START treaty, whose final days coincided with the identifiable-victim media storm surrounding the Guthrie kidnapping; and outlines a three-study program testing the mechanism at laboratory and short-term scales, with policy-window demobilization as its projected implication.

title: Neighbourhood-Level Alcohol-Related Social Disorder and Subjective Well-Being: A Multilevel Analysis
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Roorkee and Imperial College London

detail.title: Neighbourhood-Level Alcohol-Related Social Disorder and Subjective Well-Being: A Multilevel Analysis
detail.abstract: Alcohol-related neighbourhood disorder has been increasingly recognised as a social and public health concern, yet its relationship with subjective well-being remains underexplored particularly in India. This study examines the association between perceived neighbourhood alcohol-related disorder and subjective well-being and assesses whether neighbourhood trust moderates this relationship. Multilevel linear mixed-effects models are estimated to account for clustering at the neighbourhood level while controlling for demographic and socioeconomic characteristics. The findings indicate that perceived alcohol-related neighbourhood disorder is associated with lower levels of subjective well-being (β =-0.07, 95% CI:-0.14 to-0.00). Similarly neighbourhood trust is positively associated with subjective well-being only in neighbourhoods without alcohol-related disorder, suggesting that the benefits of trust may be diminished in disorderly environments. These findings highlight the importance of local social environments and the need to consider both structural and social dimensions of local neighbourhoods when evaluating policies aimed at improving community well-being.

title: Exploratory Network Analysis, Identifying factors, and a Transfer Destinations Predictor for College Football Transfer Portal
affiliations: and State University of New York (SUNY) - University at Buffalo

detail.title: Exploratory Network Analysis, Identifying factors, and a Transfer Destinations Predictor for College Football Transfer Portal
detail.abstract: The College Football Transfer Portal along with Name, Image, and Likeness is the collegiate version of the professional football transfer market. Since its creation in 2018, both student-athletes and colleges have utilized it. For example, student-athletes have utilized it to achieve their goals and chase their dreams. While College Football programs utilize it to improve their rosters in the race towards College Football Playoff. While this portal is widely used in College Football, there is limited research on this topic. This study aims at overcoming this by using exploratory data analysis (EDA) and network-based machine learning methods to explore the most recent data set from the network science perspective, along with providing a comprehensive overview of the transfer portal. Its goal is to show how EDA, network analysis, and machine learning can support the public, researchers and policymakers in sports management. Our findings show the transfer trends over time and a clear hierarchy in the portal among different levels of College Football. Meanwhile, we also explored the relationships between the quality of incoming transfers and associated factors (e.g., team performance and pro potential). Finally, we develop a model to predict College Football transfer destinations which demonstrates the potential of utilizing machine learning in sports analytics.

title: A Behavior-Based Targeting Framework for Equitable Allocation of Vaccination and Telehealth Resources: Evidence from COVID-19
affiliations: University of Missouri at Saint Louis, affiliation not provided to SSRN and George Mason University - Department of Health Administration and Policy

detail.title: A Behavior-Based Targeting Framework for Equitable Allocation of Vaccination and Telehealth Resources: Evidence from COVID-19
detail.abstract: Public agencies must allocate scarce outreach and infrastructure resources during health crises, yet lack data-driven tools to decide where to direct them. Using a nationally calibrated non-probability survey of U.S. adults from the COVID-19 pandemic (Climate Nexus Polling), we develop a two-stage analytics pipeline and translate it into a conceptual decision-support framework for equitable resource targeting. In the first stage, association rule mining describes how sociodemographic attributes and non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) co-occur with vaccination and telehealth adoption across geographic, regional, racial, and age subgroups. In the second stage, four supervised learning models (logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, and neural network) predict each behavior under four scenarios, and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis identifies which features drive each prediction. We then organize the results into a targeting framework that segments subgroups by their vaccination–telehealth co-occurrence pattern, classifies each segment by barrier type (structural access versus attitudinal trust), and prioritizes resources using a transparent score combining unmet need, predicted reachability, and an equity weight. A key decision-relevant finding is that telehealth adoption is predicted more accurately from specific proactive, exposure-reducing behaviors (AUC 0.77) than from models that add demographic variables (AUC 0.61), and SHAP analysis confirms these behaviors — not generic hygiene NPIs or demographics — carry the predictive signal, implying that targeting on observed behavior is both more accurate and more equitable than demographic profiling. The framework offers planners a structured, interpretable basis for allocating vaccination outreach and telehealth investment, and can be extended to a formal cost-constrained optimization when programmatic cost and capacity data are available.

title: The Intrinsic Advantage: Self-Determination, The Automation of Purpose, and the Case for Interest-Driven Education in a Post-Scarcity Economy

detail.title: The Intrinsic Advantage: Self-Determination, The Automation of Purpose, and the Case for Interest-Driven Education in a Post-Scarcity Economy
detail.abstract: The displacement debate around advanced automation has concentrated on employment and income. This paper argues that the more durable casualty is purpose. For a large share of the workforce, a sense of mattering has been wired to externally imposed structure and to productive output, and the removal of that structure produces a crisis that income replacement alone does not resolve. A subpopulation appears insulated from this crisis. Their motivation is intrinsic rather than extrinsic, organized around self-chosen interest rather than external demand, and that orientation does not depend on the labor economy for its survival. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, this paper characterizes the insulation as a function of motivational orientation rather than a fixed personality trait, which means it is in principle cultivable. Interest-driven and self-directed education is proposed as the mechanism by which the orientation could be scaled from a minority adaptation toward a general one, built before the economic transition arrives rather than improvised after it. The argument is deliberately bounded. It addresses the meaning dimension of post-scarcity, not the material dimension. The distribution of abundance is a separate problem on a separate front, and the cultivation of intrinsic motivation does not resolve it. What interest-driven education can do is determine which side of the coming purpose divide a person is prepared to stand on.

detail.title: Construction of an Evaluation Index System for Emergency Response Capacity for Adverse Events Following Immunisation in Secondary and Tertiary Hospitals across Guangxi
detail.abstract: This study aimed to develop an evaluation index system to assess hospitals’ emergency response capacity for Adverse Events Following Immunisation (AEFI) in secondary and tertiary facilities in Guangxi, China. The findings intend to inform the assessment and systematic improvement of AEFI emergency preparedness within regional hospitals, ultimately safeguarding the overall safety of vaccination programmes.A preliminary framework and draft indicators were established through comprehensive literature review. Two rounds of the Delphi method were implemented, with indicators screened and revised iteratively based on expert feedback and group discussion. The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) was subsequently adopted to refine the index system. A hierarchical structure and pairwise comparison matrices were constructed, and SPSS AU software was used to calculate the weight of each indicator, conduct hierarchical ranking and consistency tests. Combined weights for tertiary indicators were computed via multiplicative probability.The weights of primary indicators, ranked in descending order, were as follows: first-aid knowledge (0.11338), first-aid command and coordination (0.1129), first-aid personnel (0.11241), first-aid techniques and equipment (0.11241), emergency medicine reserves (0.11241), emergency response plans (0.11192), digitalised emergency management (0.10949), on-site emergency facilities (0.10803), and monitoring, early warning and reporting (0.10706). Consensus was achieved among participating experts after two rounds of consultation. The final system comprised 9 primary indicators, 25 secondary indicators and 55 tertiary indicators, totalling 89 individual items. Weighting analysis demonstrated that first-aid knowledge, command and coordination, staffing, alongside technical and equipment provision, represented the most critical dimensions of AEFI emergency capacity.

detail.abstract: We use a randomized controlled trial to examine how out-of-pocket costs affect contraceptive method choice, pregnancy, abortion, and childbirth among uninsured U.S. women. The study recruited women seeking care through Title X, a national family planning program subsidizing reproductive health services for low-income Americans– and randomized vouchers, making the full spectrum of contraception highly discounted or free. We find that subsidizing contraception has large and persistent effects on the choice of contraceptive method, resulting in significantly fewer pregnancies and abortions at 26 months. The effects on births are inconclusive.

title: Bad Neighbors: Bordering Institutions as Comparative (Dis)Advantage
affiliations: Universidad Adolfo Ibañez, Universidad Adolfo Ibanez and Universidad de Chile

detail.title: Bad Neighbors: Bordering Institutions as Comparative (Dis)Advantage
detail.abstract: Research has shown how domestic institutions shape comparative advantage. But for most countries in the world, contract-intensive supply chains tend to go beyond national borders. We show that-all else equal-countries with stronger neighboring institutions also export relatively more in contract-intensive industries. A one-standard-deviation increase in neighbors' institutions is associated with 0.14-0.25 standard deviations higher exports of contract-intensive goods. This is similar in magnitude to estimates for domestic institutions. Our results remain qualitatively robust to a wide range of potential concerns, including collinearity and endogeneity of institutions, as well as measurement of judicial quality and contract intensity. We also test the robustness of our results using U.S. imports, industrial production, imports of intermediate inputs, and domestic value added. Over two decades of data, the role of neighboring institutions remains stable. Taken together, our findings suggest a relevant role for regional value chains and cross-border contract enforcement.

title: Nonbank Subsidiaries and the Hidden Fragility of Internal Capital Markets Reallocation

detail.title: Nonbank Subsidiaries and the Hidden Fragility of Internal Capital Markets Reallocation

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Banks became safer after Basel III. Whether it made the broader organization safer is less clear. We document that bank subsidiaries accumulated capital, improved asset quality, and reduced risk. But holding companies built that capital largely by drawing on their nonbank affiliates. Did the reallocation reduce risk for the organization as a whole or merely move it to a less visible part of the firm? Our evidence points to the latter: the same internal capital markets that helped banks meet tighter requirements left nonbank affiliates with thinner buffers and riskier business models, and a greater capacity to transmit distress back to the organizations that own them.
