detail.abstract: Deciding where to live involves a complex balance between commuting and moving, as households must weigh housing affordability, transportation expenses, access to workplaces, and social ties. Traditional urban economic theories focus on the balance between housing expenses and commuting costs, while modern studies also consider housing affordability, transportation access, and utility maximization. However, few studies have combined these elements into a clear mathematical model that can be used for both policy analysis and household decision-making. This paper introduces an algebraic model for deciding whether to commute or move, expanding on traditional residential location theories by including direct housing and commuting expenses, income-related affordability limits, indirect social and service access costs, and location-based utility within a single utility-maximization framework. The model uses the common 30% housing affordability rule as a constraint, acknowledging that residential choices are also shaped by social networks, access to institutions, neighborhood ties, and quality-of-life factors. The decision rule derived from the model integrates direct financial costs with weighted social benefits and indirect access costs to assess when moving offers more overall utility than staying put and commuting. Unlike complex discrete-choice, nested-logit, or agentbased models, this framework offers a mathematically clear, understandable, and flexible decision model that can easily be expanded to include more household characteristics, transportation options, or policy factors. The model advances urban economics, migration studies, and housing affordability research by providing a practical analytical tool for assessing residential mobility decisions within financial and behavioral limits.

title: Extractive Stagnationary Diffusion: Compute Lock-In, the Productivity Paradox, and the Political Economy of AI
affiliations: University of Ontario Institute of Technology (UOIT)

detail.title: Extractive Stagnationary Diffusion: Compute Lock-In, the Productivity Paradox, and the Political Economy of AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no financial or other relations with the organizations that are the topic of this work

detail.abstract: The international build-out of artificial-intelligence infrastructure is among the largest concentrated capital commitments in history, yet the productivity gains meant to justify it remain difficult to detect. Commentary has organised around two expectations: vindication or financial bust. This article argues it may be neither. Adapting carbon lock-in theory from energy research to computing power, while drawing on organisational sociology and the political economy, we develop a theory of extractive compute lock-in driven by a selfreinforcing AI techno-institutional complex. Its signature is extractive stagnationary diffusion: AI spreading into ever more areas while economy-wide productivity stays flat or falls. The argument turns on a distinction the dominant framings miss: task-level efficiency need not aggregate to economy-level efficiency. Economics has noted this aggregation gap but explained it with neutral mechanisms that predict eventual resolution. In contrast, we supply a structural political-economy explanation for the gap's persistence: AI lock-in spurs inefficient resource allocation while value is captured by AI supply oligopolies, shielded from correction by political protection and information opacity. Ten measurable indicators developed here as a monitoring instrument are evaluated against early-2026 data. That evidence is consistent with extractive stagnationary diffusion, though definitive judgement awaits possible resolution due to information and depreciation lags.

title: The Hermite Latent: Natural Representations for Sums of Correlated Lognormals

detail.title: The Hermite Latent: Natural Representations for Sums of Correlated Lognormals
detail.abstract:
The moment-based Latent representation of correlated lognormal sums (Nagy, 2026h) relies on scaled moments 𝑐𝑘 = 𝑚𝑘/𝑘! that grow as 𝑒𝜎2max𝑘2/2. This super-exponential growth is the root cause of ill-conditioning in the Padé resummation step: the moment Toeplitz matrix has condition number ∼ 𝑒𝑂(𝑁2 𝑃), making the method impractical for 𝜎max > 0.8. The Smooth Latent Operator (Nagy, 2026j) mitigates this through regularization but cannot overcome the information-theoretic limit imposed by the growth rate.
We show that the moments are the Latent representation of the wrong generating function. The moments are Taylor coefficients of the moment generating function 𝑀(𝑧) = 𝐸[𝑒𝑧𝑆], which has zero convergence radius for lognormal sums. By contrast, the Hermite-chaos expansion — the Wiener polynomial chaos of 𝑆 in the underlying Gaussian variables — has coefficients that decay factorially. This is because the exponential function 𝑒𝑌 has a convergent Hermite series for 𝑌 ∼𝑁(𝜇,𝜎2), with coefficients 𝜎𝑘/𝑘!.
The resulting Hermite Latent Λ𝐻 = {𝑐𝐻 k} lives in ℓ2 (no Gaussian weight needed), the character istic function is recovered by a convergent inner product (no Padé resummation needed), and the CDF follows by Fourier-cosine inversion (Fang and Oosterlee, 2008). The entire chain is closed-form and well-conditioned for all 𝜎.
We formalize this as a grade-3 Latent: the optimal choice of representation basis. The grade 3 Latent for lognormal sums is the Hermite-chaos basis, selected by matching the basis to the problem’s generative structure (Gaussian → exponential → sum). The three-body problem’s use of Fourier coefficients (instead of Taylor coefficients) is the same grade-3 choice, matched to the problem’s periodic structure.

title: Economic Incentives in the Digital Art Market

detail.title: Economic Incentives in the Digital Art Market
detail.abstract: Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are assets on a blockchain that represent ownership of digital art and are traded on NFT marketplaces. The NFT market on the Ethereum blockchain was monopolistic until the end of 2022, when a new marketplace entered and captured a significant market share. This paper collects transactions from these marketplaces to study the effects of increased competition on the incumbent marketplace, artists, and investors. While competition had positive effects by reducing transaction costs, increasing trading volume and attracting new users, it decreased the profits of artists, discouraged them from creating new artwork, and thereby reduced the supply of new assets. I also study user migration, multi-homing behavior, and market segmentation, and compares the results with the predictions from theories of platform economics.

title: A Treatment of Spatial Omitted Variable Bias in Hedonic Pricing Based on Comparables
affiliations: University of Manchester - School of Environment and Development and École supérieure d'aménagement du territoire et de développement régional (ÉSAD)

detail.title: A Treatment of Spatial Omitted Variable Bias in Hedonic Pricing Based on Comparables
detail.abstract: Hedonic Pricing (HP) is a key method across many subfields of economics and the most extensively applied revealed preference method for non-market valuation of spatial and environmental amenities. However, empirical applications of HP suffer from spatial omitted variable bias (OVB), which can compromise estimation and interpretation of results. The common OVB treatment in HP relies on small-area fixed effects (FEs), which decrease the degrees of freedom for estimation. There are no widely accepted tests for selecting the size/number of areas as FEs that are sufficient for spatial OVB treatment. As an alternative, we propose a “differenced Comparables Sales Approach” (dCSA) that is based on sales occurring in close spatial proximity and tight time-window before a house sale. By differencing out common spatial observable and unobservable amenities between comparables, dCSA is evidenced to provide a solution for spatial OVB treatment without relying on FEs. An additional novel aspect of this approach is to formalise tests for robustly selecting the number of comparables that deliver spatial OVB treatment.

title: The Spectral Tensor Representation of Stochastic Processes

detail.title: The Spectral Tensor Representation of Stochastic Processes
detail.abstract: We prove that every Ito diffusion dX = mu(X) dt + sigma(X) dW admits a complete, finite-dimensional representation through its Fokker-Planck generator discretized in a cosine basis. The generator matrix M (N x N), computed via the integration-by-parts weak form with reflecting boundary conditions, is a sufficient statistic for the entire stochastic system: time-dependent distributions, all moments, option prices, Greeks, Value-at-Risk, Expected Shortfall, stationary distributions, spectral gaps, and autocorrelation functions are all computable from M alone, without Monte Carlo simulation. For time-homogeneous diffusions M is a matrix; for time-inhomogeneous processes it extends to a 3-tensor; for multi-dimensional systems, to higher-order tensors. A universal-representation bound guarantees that N = Theta(log(1/eps) / log rho) basis functions suffice regardless of dimension or the property being computed, where rho > 1 is the spectral decay rate of the process. We validate the completeness theorem by three-way comparison (spectral vs analytical vs Monte Carlo) on the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, demonstrate it on a nonlinear double-well potential with bimodal dynamics, and apply it to mean-reverting energy pricing, where a single 48 x 48 matrix produces the complete term structure of prices, risk measures, and Greeks.

title: Noise Valuation Through the House Price Shock of Airport Closure
affiliations: University of Manchester - School of Environment and Development and École supérieure d'aménagement du territoire et de développement régional (ÉSAD)

detail.title: Noise Valuation Through the House Price Shock of Airport Closure
detail.abstract: The expansion, opening or closure of an international airport is an ‘ideal’, but very rare, external shock for monetising aviation noise. There are only a hand-full of quasi-experimental studies on the valuation of aviation noise, and none that employ a complete airport closure to estimate marginal (per decibel) values of noise nuisance. This paper exploits the closure of a major international airport in Greece as a quasi-natural experiment on noise removal. We propose an extension of the difference-in-differences hedonic pricing to include a ‘differenced Comparable Sales’ approach inspired by a type of first-difference transformation widely employed in real estate industry. This approach treats omitted variable bias without requiring any small-area fixed-effects, which is especially useful in cases of sparse and challenging data. We contribute to the literature by estimating a marginal willingness to pay of 0.74% price increase per decibel of noise reduction from an airport closure quasi-natural experiment. The airport closure results on average to a 5.4% price increase, which provides a tentative estimate of over €1 billion benefits from aircraft noise removal capitalised in the local housing market. We also find that noise reductions are not valued linearly above 65 decibels.

title: The Spectral Lognormal Distribution, The Distribution of Portfolio Value

detail.title: The Spectral Lognormal Distribution, The Distribution of Portfolio Value
detail.abstract:
The CDF of a weighted sum of correlated lognormal random variables has lacked a tractable characterization since Fenton (1960). We show that eigenvalue conditioning of the correlation matrix, followed by Fourier-cosine inversion, yields an analytic, grid-free N-term spectral representation of that CDF: the Spectral Lognormal Distribution. The central point is not an elementary closed form, but a reusable analytic object whose dominant approximation error is controlled by residual correlation after conditioning rather than by the spectral inversion itself.

The total CDF error decomposes into six independent components. Within the target parameter regime studied in Section 5, five are saturated at double-precision noise; the remaining dominant term is the residual-correlation error induced by finite-K conditioning. This yields a smooth deterministic CDF and quantile map, addressing a constraint identified by Acerbi (2002, Section 5): non-parametric evaluation of the full class of spectral risk measures for weighted sums of correlated lognormals.

title: Yes, Karmic Theory Is Testable
affiliations: UCLA Anderson

detail.title: Yes, Karmic Theory Is Testable
detail.abstract: The doctrine of karma that good actions cause good outcomes and bad actions bad onesis widely held to be untestable. Anyone who prospers despite wickedness, or suers despite virtue, can be explained by an unobserved ledger of past deeds, possibly carried over from earlier lives. I show that this individual-level unfalsiability does not imply cross-sectional unfalsiability. If inherited karma is uncorrelated with current action, ordinary least squares recovers the causal eect of actions on outcomes even though the karmic stock is never observed. I derive the bias when that orthogonality fails, show that the doctrine's own psychology biases naive tests in karma's favor, and prove that purely trans-life karma is either undetectable or unidentied. I propose an instrumental-variables design with independently coded actions and outcomes, and show that the same instrument purges both the disposition confound and classical measurement error. A Monte Carlo delivers a sharp warning: where disposition persists, statistical power works against the naive testlarger samples drive its false-positive rate toward oneso credible inference requires exogenous variation, not merely big data.

title: Asymmetric and Multi-Horizon Transmission of Fiscal Dominance and Exchange Rate Pass-Through to Inflation: Evidence from Ghana
affiliations: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) and Transilvania University of Brasov

detail.title: Asymmetric and Multi-Horizon Transmission of Fiscal Dominance and Exchange Rate Pass-Through to Inflation: Evidence from Ghana

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available secondary macroeconomic data and does not involve human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract: This study examines fiscal dominance, exchange rate pass-through, and inflation dynamics in Ghana over 1970-2024 (N = 55), combining ARDL bounds testing, Quantile Regression (QR), Nonlinear ARDL (NARDL), and Wavelet Coherence Analysis on data rebuilt directly from World Bank World Development Indicators. DF-GLS, Phillips-Perron, and Zivot-Andrews structural-break unit root tests confirm a mixed I(0)/I(1) order with no I(2) series, supporting the ARDL bounds-testing framework. At the BIC-preferred lag specification, cointegration is confirmed for both the PDS model (F = 8.87, K = 6) and the SPD model (F = 9.08, K = 6). Contrary to the crowding-out hypothesis in the original specification, public debt servicing (PDS) is positively associated with inflation across most of the conditional distribution, peaking at the median (0.75, p < 0.05), consistent with a fiscal-dominance/monetisation channel and aligning with Aimola and Odhiambo's (2021) standard-ARDL finding for Ghana. The static quantile-regression coefficient on the exchange rate is negative, plausibly reflecting collinearity with global oil prices (VIF = 5.93) rather than a genuine reversal of pass-through; the dynamic NARDL specification instead shows a robust, theory-consistent short-run pass-through of currency depreciation to inflation (β = 1.11, p = 0.003), while asymmetry between depreciation and appreciation is only marginal in the long run (p = 0.085) and not significant in the short run (p = 0.363). A joint test of slope equality across quantiles does not reject homogeneity (χ² = 22.6, df = 24, p = 0.544), and a BDS test on the ARDL residuals finds no significant nonlinear dependence (p > 0.32); both results temper the case for the nonlinear and distributional extensions relative to a linear benchmark, without eliminating it. Wavelet coherence confirms exchange rate-inflation co-movement concentrated at the 2-4 year band, but roughly half of the 8-16 year band lies outside the cone of influence and is not interpreted. Together, the results support a more measured account of Ghana's inflation dynamics: real, short-run, theory-consistent exchange rate pass-through and a debt-servicing effect consistent with fiscal dominance, alongside more limited evidence for distributional heterogeneity and pass-through asymmetry than initially hypothesised.

title: Digital Learning Tools and Teachers’ Effectiveness in Curriculum Implementation: Evidence from Selected Secondary Schools in Nkozoa Municipality, Centre Region of Cameroon

detail.title: Digital Learning Tools and Teachers’ Effectiveness in Curriculum Implementation: Evidence from Selected Secondary Schools in Nkozoa Municipality, Centre Region of Cameroon
detail.abstract: The integration of digital learning tools into classroom instruction has transformed teaching practices and curriculum implementation across educational systems. In Cameroon, efforts to promote the use of information and communication technologies (ICT) in education have increased, yet many secondary schools continue to experience challenges in the effective use of digital tools for teaching. This study examined the impact of digital learning tools on teachers' effectiveness in curriculum implementation in selected secondary schools in Nkozoa Municipality, Centre Region of Cameroon. Specifically, the study identified the digital learning tools available to teachers, examined how these tools are used in curriculum implementation, assessed their influence on teachers' effectiveness, and investigated the challenges affecting their use. A descriptive survey research design was adopted. Data were collected from teachers using structured questionnaires and analysed using descriptive and inferential statistical techniques. The findings revealed that computers, laptops, projectors, smartphones, and educational software were the most commonly used digital learning tools. The study further established that the effective use of these tools enhanced lesson preparation, instructional delivery, learner engagement, classroom management, and assessment practices. However, inadequate ICT infrastructure, limited internet connectivity, insufficient professional training, irregular electricity supply, and inadequate institutional support constrained teachers' effective integration of digital technologies into classroom practice. The study concludes that digital learning tools significantly improve teachers' effectiveness in curriculum implementation when adequate resources, training, and institutional support are available. It recommends increased investment in ICT infrastructure, continuous professional development for teachers, improved internet access, and strengthened policy implementation to promote effective digital learning in secondary schools.

title: Beyond Nash: Threshold-Constrained Admissibility and Regime-Switching Equilibria in Endogenous-Feasibility Systems

detail.title: Beyond Nash: Threshold-Constrained Admissibility and Regime-Switching Equilibria in Endogenous-Feasibility Systems
detail.abstract: Classical game theory assumes strategy sets, feasibility constraints, and payoff mappings are exogenous and fixed. This assumption fails systematically in endogenous-feasibility systemsenvironments such as state collapse, financial contagion, and institutional decay where the admissible strategy set is itself a function of cumulative player behaviour, and individual rationality produces collective ruin because the game board itself evolves endogenously. This paper introduces Societrics Game Theory (SGT), a framework in which strategy admissibility is endogenously constrained by a threshold ratio Θt = WSIt/SOCt. When Θt > 1, strategies are excluded from the admissible set through domain collapse, not payoff penalty. We define two equilibrium concepts in a refinement hierarchy: the Structural-Strategic Equilibrium (SSE), satisfying structural feasibility (C1) and strategic stability (C2), and the Societrics Equilibrium (σe), an SSE additionally satisfying systemic sustainability (C3). Theorem 1 proves SSE existence via Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem. Theorem 1R proves σe existence as a sustainability refinement via the Intermediate Value Theorem on the path-connected SSE set, under an explicit Sustainability Traversal assumption (A6). The Separation Theorem establishes SE ⊊ SSE ⊊ NEen, where NEen is Nash in the enriched game. The Canonical SGT Model — the Continuous Effort Game — derives threshold crossing endogenously from a complementarity payoff structure, demonstrating that the low-effort Nash equilibrium is excluded from SSE by (C1) alone, without moral filtering or tie-breaking. The non-commutativity of recovery phases is a structural theorem, derivable directly from the SIP Trap definition without simulation, and is confirmed computationally across three parameter sets with formal robustness proof (Proposition 4). The framework is positioned against GNE, stochastic games, global games, viability theory, and state constrained differential games. Fragile-state dynamics and financial-system cascades are developed as two application domains of a common endogenous-feasibility architecture, with Nigeria 2015–2024 as the primary worked case and the 2008 Lehman cascade as the secondary instance. The residual contribution is stated precisely as architectural integration of (F1)–(F4) within a unified discrete-time noncooperative equilibrium concept. Empirical validation against Afrobarometer Round 10 probability-sampled data for Nigeria (n = 1,600) produces a weighted Fundamentals-layer reading (WSI strain 4.56 on the Moderacy 1–7 scale; 95% confidence interval [4.50, 4.61]) that converges qualitatively with the stylised MVD Θ trajectory (Θ = 1.20, Crisis-moderating) for the same 2024 state, establishing measurement consistency across institutional-index and perception-survey pathways.

title: Stabilization without Inclusive Development: Neoliberalism, Economic Liberalization, Poverty, and Inequality in Bolivia

detail.title: Stabilization without Inclusive Development: Neoliberalism, Economic Liberalization, Poverty, and Inequality in Bolivia
detail.abstract: This article reconstructs the economic and social history of Bolivian neoliberalism and evaluates whether economic liberalization reduced or increased poverty and inequality in Bolivia. The historical argument is that the Bolivian neoliberal cycle was not a single event but a layered sequence: hyperinflation and emergency stabilization, the 1985 New Economic Policy, labor displacement and mining restructuring, second-generation reform in the 1990s, capitalization, decentralized state restructuring, commodity dependence, and the social conflicts that culminated in the collapse of the party system. The empirical contribution is to integrate macroeconomic indicators, economic-freedom indices, poverty and inequality series, IMF and financial-reform data, commodity and disaster controls, Bolivian export aggregates, and harmonized historical survey indicators. The preferred design is a heterogeneous instrumental-variables model that instruments domestic liberalization with lagged regional leave-one-out policy diffusion and allows Bolivia to differ from the Latin American average. The central estimate is that a 10-point increase in the Heritage economic-freedom score is associated, for Bolivia, with approximately +4.46 percentage points of poverty at the USD 4.20/day line, +3.61 percentage points at the USD 3/day line, +7.40 percentage points at the USD 8.30/day line, and +3.91 Gini points. These results remain socially regressive in sign after adding export-structure controls to the poverty specifications, although the causal interpretation remains conditional on the exclusion restriction. The article therefore advances a qualified conclusion: Bolivian neoliberalism stabilized hyperinflation, but the historically specific liberalization package appears to have increased social vulnerability and inequality rather than producing inclusive development.

title: Cognitive Costs in Consumer Search
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Illinois at Chicago - College of Business Administration, New York University (NYU) and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Cognitive Costs in Consumer Search

declarations.ethicsApproval: Experiment ethics were approved by the University of Chicago IRB: IRB24-1509. All participants consented prior to participation.

detail.abstract: Online shopping and home delivery have minimized the physical and financial costs consumers experience while shopping. Nevertheless, consumers behave as if searching for products is costly, examining fewer products than they should if search were free. Existing models of consumer search incorporate `search costs', but it is unclear what aspects of search are experienced as costly by the consumer and whether cognitive costs (such as the costs of attention and memory) are part of the equation. Across three multi-stage incentivized lab experiments (N = 549) we assess how changes in the complexity of the search environment affect how consumers search for products in an online shopping task. We manipulate two aspects of the shopping task: the number of relevant attributes of each product (placing greater demands on attention), and whether information about searched products needs to be remembered (or remains on screen). We use conjoint choice tasks to estimate participants' true preferences, in addition to a task where explicit preferences and rules (which govern utility and payoffs) are provided. In our experiments we find manipulating complexity, via the number of relevant attributes and the memory demands of the task, impacts search: consumers search fewer unique products as complexity rises. We fit the behavioral data to the Weitzman sequential search model to quantify how these behavioral changes map onto the `search cost' parameter in such models.

title: Enhancing Economic Growth through Public Investment in Ethiopia: Long-Run Evidence and Policy Insights
affiliations: Department of Economics, East West University

detail.title: Enhancing Economic Growth through Public Investment in Ethiopia: Long-Run Evidence and Policy Insights
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of public investment on economic growth in Ethiopia, focusing on both long-run dynamics and short-run adjustments while accounting for key macroeconomic determinants. The study adopts a quantitative time-series approach using annual data from 1983 to 2024. An autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) model is employed to estimate long-run and short-run relationships. Unit root and bounds tests are conducted to establish stationarity and cointegration, followed by an error correction model (ECM). Diagnostic and stability tests ensure model robustness, and Granger causality analysis examines directional relationships. The results confirm a long-run equilibrium relationship among the variables. Public investment has a positive and significant long-run effect on economic growth, while it remains insignificant in the short run, indicating delayed impact. Labour force and gross capital formation significantly promote growth, whereas inflation, interest rates, and external debt service exert negative effects. Foreign aid shows a weak negative influence, suggesting inefficiencies in its utilization. The error correction term indicates a moderate speed of adjustment toward equilibrium. Causality results reveal a unidirectional relationship from public investment to economic growth. The study contributes by constructing a composite index of public investment and providing updated empirical evidence for Ethiopia, offering policy-relevant insights on enhancing the efficiency of public investment for sustainable growth.

title: Selling Control Without a Backstop: AI Governance Frameworks, the Uninsurability of Artificial Intelligence, and the Vendor in the Civil Liability Chain

detail.title: Selling Control Without a Backstop: AI Governance Frameworks, the Uninsurability of Artificial Intelligence, and the Vendor in the Civil Liability Chain
detail.abstract: A market has formed around the sale of artificial intelligence governance. Vendors offer frameworks, audits, maturity models, and certifications that promise an enterprise it can deploy AI responsibly and demonstrate that it did. This article argues that the governance market is selling a form of control over a risk that the insurance market has just declared it will not underwrite, and that the gap between those two facts has a legal shape. As of late 2025 and into 2026, major carriers filed to exclude artificial intelligence liabilities from standard corporate policies, and the standard form publisher for United States commercial general liability released endorsements that carve generative AI out of the baseline coverage that most businesses carry. Regulatory enforcement, where it reaches at all, terminates at the deployer. The result is a civil loss-allocation vacuum: when a deployed system causes a third party harm, the loss lands on the deployer's balance sheet with no insurer behind it and no statute reallocating it. Into that vacuum the governance vendor has inserted itself, not by accident but through its own marketing, holding out its framework as the thing that makes deployment safe and defensible. This article develops three claims. First, control over a contemporary AI system cannot honestly be sold, because the system is stochastic in output, open in action space, and indifferent as to substrate, so no framework can promise the determinacy the sale implies. Second, when a framework is marketed as the assurance on which a deployer reasonably relied, the vendor has volunteered for a place in the civil liability chain that regulation does not give it and that an indemnity clause cannot fully cure. Third, the governance genre asks four familiar questions and never asks the fifth, which is whether the buyer and the people the buyer's system will affect have been told, in plain terms, that the risk is uninsured. The article closes on that fifth question.

title: Inelastic Integration: The Price of Market Access
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU), City University of Hong Kong (CityU),  and

detail.title: Inelastic Integration: The Price of Market Access
detail.abstract: Standard theory predicts that market integration compresses valuation differences through risk-sharing. We show that this prediction reverses when entering investors are price-inelastic. China's Stock Connect simultaneously granted foreign investors access to A-shares and Mainland investors access to Hong Kong H-shares for the same dual-listed firms Instead of converging, the AH premium widened. Estimating a demand system from investor-level holdings, we find that Northbound investors are substantially less elastic than Southbound investors, with median elasticities of roughly 0.2 and 0.6, consistent with A-shares offering greater unspanned diversification value to global portfolios. This elasticity asymmetry correctly predicts the direction of the premium change, suggesting that demand elasticities of entering investors shape integration's price effects.

title: The Accommodation Axis: Disability Discrimination, Algorithmic Opacity, and the Deployers That Anti-Discrimination Scholarship Overlooks

detail.title: The Accommodation Axis: Disability Discrimination, Algorithmic Opacity, and the Deployers That Anti-Discrimination Scholarship Overlooks
detail.abstract: A growing body of scholarship warns that the economic and training logic of modern artificial intelligence drives automated decision systems to target the vulnerable, conceal discrimination, and resist detection, defeating both the disparate treatment and disparate impact theories on which anti-discrimination enforcement has relied. That work is largely correct, but it runs on a single axis: intent versus impact. Both engines it analyzes are Title VII engines, and the analysis treats disability as one more protected class to be fed through the same machinery. This Article argues that disability discrimination law occupies a different axis entirely. The Rehabilitation Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act add an affirmative-duty engine, reasonable accommodation and meaningful access, that is structurally immune to the three capabilities said to make algorithmic discrimination undetectable. A failure-to-accommodate claim requires no proof of intent, so a system that hides its reasons defeats nothing; it requires no comparator, so a system that eliminates comparators defeats nothing; and it shifts the burden of justification to the deployer, so a system that manufactures a plausible pretext shifts nothing. The Article then turns the opacity argument around. The unexplainable model that shields a Title VII defendant indicts a disability defendant, because a selection device the deployer cannot validate fails the business-necessity requirement as a matter of law, and a leading developer's own research forecloses curing that failure through the model's stated reasons. Finally, the Article identifies the deployers this literature has overlooked, universities and public agencies, which are paradigmatic recipients of federal financial assistance and are now routing admissions, accommodation, and eligibility decisions through systems no human can explain. The doctrine to reach them already exists. No new statute is required.

title: Do Focal Entities Coordinate their Industries? An Empirical Falsification Study

detail.title: Do Focal Entities Coordinate their Industries? An Empirical Falsification Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: The author declares no conflicts of interest. AI tools (Claude, Anthropic) were used for editing assistance and feedback during the drafting process. All substantive intellectual content, theoretical development, and argumentation are the author's own.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: A companion paper to Price as a Construct of Time advances two empirically load-bearing claims: that "boundary entities" exert asymmetric synchronization spillovers on other firms in their industry, and that such entities occupy an intermediate position in tangible/intangible balance-sheet space rather than the pure-intangible corner. We subject both claims to a falsification standard: an effect counts only if it survives the benchmarks a sophisticated desk already owns. These refer to large-cap-leads-small-cap lead-lag, sector beta, a common "AI factor," liquidity, and documented economic-link return predictability. Using NVIDIA, Tesla and Meta as candidate boundary entities and the January 27, 2025 DeepSeek episode together with the April 2025 H20 export-control charge as the two cleanest natural experiments, we find: (i) focal→ecosystem repricing is real and directionally asymmetric, but its channels are individually identical to pre-existing mechanical anomalies, and it does not separate from size plus a common AI factor in a single correlated episode; (ii) all three candidate entities are genuinely intermediate in composition. Each retains a non-trivial tangible anchor unlike a pure software firm yet a focality composite is so collinear with log market capitalization and AI-membership that "boundary status" is, on present evidence, largely size relabeled. The headline result is negative, and we report it as the finding: the boundary construct is descriptively valid and analytically useful for risk, but is not a standalone source of alpha. We distinguish a falsifiable residual, a shock taxonomy separating narrative-reabsorbable from tangible-constraint events, that does survive.

title: No More Tiers: Rebuilding Auditability in Partnership Taxation
affiliations: Loyola Law School Los Angeles

detail.title: No More Tiers: Rebuilding Auditability in Partnership Taxation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: No one

detail.abstract:
Over the past two decades, large partnerships have proliferated and grown dramatically more complex, with ownership chains commonly extending ten, twenty, or more tiers. As the Article documents, this complexity has rendered Subchapter K effectively unauditable: tracing allocations, basis, and liability shares across multiple interdependent entities requires simultaneous examination of every partnership above and below the audit target, often across jurisdictions and tax years. GAO and TIGTA reports confirm that audit rates for large partnerships have fallen near zero, that most audits yield no adjustments, and that the IRS lacks the capacity to enforce even the most basic rules of partnership taxation. The Article demonstrates that tiering creates exponential audit‑scope expansion, severe timing mismatches under § 706, and cascading basis effects under § 752, making meaningful enforcement practically impossible.

The Article proposes a categorical structural solution: prohibit entities from qualifying for partnership treatment if any of their interests are owned, directly or indirectly through disregarded entities, by partnerships. In short: no more tiers. This rule would restore the factual predicates assumed by Subchapter K’s drafters, reactivate the centralized audit regime enacted in 2015, and generate substantial revenue through both direct enforcement and deterrence. The Article concludes that a prohibition on partnership‑on‑partnership ownership can rebuild auditability, restore legal determinacy, and prevent the partnership tax system from devolving into what the Article describes as a “voluntary donation system.”

title: Margin Illusion in Commodity-based Industries: Evidence from Polyethylene Markets

detail.title: Margin Illusion in Commodity-based Industries: Evidence from Polyethylene Markets
detail.abstract:
Reported margins in commodity industries often rise sharply during price upcycles, and are
frequently interpreted as evidence of improved structural profitability. This paper argues
that such interpretations can be misleading. In practice, reported margins may diverge
significantly from underlying economic profitability due to a combination of inventory
accounting effects, lagged cost pass-through, and global arbitrage dynamics.
Using polyethylene (PE) markets as an empirical setting, this study introduces the concept
of Margin Illusion—a systematic overstatement of profitability that emerges when rising
prices are measured against historically lagged costs. Building on Cost of Supply Analysis
(COSA), the paper develops a simple framework to distinguish between accounting
margins and economically meaningful returns under dynamic pricing conditions.
Drawing on a panel dataset of regional PE prices, feedstock costs, and export flows, the
analysis shows that periods of margin expansion are followed by supply responses and
margin normalization. This pattern suggests that what appears to be sustained profitability
is often temporary and self-correcting.
The paper contributes both conceptually and practically by proposing a Margin Illusion
Index (MII) to quantify the divergence between reported and economic margins, offering a
more reliable lens for evaluating performance, investment decisions, and market cycles in
commodity-based industries.

title: The Role of External Sector Dynamics in Food Production in Ethiopia: Evidence from Foreign Aid, FDI, Trade Openness, and Remittances
affiliations: Department of Economics, East West University

detail.title: The Role of External Sector Dynamics in Food Production in Ethiopia: Evidence from Foreign Aid, FDI, Trade Openness, and Remittances
detail.abstract: This paper examines the macro-econometric relationship between external sector dynamics and agricultural food production in Ethiopia. Utilizing a comprehensive structural framework, this study investigates the long-run and short-run impacts of official development assistance (ODA), foreign direct investment (FDI), trade openness, and personal remittances on the Ethiopian Food Production Index. Using annual time-series data spanning from 1990 to 2024 and employing a Vector Error Correction Model (VECM), the framework captures complex cointegrating properties and systemic feedback mechanisms. The empirical findings indicate that trade openness and macroeconomic remittances exert statistically significant positive effects on food production in the long run. Foreign direct investment demonstrates a positive but modest long-run contribution, while official development assistance exhibits a minor negative impact, highlighting potential aid-dependency distortions and structural misallocation. The error correction term is found to be-0.65, implying a robust and rapid adjustment speed toward long-run equilibrium. These insights indicate that Ethiopia can structurally optimize its food production systems by deepening regional and global trade integration, creating targeted agroindustrial investment frameworks, and formalizing diaspora resource channels.

title: Smallholder Farmers' Integration into Edible Oilseeds Value Chains: A Multivariate Probit Analysis of Market Outlets Choice in Hararghe Zones, Ethiopia

detail.title: Smallholder Farmers' Integration into Edible Oilseeds Value Chains: A Multivariate Probit Analysis of Market Outlets Choice in Hararghe Zones, Ethiopia
detail.abstract: This study aims to examine determinants market outlet choices among smallholder producing edible oilseeds crops in Hararghe, Ethiopia, utilizing multivariate probit model(N=383). The results indicates significant interrelated and interdependent markets outlets. Access to market information's and extension services shifts significantly smallholder from collectors and retailors towards wholesale and cooperative market outlets. The larger volumes, male-headed household and access to credit services significantly increase the probability to sell to wholesales, while farmers at distance from the main markets outlets heavily rely on cooperative market outlets to reduce transactions. Smallholder producing groundnuts highly commercialized as compared to soybean producers across wholesales, retailors, and cooperative market outlets. It is vital to focus on the orientation of the extension services to market outlets choices in addition to assisting smallholder farmers to improve their agricultural productivity. Providing digitalized platforms reduce market information asymmetry. It is also quite essential to provide access to agricultural credit to improve smallholder farmers' capacity to invest in agricultural technologies to increase surplus produces for the market. To accelerate smallholder integration into high-value market chains, policy interventions must prioritize strengthening targeted extension, market information systems, and credit access.

title: Modelling the Transition to High-Efficiency Industrial Motor Systems in India: A System Dynamics Perspective
affiliations: Tyche Investments - Climate Consulting Group

detail.title: Modelling the Transition to High-Efficiency Industrial Motor Systems in India: A System Dynamics Perspective
detail.abstract: Industrial electric motor-driven systems (EMDS) consume a large share of electricity and contribute significantly to greenhouse gas emissions in India. Improving the energy efficiency of these systems is therefore essential for reducing energy use, lowering operating costs, and supporting industrial decarbonization. However, existing studies often focus on technical or economic aspects separately and do not capture the dynamic interactions among technology adoption, digitalization, climate finance, and circular economy practices. This study develops an integrated System Dynamics (SD) model to evaluate the long-term energy efficiency and lifecycle sustainability of industrial EMDS in India. The research follows five stages: model development, calibration, mathematical formulation, simulation, and validation. The model is implemented in a dynamic Microsoft Excel-based simulation platform and evaluates six policy scenarios, including Business-as-Usual, energy efficiency, climate finance, digitalization, circular economy, and an integrated policy scenario. The results show that increasing the retrofit rate has the greatest impact on reducing electricity consumption and carbon emissions. Digitalization improves equipment reliability and reduces lifecycle costs, while climate finance accelerates the adoption of energyefficient motor technologies. Among all scenarios, the integrated policy approach delivers the best overall performance by achieving the largest reductions in energy use and emissions, with 50% reduction in electricity consumption and carbon emissions by 2050. The proposed framework provides a practical decision-support tool for policymakers, industries, and financial institutions to design effective energy efficiency strategies and support India's transition toward sustainable and low-carbon industrial development.

title: Beyond Black Scholes--Intrinsic Geometry and Endogenous Drift in Modern Options Pricing: A Unified Field Approach
affiliations: University of Toledo

detail.title: Beyond Black Scholes--Intrinsic Geometry and Endogenous Drift in Modern Options Pricing: A Unified Field Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No financial interests.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a unified conceptual reconciliation between the intrinsic information-geometric framework of Dean (2026) and the extrinsic variable-drift Fokker-Planck framework of the Moore Model (Moore's R). For over fifty years, the quantitative finance industry has relied on ad-hoc practitioner patches-manually smoothing a fictional "volatility smile" over a flat Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) baseline-to mask systemic mispricing in out-of-the-money (OTM) and long-dated options. Dean (2026) isolates the exact boundary condition under which BSM operates as a flat sub-manifold slice, treating the volatility smile as an intrinsic geometric penalty for ignoring the broader curved Gaussian Fisher information manifold. Conversely, the Moore Model implements an extrinsic physical architecture, proving that this apparent topological curvature is the rational byproduct of a strike-specific, dynamic Fokker-Planck drift bound by endogenous discounted cash flow (DCF) replication limits. To evaluate these paradigms against traditional methods, a localized 500-step numerical tracking simulation was executed in a high-volatility regime for deep OTM LEAP options. The results reveal that while the Practitioner model suffers from severe unhedged equity bias (accruing $4.12 of tracking slip per contract), Dean's post-hoc tensor corrections significantly smooth the replication boundary ($0.85 of slip). The Moore Model demonstrates the highest tracking stability ($0.18 of slip) by allowing the asset to adjust natively through its endogenous discount rate. While these simulation results are explicitly acknowledged as limited and localized, they suggest a mathematically rigorous alternative to empirical smoothing, offering a framework grounded in absolute field continuity and rational market mechanics.

detail.title: Timing Selection and Counterfactual Reconstruction in Synthetic Control Designs: A Placebo-in-Time Decomposition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, animals, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper separates benchmark reconstruction error from benchmark-relative timing reweighting in synthetic-control designs with candidate treatment dates. Given a benchmark timing distribution, the mean untreated reconstruction error under actual timing equals the benchmark mean error plus a covariance term that measures how actual timing reweights candidate-date errors. Both components are benchmark-relative: changing the benchmark reallocates the fixed actual-timing error between them. The decomposition is therefore an accounting device, not a unique partition into primitive causes. We also adapt weighted randomization inference to placebo-in-time diagnostics: holding uncontaminated placebo dates fixed, unit-label permutations yield date-specific and max-over-dates omnibus tests, whereas permutation over event dates is exact only under an explicit as-if-random timing law. We state conditions under which placebo-in-time comparisons admit these interpretations and develop a joint sensitivity analysis for single-event applications with uncertainty about the actual timing law, the benchmark timing law, and unobserved post-event errors. A synthetic-control simulation shows that signalbased timing can generate non-negligible bias-about 12 percent of the treatment effect in our baseline calibration-even when pre-treatment fit is strong.

detail.title: Camel Rating Model: An Effective Parameter for Predicting Bank Distress in Nigeria

keywords: Multiple Discriminant Analysis and Multiple Regression Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: Calabar Journal of Finance and Banking, Volume 2, Issue 1. Pp. 1-15

detail.abstract: The paper tested the efficacy of the use of the CAMEL Rating Model to predict bank distress in Nigeria during the period 2009-2018. Data for the study were collated from published annual reports and accounts of a sample of 10 deposit money banks. The study employed the techniques of Multiple Discriminant (MDA) and Multiple Regression Analyses on the data. The MDA results revealed that 5 out of the 10 sampled banks obtained Z-score values within the region of distress. Using the CAMEL Rating Model, banks were categorized as distressed and non-distressed banks. The result further revealed that all distressed banks fell under the marginal category, indicating symptoms of financial deterioration in their asset quality ratios. Again, the CAMEL Rating values were regressed against the Z-score values to provide further impetus to distress prediction. The regressed estimates showed the quality of assets, efficiency of management and the state of liquidity impact significantly on bank distress. On the other hand, capital adequacy and earning strength had an insignificant effect on bank distress. Therefore, CAMEL variables were effective in predicting bank distress in Nigeria in the period of study. Based on these results, it was recommended, among other things that the Central Bank of Nigeria should ensure strict compliance with prudential guidelines by banks in granting loans and advances to customers to enhance liquidity strength, asset quality, earning strength and management efficiency among deposit money banks, hence a sound and safe banking industry in Nigeria.

title: Animal Magnetism: A Bull-bear Polarisation Model of Endogenous Market Volatility
affiliations: Averisera Ltd

detail.title: Animal Magnetism: A Bull-bear Polarisation Model of Endogenous Market Volatility
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces animal magnetism: a structural model of market volatility inspired by two classical ideas, Keynes's animal spirits and Anderson's principle that "more is different". Keynes gives the economic intuition: markets are moved not only by calculation, but also by confidence, fear, positioning, liquidity pressure, and the urge to act under uncertainty. Anderson gives the physical intuition: when many simple components interact, collective behaviour can emerge that is not visible at the level of the individual component.

We model unresolved bullish and bearish market pressures as interacting binary variables in an Ising-type hidden layer. Their aggregate state is the hidden bull--bear polarisation. When these pressures weakly interact, the market remains balanced and well anchored. When interaction strengthens, the market can become crowded, reactive, and fragile. Near the critical threshold, small disturbances can be amplified because the hidden state has lost resistance.

Coupling this hidden pressure layer to prices gives a structural stochastic-volatility model in which volatility clustering, fat-tailed returns, regime changes, and crash-like transitions arise as different visible consequences of the same hidden interaction structure. An empirical illustration from 2005--2026 constructs an animal-magnetism fragility score from visible stress, one-sided pressure, hidden activity, shock amplification, and loss of effective diversity. High-fragility days are followed by substantially higher realised variance, larger drawdown stress, and stronger common-mode concentration.

The result is a distinction between ordinary volatility and structural fragility. Market risk depends not only on how much prices are moving, but on the hidden collective state in which the next shock arrives.

title: Optimal Leverage Sequencing in Leveraged Dollar Cost Averaging: Theory and Multi-asset Evidence

detail.title: Optimal Leverage Sequencing in Leveraged Dollar Cost Averaging: Theory and Multi-asset Evidence
detail.abstract:
This paper proves that among all leverage sequences with fixed total leverage
applied to a Dollar Cost Averaging (DCA) entry schedule, the non-decreasing
(increasing) sequence uniquely minimises the weighted average entry price
whenever entry prices are non-increasing. The proof uses the rearrangement
inequality and establishes a formally optimal allocation rule for practitioners
who combine DCA with leverage in derivatives markets: assign lower leverage
to earlier, higher-priced entries and higher leverage to later, lower-priced entries.
We formalise this result within a parametric DCA framework whose entry
drawdown schedule is:
Dk = f + k M − f
n , k = 0, 1, . . . , n,
where f is the initial trigger drawdown, M is a user-defined maximum drawdown
threshold, and n is the number of DCA intervals. Analytical comparison
across increasing, decreasing, and uniform leverage sequences—all with identical
average leverage 6×—demonstrates that the increasing sequence achieves the
lowest weighted average entry (86.7 vs. 90.0 and 93.3), the largest reference-to-
entry span (13.3% vs. 10.0% and 6.7%), and the highest return at every tested
recovery threshold. We further clarify the distinction between the reference-to-
entry span—a portfolio-level measure of how far below the reference high the
average cost basis sits—and the per-position liquidation price, which is a separate
exchange-determined quantity. Empirical validation on 9.5 million one-minute
bars across five markets—XAUUSD Gold, Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH),S&P 500 ETF (SPY), and NASDAQ 100 ETF (QQQ)—confirms that the
increasing leverage sequence achieves the highest risk-adjusted return (Sharpe
ratio) and the fewest liquidation events in every market without exception. On
QQQ the increasing sequence records zero liquidation events over five years
versus 14 for the decreasing sequence. A five-market replication yields an
approximate p-value of 0.004 for the Sharpe-ranking result. This work does not
claim that the strategy is profitable in absolute terms; the contribution is a
proof of comparative optimality and empirical confirmation of the theoretical
ordering across independent markets and asset classes.

title: Decarbonising India's Urban Thermal Energy Systems: An Hybrid Model Approach for Policy and Investment Planning
affiliations: Tyche Investments - Climate Consulting Group

detail.title: Decarbonising India's Urban Thermal Energy Systems: An Hybrid Model Approach for Policy and Investment Planning
detail.abstract:
India's cities are getting hotter, and the demand for cooling in homes, offices, hospitals, and industries is growing rapidly. If current trends continue, the electricity needed for cooling could triple by 2050, placing enormous pressure on power grids and significantly increasing carbon emissions. This study examines how Indian cities can meet future cooling needs while reducing pollution and improving energy efficiency.

The research develops an computer simulation model that combines long-term energy planning with the behavior of key decision-makers, including households, industries, utilities, and governments. Five future scenarios were evaluated, ranging from continuing current practices to adopting advanced solutions such as waste heat recovery, thermal energy storage, sector coupling, and coordinated policy measures.

The results show that no single technology can solve the problem. However, when these solutions are implemented together, carbon emissions from urban heating and cooling can be reduced by about 71%, peak electricity demand can fall by 63%, and cooling energy demand can be reduced by nearly 48% by 2050 compared with current trends. Although the integrated approach requires an estimated US$68.2 billion in infrastructure investment over 25 years, it also delivers US$7.6 billion in long-term cost savings through lower energy use and greater system efficiency.

The study also finds that people's behavior and effective government implementation have a greater influence on success than technology alone. Overall, the research provides a practical roadmap for policymakers, city planners, utilities, and investors to build cleaner, more affordable, and climate-resilient urban energy systems in India, with lessons that can also benefit other rapidly urbanizing developing countries.

detail.title: Financial Inclusion in Rural India: Challenges, Digital Transformation, and Policy Implications
detail.abstract: In this way, the issue of financial inclusion has become one of the leading ones that contributes largely to socioeconomic development and poverty alleviation in India. It is critical for people living in rural areas, farmers, and small businesses to have access to banking facilities because they must get access to institutional financing. In recent years, much progress has been achieved through various programs such as the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, Unified Payments Interface, Aadhaar Enabled Payment System (AePS), and m-banking. However, at the same time, there are many barriers that hinder the achievement of true financial inclusion. In particular, the paper will focus on the problem of financial inclusion and the main barriers to it that are related to the issues of financial literacy, lack of digital infrastructure, poor access to institutional financing, language problems, cybersecurity risks, and discrimination based on gender in the field of finance. Research will use secondary data collected from government and scientific publications, RBI, and NABARD materials. At the same time, an exploratory survey will be conducted involving 30 respondents to collect primary data. Conclusion: Financial literacy, robust digital infrastructure, technology, and proper policy intervention play key roles in ensuring financial inclusion. It was found that financial inclusion involves more than just providing people with banking services; rather, proper usage of financial services needs to be ensured as well. A collaborative effort from the government, financial institutes, fintech organizations, and even communities is necessary for proper access to financial services in India.

detail.abstract: This study examines the economic impact of the late February 2026 Middle East War on the United States, Israel, and Iran on their critical macroeconomic indicators, including Gross Domestic Product (GDP), inflation, unemployment, poverty, hunger, exports, and imports. The study is embedded on the longitudinal data of these macroeconomic indicators of the three select nations from 2015 to 2026 and used multivariate statistical operations-Auto Regression Integrated Moving Averages (ARIMA) to understand their economic prospects. The findings hint at a predominant possibility of decline in GDP and international trade, coupled with a swelling in inflation, unemployment, poverty, and hunger levels in these countries. Among the three countries, Iran in the future shall have to face adverse economic situations, and the majority of its economic indicators would be in unhealthy condition when compared to the USA and Israel. The study emphasize for restoring dialogue for constructive peace among these conflicting nations and ensuring the free flow of trade, goods, and services. This alone will reverse the ailing macroeconomic health in these nations in the future.

detail.abstract: The Unaccompanied Alien Children (UAC) program manages a multi-stage humanitarian pipeline spanning apprehension and custody by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), transfer into care administered by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and eventual discharge to a vetted sponsor. While aggregate population counts at each stage are routinely reported, process-level efficiency — how quickly and reliably children move between stages — has historically received far less structured analysis. This study reframes 720 days of daily operational data (January 12, 2023 to December 21, 2025) from a capacity-monitoring lens to a process-efficiency and outcome-evaluation lens. Five derived key performance indicators were constructed: Transfer Efficiency Ratio, Discharge Effectiveness Index, Pipeline Throughput Rate, Backlog Accumulation Rate, and Outcome Stability Score. Analysis reveals an average transfer efficiency of 0.69 (transfers per child in CBP custody), an average discharge effectiveness of 0.024, and a mean transfer backlog of approximately 43 children per day, with backlog peaking at 304 children on May 29, 2024. Approximately 24.3% of all observed days were flagged with an operational warning alert, and 21.5% of days fell within a stagnation period of five or more consecutive low-efficiency days. Weekday and weekend transfer efficiency were found to be statistically comparable (0.689 versus 0.700, a 1.6% difference), suggesting the pipeline does not suffer materially from weekend staffing constraints. Discharge effectiveness and HHS care load ratio exhibited a near-perfect inverse correlation (r = –1.00), while stagnation period length was strongly associated with both reduced transfer efficiency (r = –0.66) and reduced discharge effectiveness (r = –0.80). These findings are translated into an interactive nine-page Streamlit analytics dashboard intended to support real-time operational monitoring and policy-level decision-making aimed at reducing systemic delay and improving reunification timelines.

title: The Reform Conversion Gap

detail.title: The Reform Conversion Gap
detail.abstract: Nigeria's main policy problem is no longer a shortage of reform ideas. It is a failure of reform conversion. This white paper provides an independent, evidence-based review of the major government policies implemented in Nigeria between 2014 and 2026. It assesses their design logic, measurable outcomes, and structural gaps across twelve years of reform. It maps key developments in 2025 and early 2026, and sets out a forward agenda for accelerating meaningful change. The objective is to serve as a credible, durable policy advocacy tool-a resource for government decision-makers, legislators, development partners, and the private sector committed to accelerating Nigeria's transformation. Over the past decade, successive administrations have introduced major reforms across exchangerate policy, fuel pricing, taxation, power, agriculture, social protection, and trade. Many were economically necessary. Some were politically difficult. A few produced partial gains. Yet across sectors, outcomes have remained weaker, slower, and less durable than reform intent suggested. This paper argues that the central constraint is a Reform Conversion Gap: the distance between policy intent and measurable public outcomes. In Nigeria, reforms routinely enter systems that lack the institutional depth, delivery discipline, fiscal continuity, coordination quality, and performance visibility required to sustain them. The result is a familiar pattern: reform is announced, pressure is absorbed, execution weakens, and outcomes fall short. The evidence reviewed here points to five recurring drivers of underperformance. Institutional capacity remains too thin. Reform design often underestimates political constraints. Feedback systems are weak. Fiscal continuity remains vulnerable to oil-linked instability. Coordination across ministries, agencies, regulators, and states remains weaker than the problems being managed. This diagnosis has two implications. First, Nigeria's next phase of progress will depend less on the number of reforms announced and more on whether the state can improve its ability to convert reform intent into durable results. Second, the ambition of building a larger, more productive, and more inclusive economy, including the aspiration of reaching a $1 trillion economy, will not be realised through policy volume, statistical rebasing, or oil-price luck. It will depend on lower structural business costs, stronger non-oil fiscal depth, more reliable power, wider social resilience, greater export competitiveness, and a governing system capable of disciplined execution through difficult transitions.

title: Purchase Propensity as Adaptive Consumer Behaviour: Applying the Integrated Contextual Practice Theory (ICPT)

detail.title: Purchase Propensity as Adaptive Consumer Behaviour: Applying the Integrated Contextual Practice Theory (ICPT)

declarations.ethicsApproval: None

detail.abstract:
The Integrated Contextual Practice Theory (ICPT) is a developmental, mid-range framework proposed by the author for modelling adaptive social action: the idea that behavioural deviation from stated values often reflects rational adaptation to structural constraint rather than moral inconsistency. This paper adapts that framework, itself still unvalidated, to a long-standing problem in consumer research: why people who express strong brand preferences, ethical commitments, and purchase intentions frequently do not act on them.

Each of ICPT's five variables is reinterpreted for a business context. Consumer Purchase Habit (H) replaces Habitus, Brand and Product Value Alignment (V) replaces Values, Social Consumption Signalling (I) replaces Identity Need, Consumer Contextual Stress (Cs) captures financial and access barriers, and Market Cultural Permissibility (C) replaces the Cultural Governor. The core equation is unchanged: � � =[(𝐻× 𝑉)+𝐼 (𝐶𝑠 +𝜀) ] ×𝐶 Higher values of P indicate greater relative purchase propensity rather than an absolute probability of purchase. where P denotes Purchase Propensity. Six illustrative consumer scenarios, covering ethical retail, luxury goods, organic groceries, sustainable fashion, digital subscriptions, and electric vehicle adoption, are used to show how the equation might, in principle, separate cases where weak values are the obstacle from cases where structural stress is. The paper closes with a measurement protocol, six testable hypotheses, and an explicit statement of boundary conditions.  

As with the parent paper, this is a developmental pre-print. The numbers used throughout are illustrative, not field-derived, and the framework awaits empirical calibration before any of its claims should be treated as established.

title: The Work That GDP Forgot: Unpaid Domestic Labour and India's Shadow Economy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Work That GDP Forgot: Unpaid Domestic Labour and India's Shadow Economy
detail.abstract: Every morning, before a single rupee changes hands in the formal economy, the Indian day has already begun. Meals have been cooked, children dressed, elders bathed, vessels washed, and floors swept. None of this work appears in India's Gross Domestic Product. By the time a working professional leaves home for the office, hours of essential labour have already been done-and the people doing it, overwhelmingly women, are paid nothing. This paper investigates the size and significance of unpaid domestic labour in India and the gap between its real economic value and its statistical visibility. Drawing on the Time Use Survey 2024 released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), International Labour Organization (ILO) estimates, OECD data, and feminist economic theory, the paper finds that unpaid domestic and caregiving work in India represents an estimated 15-17% of GDP-a figure larger than India's entire manufacturing sector's contribution in some estimates. Women in India spent 289 minutes per day on unpaid domestic services in 2024, against 88 minutes for men. They spent 137 minutes per day on unpaid caregiving, against 75 minutes for men. Despite five years passing since the 2019 Time Use Survey, the gender gap in unpaid work has barely narrowed. The paper argues that this invisibility is not an accident of measurement but a structural choice-one that has direct consequences for women's labour force participation, household poverty, and the design of India's social policy. The paper closes with five policy recommendations centred on recognition (count it), reduction (invest in care infrastructure), and redistribution (share it more equally between men and women, and between households and the state). The argument throughout is that GDP, designed in the 1930s for a different economy and a different gender order, has become an increasingly unreliable mirror of what the Indian economy actually produces.

title: The Human-Animal-Welfare Trilemma
affiliations: and New York University School of Law

detail.title: The Human-Animal-Welfare Trilemma

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None to report.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: New York University School of Law; University of Michigan Law School

detail.abstract:
The “human-animal-welfare trilemma” captures the challenge of reconciling (1) a commitment to aiding the worst-off humans (“humanitarianism”), (2) a rejection of discrimination against nonhuman animals (“nonspeciesism”), and (3) an embrace of utilitarianism or prioritarianism (“welfarism”). Because so many nonhuman animals suffer severely—and because in many cases their suffering can be alleviated cheaply—nonspeciesist welfarists often will struggle to justify allocating scarce resources to the worst-off humans. 

We reject one proposed response to the trilemma: prioritizing humans for their instrumental usefulness to the planet. Even if humans are important for the planet—say, through avoiding catastrophic asteroid strikes—the worst-off humans are unlikely to be the ones who would lead those efforts. We then explore two partial solutions. One emphasizes “win-win” decisions that benefit both humans and animals, like shifting away from industrial animal agriculture. Another distinguishes between “decision rules” (rules to resolve discrete human-animal conflicts) and “meta-decision rules” (rules that select among decision rules). A welfarist could apply a nonspeciesist meta-decision rule that selects a speciesist decision rule: discounting animals enough to prevent popular backlash, but no more. Still, both of these solutions are radically incomplete, and the trilemma remains a tragic and urgent ethical challenge.

title: The Changing Distribution of EPS Forecast Errors
affiliations: and Yale School of Management

detail.title: The Changing Distribution of EPS Forecast Errors
detail.abstract: We study significant changes since 2000 in the distribution of EPS forecast errors (FE), especially variation across share price. Earlier, FE magnitudes (or standard deviations) were puzzlingly similar across low and high share prices, despite substantial variation in EPS levels. While magnitudes were similar, the means were not: mean FE increased with price from 0 to 2 cents per share. Since 2000, both FE magnitudes and means have been trending upward over time, with high price firms exhibiting the steepest increases. Our results suggest that these differential trends, which are observed across sectors, are not due to changes in earnings management, as suggested by some. They are mainly due to the universal decline in stock splits, which has resulted in higher share prices. Remarkably, investors recognize these evolving shifts in FE distributions and accordingly adapt their price responses to observed FE. We discuss two research implications of these shifting patterns: identifying firms that managed earnings to “just-meet-or-beat” analyst consensus and improved specifications for ERC-type regressions.

detail.abstract: This study examines how carbon markets shape the direction of corporate green innovation by exploiting the introduction of South Korea's emissions trading scheme (ETS) as a quasi-natural experiment. We distinguish between pure green patents, which support low-carbon alternatives, and fuel-efficiency patents, which improve fossil-fuel-based systems. We find that ETS exposure significantly reduces pure green innovation, while fuelefficiency innovation does not decline, indicating an asymmetric effect of carbon pricing across green technology domains. The fuel-efficiency response is stronger among firms with larger fuel-efficiency patent stocks, greater market power, and higher analyst coverage, suggesting that firms' technological profiles and market incentives shape their responses to carbon pricing. We find no evidence that either type of green innovation reduces emissions during the first phase of the ETS, although fuel-efficiency innovation partly mitigates the negative valuation effect of ETS exposure. Overall, the findings suggest that carbon markets can reshape the direction of green innovation, not simply its overall level, by reinforcing incremental fuel-efficiency improvements rather than promoting more transformative low-carbon technologies.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether brown discrimination is priced in the cross-section of Chinese stock returns. We define brown discrimination as mutual funds' tendency to tilt their holdings toward green firms relative to brown firms. Using Chinese mutual fund holdings and firm-level green invention patent data, we construct a market-level brown discrimination index and estimate firm-level sensitivity to this index through rolling regressions. We find that firms with higher brown discrimination sensitivity earn significantly lower subsequent returns. This return penalty remains robust to standard risk adjustment, controls for conventional firm characteristics, and alternative index constructions. We also find an information-based interpretation: the premium is attenuated when firms provide observable greentransition signals and when investor attention is higher, but it is stronger among firms with higher absolute carbon emissions. Overall, the findings suggest that the differential capital allocation between green and brown firms especially in high carbon emission markets.

detail.abstract: We develop and test a theory of how beliefs about others' responsiveness to incentives shape preferences for redistribution. In an income taxation model with heterogeneous prosocial preferences, effort distortions from higher taxes are smaller among more prosocial individuals. As a result, pessimistic beliefs about others' prosociality can reduce equilibrium redistribution even when most individuals are poor or altruistic. In a laboratory experiment, however, providing information about others' prosocial behavior does not increase support for redistribution among pessimists, whereas it reduces it among optimists. This asymmetric response is attributable to correlation between prosocial preferences and optimistic beliefs, suggesting that selfish individuals form self-serving beliefs that rationalize their choice of low redistribution.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Accounting and Economics, forthcoming

detail.abstract: Pandey et al. (2026) examine whether the auditor independence provisions of Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) impact accounting careers and human-capital development. I discuss how the paper shows that independence regulation affects not just the economic ties of auditors and clients, but also the organization of work through which auditors develop human capital. I interpret the evidence as identifying both intended and unintended consequences of independence rules on accountants' learning, networks, and mobility. The paper adds an important labor-market cost dimension to the evaluation of SOX, but I argue it should be read as informing independence regulation rather than making a case against it. The broader implication is that auditor independence and human capital are complementary inputs into audit quality, which creates a regulatory design problem of protecting auditor objectivity while sustaining expertise.

title: When Cheap Electricity Is No Longer Cheap: A Market-depth Test for Price-taking Electricity Optimization

detail.title: When Cheap Electricity Is No Longer Cheap: A Market-depth Test for Price-taking Electricity Optimization
detail.abstract: Optimization papers often schedule flexible electricity consumption by minimizing a fixed vector of day-ahead prices. That model is correct for an infinitesimal price taker. It is questionable for a MWh-scale buyer whose own order can move the auction curve. This paper proposes a transparent market-depth test for that assumption. For each period, we reconstruct offered supply and offered demand step functions from public OMIE/MIBEL aggregate dayahead curve files, anchor the counterfactual at the official marginal price, and compute the price that would be required to absorb an additional inelastic demand order. The method is not a full reimplementation of EUPHEMIA; it is an auditable local perturbation of the published auction book. In a Spain/MIBEL pilot for 1-7 January 2024, an additional 1000 MWh order has median price impact 3.775 EUR/MWh and 95th percentile impact 17.524 EUR/MWh under the anchored net-supply model. A daily flexible buyer requiring 1000 MWh with a 250 MWh perperiod cap would understate its weekly cost by 8.44 percent if it followed the published-price optimum and ignored its own price impact. The impact-aware schedule reduces actual cost by 0.85 percent in the main model. The larger contribution is diagnostic: the cheapest-hour ranking is stable at small order sizes but reverses on 42.9 percent of days at 1000 MWh, and a +1 EUR/MWh critical mass is reached within the tested order grid in 95.8 percent of hours. The conclusion is not that all price-taking papers are wrong. It is sharper: price taking is an empirical approximation, and large-load optimization should report a market-depth condition alongside the objective value.
