detail.abstract: This an abbreviated and selectiver history of Islamic finance in North America from the author's vantage. It begins with the first project financing in Saudi Arabia, which involved United States and English banks as well as Middle Eastern banks and applied Islamic Shari'ah principles in the collateral security structure. The Shari'ah-compliant collateral security satisfied credit and underwriting standards of the international banks, facilitating greater acceptance of Shari'ah-compliant financings by U.S. and European banks. The paper then focuses on developments within North America, beginning with the role of the Harvard Islamic Finance and Information Program and noting some of the fundamental interpretive letters of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Department of Financial Services of the State of New York, and the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance. The history then focuses on two developments that occurred in the United States and have had pronounced influences on internatioal practices. The first is the Dow Jones fatwa, which addresses when it is permissible to invest in an equity security. The fatwa sets for three sets of tests regarding the permisibility of different types of securities, the nature and permissible and impermissible business activities by the subject entity, and financial screens for impermissible interest income and expense. While the various sets of tests were developed for non-controlling equity investments but have broad application throughout Islamic banking and finance. The core principle of the fatwa is that some impurity or variance from strict Shari'ah principles is acceptable; the difficulties being determining how much impurity is too much. The final section discusses bifurcated ijara (lease) structures that are used for Shari'ah compliant financings in jurisdictions that have only interest-based banking and finance. Those structures are used throughout the world, including in jurisdictions that have Islamic banking and finance, and are the backbone of tradable sukuk issuances.

title: The Captive Classroom: Coercion, Consent, and the Manufacture of Belief

detail.title: The Captive Classroom: Coercion, Consent, and the Manufacture of Belief
detail.abstract: A recent wave of legislation, exemplified by a Texas mandate requiring more than five million public school students to read biblical scripture in every grade, seeks to install the scripture of one faith in the compulsory curriculum. This paper examines that project not as a legal question but as a moral and empirical one, and advances four claims. First, the categories used to defend and attack such mandates, "indoctrination" and "parental rights," function in practice as tribal markers indexed to the in-group or out-group content of the lesson rather than as principles applied to the act of compulsory instruction itself. Second, the morally decisive feature of the mandate is the coercion of a captive audience that can neither consent nor exit, which distinguishes it sharply from persuasion, however vigorous. Third, the mandate is not commanded by, and in places contradicts, the very scripture it would compel, which locates its source in a political program rather than a religious one and warrants the precise term Christian nationalism, a project the evidence shows operates most powerfully when detached from religious practice and which is therefore distinct from Christianity and from religious belief as such. Fourth, the empirical record on disaffiliation indicates that compulsion of this kind is both a symptom of declining religious adherence and an accelerant of it, so that the mandate is self-defeating on its own terms: it cannot manufacture the belief it wants, and it hastens the exit it fears, while imposing its costs on those least able to refuse. The argument throughout distinguishes a coercive political movement from ordinary religious practice, which it neither targets nor disparages.

title: Kalman Filtering in Mean-Variance Portfolios: Which Input Channel Drives Adaptive Gains?

detail.title: Kalman Filtering in Mean-Variance Portfolios: Which Input Channel Drives Adaptive Gains?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: Accurate estimation of mean-variance optimizer inputs-expected returns and the covariance matrix-is central to portfolio construction, yet standard rolling-window estimators treat all observations within the window equally, making them slow to adapt when market conditions change. Kalman filtering offers a principled alternative through recursive state updating, but prior work has not systematically isolated whether portfolio gains from Kalman filtering arise from improved expected-return estimation, improved covariance estimation, or their interaction. This paper addresses that gap by decomposing Kalman filtering across the two inputs of the mean-variance optimizer using a 2 × 2 ablation design. Three Kalman specifications are evaluated: Kalman-𝜇 MV filters only the expected-return input while retaining the rolling covariance estimator; Kalman-Σ MV retains the rolling expected-return estimator while constructing the covariance matrix from Kalman-filtered return signals; and Kalman-Full MV applies Kalman filtering to both inputs simultaneously. These are compared against Equal Weight, Rolling MV, Static MV, and Ledoit-Wolf MV benchmarks across a six-asset cross-asset ETF universe spanning US equities, bonds, gold, international equities, and real estate over a 16-year period from January 2010 to March 2026. The Kalman filter is applied at the input-estimation level using a local-level state-space model, with process noise calibrated via walk-forward cross-validation on training data using portfolio Sharpe ratio as the criterion. A regime-conditional scaling mechanism allows the filter to vary its responsiveness across four volatility regimes-LOW_VOL, MED_VOL, HIGH_VOL, and CRISIS-without requiring a fully endogenous regime-switching model. All specifications are evaluated under realistic long-only constraints with a 40% position cap. Performance is assessed using full-period and out-of-sample Sharpe ratios, maximum drawdown, turnover, transaction cost sensitivity at 0-20 basis points, regime-conditional Sharpe decomposition, and Diebold-Mariano forecast accuracy tests applied separately to each Kalman specification to assess whether forecast improvements are statistically grounded in each input channel.

title: Of This Trust: Fiduciary Prudence is Never Generic

detail.title: Of This Trust: Fiduciary Prudence is Never Generic

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Trust law does not exercise prudence in the abstract. It exercises prudence in relation to the trust under administration. The familiar phrase "of the trust" repeatedly directs fiduciary judgment toward the trust whose terms, purposes, beneficiaries, and circumstances give fiduciary obligations their legal meaning. General fiduciary principles establish standards of conduct. The trust identifies for whom, for what purpose, and under what circumstances those standards are deliberated. Institutional administration may rely upon standardized methods. The fiduciary question is whether those methods remain capable of justification by reference to this trust.

Trust law repeatedly directs fiduciary judgment back to the trust under administration: the terms of the trust, the purposes of the trust, the beneficiaries of the trust, the administration of the trust, and the circumstances affecting the trust. 1 Because these references are familiar, they are easily overlooked as drafting convention. Together they reveal a common feature of fiduciary doctrine. Fiduciary judgment is never generic. 

It is always deliberated in relation to a particular trust.

title: Does Better Data Mean Better Finances? Statistical Capacity and Fiscal Sustainability in Africa

detail.title: Does Better Data Mean Better Finances? Statistical Capacity and Fiscal Sustainability in Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: No consent
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: Despite theoretical arguments linking statistical capacity to fiscal performance, no empirical study has explicitly tested whether improvements in statistical systems enhance fiscal sustainability in Africa, nor has it identified the transmission channels. This study fills that gap. Using panel data for 54 African countries from 2016 to 2023, we employed pooled OLS, Driscoll-Kraay, quantile regression, Lewbel (2012) IV, and mediation analysis to examine the effect of the World Bank's Statistical Performance Index (SPI) on fiscal sustainability. Results consistently show that higher statistical capacity significantly improves fiscal sustainability: a one-point increase in SPI raises the primary-balance-based sustainability measure by 0.19-0.21 units. The effect is robust to alternative measures, disaggregated SPI components, outlier exclusion, and regional truncation. Quantile regressions reveal larger marginal returns for countries already in the upper tail of fiscal performance. Mediation analysis indicates that governance quality, particularly regulatory quality, corruption control, and the rule of law, accounts for 25-63% of the total effect. Policy implications include prioritising statistical investment in fiscal infrastructure, targeting governance channels, differentiating investments by capacity level, leveraging specific SPI subcomponents, and incorporating statistical capacity into debt sustainability frameworks. These findings establish statistical capacity as an actionable lever for fiscal resilience in Africa.

title: The Scroll and the Eagle: Roman Structural Erasure and the Geopolitics of Hellenistic Intellectual Lineage

detail.title: The Scroll and the Eagle: Roman Structural Erasure and the Geopolitics of Hellenistic Intellectual Lineage
detail.abstract: The destruction of the Library of Alexandria is traditionally historicized as a series of localized, catastrophic military accidents or localized religious upheavals. This study introduces an interdisciplinary revisionist framework, repositioning the library's decline not as an organic tragedy, but as a protracted, multi-century exercise in structural erasure and systemic containment executed by the Roman state apparatus. By bypassing the narrative biases of victorious Roman historiography, we cross-reference classical literary fragments with underwater maritime archaeology of Alexandria’s royal quarter (Basileia), papyrological econometrics from the Egyptian desert, and macro-environmental data tracks. We demonstrate that the Principate systematically executed an institutional demotion of Alexandrian scholarship, instituted a policy of "Caloric Imperialism" through the Cura Annonae that starved the periphery of metabolic energy, and weaponized fiscal auditing via the Lex Idios Logos. Accompanied by a deliberate campaign of philological warfare designed to reframe Hellenistic heritage as monarchical decadence, the Roman state successfully centralized intellectual hegemony within Italy while insulating itself from historical accountability. Ultimately, this paper proves that the systemic degradation of Alexandria’s independent intellectual lineage was a calculated prerequisite for Roman geopolitical legitimacy.

title: Aranceles en Puerto Rico 2025

detail.title: Aranceles en Puerto Rico 2025
detail.abstract:
En los últimos años, las dinámicas del comercio internacional han experimentado cambios importantes asociados a nuevas políticas comerciales. En este contexto, resulta relevante examinar cómo estos cambios se reflejan en Puerto Rico, particularmente debido a su dependencia de bienes importados. A partir de datos oficiales de comercio exterior, este informe analiza el comportamiento de los aranceles aplicados a las importaciones en Puerto Rico y documenta los cambios observados en años recientes. El estudio examina la evolución histórica de los aranceles durante el período 2010–2025, incluyendo su comportamiento anual y mensual en 2025, los principales países asociados a la carga arancelaria y distintos grupos de bienes importados que registraron cambios relevantes durante el período analizado. Asimismo, una de las principales aportaciones del informe consiste en estimar y analizar las tasas arancelarias efectivas, permitiendo evaluar la relación entre los aranceles pagados y el valor total de las importaciones en Puerto Rico.
Los resultados reflejan un aumento considerable en la carga arancelaria durante 2025. Los aranceles registraron un total de $919.7 millones en aranceles sobre importaciones, lo que representa un incremento de $683.1 millones en comparación con 2024 y un crecimiento interanual de 288.7%. Asimismo, la tasa arancelaria efectiva alcanzó 4.81% en 2025, el nivel más alto observado en toda la serie analizada desde 2010.
El análisis mensual evidencia que las tasas arancelarias comenzaron a aumentar principalmente a partir de abril de 2025, coincidiendo con cambios recientes en la política comercial de Estados Unidos. A lo largo del año, la tasa arancelaria efectiva alcanzó un máximo de 7.61% en noviembre y, durante varios meses, los pagos en aranceles superaron los $100 millones. Los incrementos se observaron en diversas categorías de bienes, incluyendo productos relacionados con manufactura, construcción, maquinaria, automóviles y alimentos, entre otros.
En cuanto a los países con mayor carga arancelaria asociada a importaciones hacia Puerto Rico, el informe identifica a China, Japón, México, Corea del Sur, República Dominicana, España, Brasil, Alemania, Francia y Vietnam como los principales socios comerciales impactados durante 2025. Fuera de estos países, el resto registró montos relativamente menores bajo este concepto. En términos generales, el informe documenta cambios importantes en el comportamiento reciente de los aranceles aplicados a las importaciones en Puerto Rico y presenta información que sirve de apoyo para el análisis económico y la toma de decisiones tanto en el sector público como privado.

title: Migrating for Economic Freedom: State Economic and Labor Market Freedom Institutions and the Inflow of Unauthorized Immigrants
affiliations: University of Dallas - Department of Economics

detail.title: Migrating for Economic Freedom: State Economic and Labor Market Freedom Institutions and the Inflow of Unauthorized Immigrants
detail.abstract: IN PROGRESS, DO NOT CITE: This paper examines changes in the long-run cumulative effect between state-level economic freedom institutions and the US state location choices of unauthorized immigrants within a federal system. I make two contributions to this literature. First, I use the general Error Correction Model (ECM) with two-way fixed effects to disentangle the noisy contemporaneous relationships between economic freedom institutions (and subsequent outcomes) and immigrant inflows from the long-run equilibrium associations. This is a feature that the current literature, which often works with limited time series, has not been able to make. Second, I construct an annual panel of state unauthorized-immigrant stocks spanning 1990-2022, a finer time dimension than the decennial-census snapshots common in the literature. Merging this panel with the Economic Freedom of North America (EFNA) index, I find that economic and labor market freedoms are positively associated with long-run unauthorized immigrant shares, and that the labor market channel dominates, where a one standard deviation increase in the long-run labor market freedom measure increases the unauthorized immigration fraction relative to natives by 1.27 percentage points. (where a one SD change roughly corresponds to the Pennsylvania-Texas gap in labor freedom) These results survive confounds for the state's economic standing, but not so for political constraints on immigrant mobility and enforcement, which may undermine a state's attractiveness to unauthorized immigrants, inferring another factor that unauthorized immigrants are responding to with their migration decisions. However, power concerns arising from the lack of data on political constraints along the time-series dimension may undermine statistical precision. However, deconstructing these economic and labor market freedom institutions into their constituent economic and policy outcomes finds that union density is robustly and negatively associated with unauthorized immigrants' locations. A one percentage point increase in a state's union density is associated with an estimated increase of 0.53 percentage points of the unauthorized share of the overall native population, or roughly 25% of the mean unauthorized share. Unionization effects are further developed in the Discussion, motivating a dedicated follow-up study of unions, monopsony power in the labor market, and immigration.

title: Discrimination As Exploitation: An Antidiscrimination Paradigm for the Bad Jobs Economy

detail.title: Discrimination As Exploitation: An Antidiscrimination Paradigm for the Bad Jobs Economy
detail.abstract: Employment discrimination law has failed the workers who need it most. Sixty years after Title VII became law, Black, Latino, and other workers of color are dramatically overrepresented in gig, contingent, and sub-minimum-wage work, and women still predominate in the forty lowest-paying occupations in the American economy. Most scholarship on the failures of antidiscrimination law focuses either on the evolving nature of prejudice or on judicial erosion of pro-plaintiff doctrines. In this Article, however, I argue that discrimination law fails the workers who need it most because it remains premised on an increasingly outdated understanding of where, why, and how labor market discrimination predominates. Discrimination law remains rooted in a paradigm I call discrimination as exclusion: the ways in which employers exclude marginalized workers—whether expressly, implicitly, or structurally—from better jobs and better working conditions. But today, in a fissured labor market with an ever-growing number of bad jobs, marginalized workers are more likely to experience discrimination as exploitation. I use this phrase to describe employers' preference for marginalized workers in bad and worsening jobs—a preference rooted in these workers' histories of oppression and ongoing sociolegal subordination, which enable employers to pay them less, treat them worse, and pocket the difference. The exclusion paradigm is now so embedded in antidiscrimination law that it actively inhibits the legal recognition of discriminatory exploitation. Here, I identify potential doctrinal openings within discrimination law—ways to challenge biased selection processes, workplace segregation, and the discriminatory degradation of job conditions—and I argue for recognizing the antidiscrimination potential of a broader range of laws, among them, immigration law, minimum standards law, and labor law.

title: The Magnitude Classification Matrix for Errors and Omissions in the Balance of Payments

detail.title: The Magnitude Classification Matrix for Errors and Omissions in the Balance of Payments
detail.abstract:
Errors and Omissions (E&O) in the Balance of Payments constitute the residual mechanism that ensures accounting balance between external credits and debits, as defined in the International Monetary Fund's BPM6 Manual. Despite their technical nature, the persistent magnitude of E&O has been associated in the literature both with statistical imperfections and with potential unrecorded financial flows. However, a standardized comparative classification instrument capable of assessing the relative magnitude of E&O across heterogeneous economies remains absent. 
This article provides international validation of the Magnitude Classification Matrix (MCM), originally proposed in Mateus (2026), applying it to a sample of 17 economies for the period 2012-2024. The central contribution is twofold: (i) cross-sectional validation of the instrument across diverse macroeconomic contexts; and (ii) explicit formalization of the asymmetric architecture of the MCM ratio, distinguishing the substantive function of the numerator from the purely scalar function of the denominator. 
The results demonstrate that using the sum of the absolute values of the Current Account as the denominator eliminates arithmetic distortions associated with sign compensation, ensuring classificatory stability between deficit and surplus economies. The resulting distribution confirms that the MCM does not automatically reproduce traditional structural typologies, reinforcing its usefulness as an analytical instrument independent of productive structure. The study does not aim to causally test the determinants of E&O, but rather to verify the classificatory robustness of the MCM as an international comparative tool.

title: The Second Wave: Becoming, Infrastructure, and the Pattern That May Not Hold

detail.title: The Second Wave: Becoming, Infrastructure, and the Pattern That May Not Hold

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent researcher who develops AI-oversight technology; a related system is the subject of a separate paper and a provisional patent application. This philosophical argument stands independently of that work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable; this work involved no human or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: History shows that foundational capabilities become transformative not at the moment of discovery but when infrastructure forms around them and reorganizes ordinary life. Electrification, sanitation, industrial fertilizer, and digital computing each followed a recognizable cycle: a new force became infrastructural, older constraints weakened, inherited institutions destabilized, and a later settlement eventually made the capability ordinary. This paper retraces that cycle, but not in order to place artificial intelligence as its next instance. It retraces the cycle in order to expose a premise the pattern has always carried silently — a premise so constant across every prior case that it never had to be stated: that man is the one who becomes, and the technology is an instrument that holds still long enough to be corrected. Each prior settlement was survivable because that premise held. Damage was done, seen, and eventually — late, and partially — corrected, because the tool waited while we deliberated and because man kept the pen. The argument of this paper is that artificial intelligence may be the first foundational force to violate that premise. It stands against the recent thesis that AI is a normal technology, continuous with prior general-purpose technologies (Narayanan & Kapoor, 2025); it concedes that the alarm it draws on — that a self-improving system may resist correction — is not new but canonical (Omohundro, 2008; Bostrom, 2014; Soares et al., 2015), and that the intuition of technological autonomy is older still (Ellul, 1954; Winner, 1977). Its contribution is a synthesis those literatures have not made: reading the disciplined economic-history cycle of general-purpose technologies as a foil, and locating the break precisely where the corrigibility problem voids the cycle's tacit premise of correction. This is not a forecast. It is an interpretation of what would have to be true for the pattern to break, and of why this is the first force to make that question live.

title: When Is Bayes Gaussian? Curvature of the Rate Function, from Bernstein-von Mises to Ghosh
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: When Is Bayes Gaussian? Curvature of the Rate Function, from Bernstein-von Mises to Ghosh
detail.abstract:
The Bayesian posterior is the exponential of a rate function, and it is Gaussian exactly when that rate is a single fixed nondegenerate paraboloid. This one sentence organizes the asymptotics. The rate is the one governing the posterior’s own large deviations: by the inverse Sanov theorem of Ganesh and O’Connell the posterior obeys a large deviation principle with rate J(θ) = D(pθ0 ∥pθ), and the Fisher information is precisely its Hessian at the truth, I = ∇2J|θ0 . Bernstein–von Mises is that curvature exponentiated, the moderate-deviation principle of Eichelsbacher and Ganesh is the rung between the two, and regularity, the Gaussian posterior, and a nondegenerate Hessian are three names for one condition. We prove that both orderings of relative entropy share this Hessian, so Bernstein–von Mises is blind to the direction of the divergence and only the large-deviation scale sees the asymmetry of Kullback–Leibler.
Everything else is a way the curvature degenerates, and each is a common Bayesian model. J. K. Ghosh’s non-regular problems put a corner in the rate, and for the conjugate Uniform Pareto pair we prove the resulting non-regular inverse-Sanov statement outright: a linear rate, an exponential posterior, contraction at rate n. Mixture and sparse priors put two minima and a corner between them, which every unimodal approximation convexifies, so Laplace and mean-field variational posteriors misreport component and inclusion probabilities in the limit, not merely at small samples. Non-ergodic processes make the curvature random, the observed information being the quadratic variation of the score: the estimator is mixed normal while the posterior, conditioning on the realized information, stays Gaussian, which is the Heyde–Johnstone robustness and, through Polson–Roberts, a statement about expected utility. Misspecification splits the curvature, and we show the split is exactly the failure of the Bartlett identity, not a swap of the divergence’s arguments; the posterior stays Gaussian and lies only about its width. In infinite dimensions the curvature becomes an unbounded operator and Bernstein–von Mises fails outright, the Dirichlet process, whose rate is regular, being the clean exception. We close with the computational moral: the safe algorithm is the one that respects the actual shape of the rate near its minima.

title: Spectral Risk Parity
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Cornell University - Operations Research & Industrial Engineering and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority

detail.title: Spectral Risk Parity

keywords: Portfolio Construction JEL classification codes: G0

detail.abstract: Utilizing concepts from random matrix theory (RMT), we propose a spectral approach to constructing risk parity portfolios. This portfolio tracks the principal component portfolio while explicitly penalizing the exposure to noise. The principal components and noisy components are identified using the Marčenko-Pastur distribution associated with the covariance (correlation) matrix. Such portfolios are robust to noise by construction. We provide empirical evidence to show the out-performance over the equal-risk-contribution (ERC) and minimum variance (MinVar) portfolios. Key Takeaways • Spectral Risk Parity Approach: A new approach to building risk parity portfolios based on the eigenspectrum of the covariance matrix of asset returns is presented. We refer to this approach as the spectral risk parity (SRP) approach. • Noise Resilience: The SRP portfolios explicitly penalize the exposure to these noisy components, making them inherently less sensitive to noise. Noisy components of the eigenspectrum are identified using the Marčenko-Pastur distribution. • Empirical Results: Empirical evidence for demonstrating the outperformance of SRP portfolios over equal-risk-contribution (ERC) and minimum variance (MinVar) portfolios is provided.

title: Optimal Control of Stochastic Differential Delay Equations (SDDE) with Jumps and Markov Switching, and with an Application in Economics
affiliations: University of Calgary and Mount Royal University

detail.title: Optimal Control of Stochastic Differential Delay Equations (SDDE) with Jumps and Markov Switching, and with an Application in Economics
detail.abstract: This paper considers stochastic optimal control of stochastic differential delay equations (SDDEs) with jumps and Markov switching, and its economical applications. The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation and the inverse HJB-equation are derived by applying the Dynkin's formula and solution of the Dirichlet-Poisson problem for those SDDEs. Three cases of modified Ramsey stochastic models in economics are studied; namely, a Ramsey diffusion model with jumps, a Ramsey diffusion model with Markov switching, and a Ramsey diffusion model with jumps and Markov switching. We also present numerical examples for all three cases. The contributions of the paper are four-fold: introducing and studying three new models for SDDEs: with jumps, Markov switching and both; studying optimal control for those models; applications of these results to economics with Ramsey's stochastic models; and numerical examples for these different models.

title: Circularity in the Decommissioning of Petroleum Activities
affiliations: University of Bergen, Faculty of Law, University of Bergen - Faculty of Law, University of Bergen - Faculty of Law, University of Bergen - Faculty of Law, University of Bergen - Faculty of Law, University of Bergen - Faculty of Law and University of Bergen - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Circularity in the Decommissioning of Petroleum Activities
detail.abstract: This report examines how legal and regulatory frameworks influence circularity in the decommissioning of offshore petroleum installations. Against the backdrop of increasing decommissioning activity on the Norwegian continental shelf and broader energy transition goals, it evaluates whether existing rules facilitate reuse, repurposing, upcycling, and recycling of offshore infrastructure. Through a comparative analysis of Norway, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Australia, the report identifies key barriers to circularity, including liability regimes, export controls, regulatory uncertainty, insufficient secondary markets, contractual restrictions, and limited coordination among stakeholders. While circular economy strategies have become prominent in public policy, the analysis shows that petroleum regulation continues to prioritize safe removal and environmental protection, with relatively few concrete incentives for higher-value circular solutions. The report argues that achieving greater circularity requires targeted regulatory reform, stronger collaboration between public authorities and industry, and the development of markets and standards that make reuse commercially viable. It concludes with recommendations aimed at aligning decommissioning practices with broader sustainability and resource-efficiency objectives.

title: Multivariate Generative Bayesian Computation
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Multivariate Generative Bayesian Computation
detail.abstract: We develop a theory of Multivariate Generative Bayesian Computation (MGBC): the use of a learned transport map H to carry multivariate base-distribution noise onto the joint posterior of a d-dimensional parameter vector θ. In one dimension GBC reduces to learning the inverse CDF, an approach elicited by the pinball loss and therefore provably calibrated. We show that three natural multivariate generalisations-(i) the Knothe-Rosenblatt (KR) triangular map, equivalent to a masked autoregressive flow with cosine-embedded IQN conditionals; (ii) the Monge-Kantorovich (MK) vector quantile, realised as the gradient of an Input Convex Neural Network (ICNN); and (iii) the tensor-product cosine expansion with a horseshoe prior-each recovers a distinct notion of multivariate quantile. We establish consistency, optimal posterior contraction rates, and a minimax elicitability result that clarifies which loss is proper for each definition. The KR/autoregressive route avoids the curse of dimensionality by decomposing the d-dimensional problem into d scalar regressions, each at the univariate minimax rate. The MK/ICNN route is affine-equivariant and theoretically canonical but requires an adversarial semi-dual training objective. We propose a practical hybrid architecture-autoregressive at the outer level, ICNN-convex per conditional-that combines scalability with monotonicity guarantees. Empirical results on synthetic benchmarks and financial return data demonstrate that MGBC achieves competitive joint coverage, correct tail-dependence recovery, and significant computational advantages over density-based competitors.

title: Bad Neighbors: Bordering Institutions as Comparative (Dis)Advantage
affiliations: Universidad Adolfo Ibañez, UAI Business School  and Universidad de Chile

detail.title: Bad Neighbors: Bordering Institutions as Comparative (Dis)Advantage
detail.abstract: Research has shown how domestic institutions shape comparative advantage. But for most countries in the world, contract-intensive supply chains tend to go beyond national borders. We show that-all else equal-countries with stronger neighboring institutions also export relatively more in contract-intensive industries. A one-standard-deviation increase in neighbors' institutions is associated with 0.14-0.25 standard deviations higher exports of contract-intensive goods. This is similar in magnitude to estimates for domestic institutions. Our results remain qualitatively robust to a wide range of potential concerns, including collinearity and endogeneity of institutions, as well as measurement of judicial quality and contract intensity. We also test the robustness of our results using U.S. imports, industrial production, imports of intermediate inputs, and domestic value added. Over two decades of data, the role of neighboring institutions remains stable. Taken together, our findings suggest a relevant role for regional value chains and cross-border contract enforcement.

title: The Phillips Multiplier and the Two Sides of Inflation
affiliations: Universidad del Pacifico

detail.title: The Phillips Multiplier and the Two Sides of Inflation
detail.abstract: The inflation-unemployment trade-off faced by a central bank can be characterised non-parametrically by the Phillips multiplier of Barnichon and Mesters (2021). Because the multiplier is linear in inflation, it inherits any exact decomposition of it. We split it into the two directional margins of price adjustment of Quineche and Zapata (2026). Before 1990, a policy-induced one-percentage-point rise in the cumulative unemployment gap raises cumulative deflationary pressure by 0.4pp: the identified trade-off runs through price cuts. After 1990, excluding the zero lower bound, nothing is identified: neither the multiplier nor either margin. The instruments carry too little exogenous variation.

title: GenAI as Fictional Author: Statutory Attribution of Copyright in AIGC

detail.title: GenAI as Fictional Author: Statutory Attribution of Copyright in AIGC
detail.abstract: The capacity of GenAI to produce content autonomously and at scale challenges copyright doctrine because the machine-generated portions of AIGC may satisfy originality thresholds in a factual sense while lacking a qualified legal author. This tension is especially visible in the divergence between the United States, which continues to insist on human authorship, and China, where some courts have been more willing to protect AI-related outputs through human attribution or pragmatic reasoning. A further doctrinal distinction is required between the copyrightability of user inputs, including prompts and subsequent edits, and the copyrightability and ownership of the final AI-generated output. Against this background, two routes are examined. The first treats GenAI as an electronic person or juridical person for limited attributional purposes, but it is ultimately rejected because it currently faces substantial ethical and institutional barriers. The proposed framework instead treats GenAI as the fictional factual author of the machine-generated portions of AIGC and attributes legal authorship, as a matter of statutory allocation, to the developer or other controlling deployer, while preserving user rights in copyrightable prompts, selection, arrangement, or revision. This framework seeks to clarify authorship, ownership, and accountability without requiring full legal personhood for AI.

title: Shipping Strategy Selection in Cross-Border E-Commerce Supply Chain Under Exchange-Rate Risk
affiliations: School of Management, Jinan University, , Jinan University, University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee - Sheldon B. Lubar School of Business and University of Southampton

detail.title: Shipping Strategy Selection in Cross-Border E-Commerce Supply Chain Under Exchange-Rate Risk
detail.abstract: Exchange-rate fluctuations expose small and medium-sized enterprise sellers to exchange-rate risk in the agency channel, incentivizing risk-averse sellers to shift sales to the reselling channel, where the wholesale transaction is settled in domestic currency and the seller's revenue is insulated from exchange-rate volatility. Considering this shift intensifies downstream competition, both the seller and the platform might independently select between direct shipping and overseas warehouse shipping for their respective sales channels to mitigate channel conflict. We develop a game-theoretic model to analyze the seller's sales channel decision and both members' shipping strategy selections under exchange-rate volatility. Our analysis reveals three findings: First, symmetric shipping strategies never emerge in equilibrium. Both members spontaneously select differentiated shipping to mitigate channel conflict and facilitate risk-hedging profit-shifting. Second, the seller achieves the most cost-effective profit shifting when it alone adopts direct shipping under low volatility, whereas adopting overseas warehouse shipping alone proves superior under high volatility. Third, when volatility is moderate, the strategy combination in which the seller adopts overseas warehouse shipping and the platform selects direct shipping achieves a Pareto improvement. Managerially, our work highlights a strategy combination that remains robust across a broad range of 1 volatility, enabling the seller to manage exchange-rate risk while allowing the platform to enhance revenue.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that carefully designed lay participation in administrative processes can reinforce democratic resilience by linking law, mass beliefs, and institutional design. I advance four claims. First, European hard and soft law establishes a practicable framework of authorized discretion that ties bureaucratic decision-making to democratically sanctioned principles. Second, these principles occupy a coherent and resilient position within mass political belief systems. Third, authorized discretion provides a publicly intelligible standard of administrative responsibility, and concrete encounters sharpen citizens’ reasoning about it. Fourth, the structural integrity principle embedded in authorized discretion protects democratic governance against destabilizing challenges, such as populist politics. Together, these claims support a normative and practical case for institutional designs that empower citizens to help defend democratic governance against partisan capture.

title: The Church as an Alternative Field: Institutional Mechanisms of Immigrant Mobility among Nikkei Peruvians in Japan

detail.title: The Church as an Alternative Field: Institutional Mechanisms of Immigrant Mobility among Nikkei Peruvians in Japan
detail.abstract: This article examines the institutional mechanisms that facilitate upward social mobility for second-generation Nikkei Peruvians in Japan, a group facing a "credential paradox" where human capital gains do not yield proportional socioeconomic returns. Moving beyond standard network analysis, this study is positioned as an interpretive qualitative inquiry with a supplementary quantitative component to analyze multicultural Christian churches in Aichi as unique institutional actors. Integrating James Coleman's framework of the "social capital multiplier" with Pierre Bourdieu's concept of the "field," the article argues that these churches function as "alternative fields" of value. Within these spaces, migrants' cultural capital (e.g., bilingualism), often devalued in the mainstream labor market, is actively incubated and converted into highstatus social capital. This newly acquired capital is then leveraged to circumvent structural barriers through trusted job referrals, facilitating a direct transition from manual to non-manual labor. The findings reveal a model of "circumstantial mobility," demonstrating how meso-level civil society institutions create parallel systems of value where state and market institutions structurally fail. However, the study also identifies a "network ceiling effect," revealing that this pathway constitutes a form of "bounded mobility" that provides an alternative to, and negatively correlates with, higher educational attainment. Ultimately, this research contributes to International Development Studies by demonstrating that addressing systemic inequality requires actively cultivating the meso-level infrastructure of civil society, rather than relying solely on individual capacity-building.

detail.title: Exploring Preferred Leadership Styles Across Industries: Perspectives of Followers
detail.abstract: Introduction/ Main Objective: This study investigated preferred leadership styles, considered by many to be the most prevalent styles: autocratic, participative, and laissez-faire. We assessed ‘preferred leadership style’ from the perspective of the follower. The study aimed at exploring the variations in the preference for leadership styles across selected industries, namely the food/beverage industry, the retail industry, and the financial industry. Novelty: Leadership styles and perspectives have been investigated from divergent angles; but the preferred leadership styles have not been explored adequately across industries. This study endeavored at filling the gap in literature, and to provide direction to stakeholders, as regards followers’ perspectives. Research Methods: Our convenience sample was a result of a targeted effort to query respondents from three distinct samples: retail, restaurant/drink establishments, and consumer finance institutions (primarily banks). In addition to the preferred leadership from the perspective of the follower, we also collected demographic data including gender and age of the follower, in order to get critical insights from demographic lenses. Our survey included the leader behavior questions that are borrowed from the LBDQ XII manual provided by Stogdill (1962), and involved an examination of the studies conducted by Van Eeden, et al.(2008) for examples of behaviors attributed to the various leadership styles. Finding/Results: Our results were mixed. In some analyses, our results were reflective of the literature. However, in other analyses, our results differed from the literature. The study evinced tolerance for autocratic leadership, particularly in retailing, much against the pre-conceived notion. Conclusion: The study confirmed the generally- accepted hypothesis that employees from the food/beverage industry, the retail industry, and the financial industry all prefer participative leadership significantly more than autocratic or laissez-faire styles.

title: Local Opioid Exposure and Corporate Debt Structure
affiliations: University of Bradford,  and University of Bradford - School of Management

detail.title: Local Opioid Exposure and Corporate Debt Structure
detail.abstract: This paper examines how local opioid exposure affects firms’ debt structure. Motivated by evidence that the opioid crisis weakens labor supply, impairs human capital, and increases operating uncertainty, we argue that firms exposed to greater local opioid distress rely more heavily on bank debt because bank lenders provide monitoring, private information production, and renegotiation flexibility that become more valuable when borrower risk is harder to assess. Using a panel of 5,424 U.S. public firms from 2003 to 2020, we find that greater local opioid exposure, measured by county-level opioid-related mortality, is associated with a greater share of bank debt and a lower share of public debt. To strengthen identification, we exploit the staggered adoption of state-level Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMPs) in a stacked difference-in-differences design. PDMP adoption is followed by reductions in local opioid exposure and a subsequent decline in firms’ reliance on bank debt. The effect is stronger among labor-intensive firms, firms located in tighter local labor markets, firms with higher R&D intensity, and firms facing greater bankruptcy and information risk. Overall, our findings suggest that opioid-related local distress alters corporate financing choices by increasing the relative attractiveness of bank debt.

detail.abstract: Introduction/Main Objectives: This study investigated preferred leadership styles across Baby Boomers, Generation X, and Millennials. The autocratic, participative, and laissez-faire were identified as most prevalent styles; and were assessed to explore how the leadership styles across generations affect the role of leadership. Background Problems: Although leadership styles and perspectives have been investigated from divergent angles, the preferred leadership styles have not been explored adequately across generations. Novelty: This study endeavored at filling the gap in literature, and to provide direction to stakeholders, as regards the preference of each generation for a particular leadership style. Research Methods: An exploratory research design was used for this study and questionnaire items were adopted from the Globe Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness (GLOBE) project. The sample was obtained from adults over the age of eighteen from the Midwest USA and Canada. Finding/Results: The study confirmed the generally- accepted hypothesis that Baby Boomers tend to be workaholics and career driven. The study provides direction and motivation for further confirmatory and exploratory studies pertaining to preferred leadership styles vis-à-vis generation as well as demographic, geographic and cross-cultural variables. Conclusion: Generation X is highly focused on family, life, and work. The millennial generation has modern values and believe in treating everyone equally, though with a desire to be the center of attention for stealing the spotlight.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a founder-centric systems framework for understanding venture scalability through the interaction between Execution Power (EP) and Internal Friction (IF). Existing entrepreneurship and organizational performance literature primarily emphasize resources, market positioning, and leadership capability as determinants of startup success. However, this study argues that sustainable venture scalability depends on the founder's ability to optimize the synergy between Human Intelligence (HI) and Human-System Integration (HSI), while minimizing Internal Friction (IF). Execution Power is conceptualized as the operational force that transforms strategic intent into measurable organizational outcomes. Internal Friction represents organizational drag arising from structural, system, and cultural inefficiencies that attenuate execution capability. The framework operationalizes these constructs through founder-centric diagnostic scaling matrices and weighted friction analysis. The study contributes theoretically by integrating systems theory, organizational behavior, and execution science into a measurable execution architecture for startups and scaling ventures. Practically, the framework provides founders with a direct diagnostic tool for identifying execution bottlenecks, reducing operational drag, and improving organizational scalability. This study builds upon the author's prior practitioner-oriented work in North Star OS (Kurva, 2026), extending those concepts into a formal theoretical and measurable framework.

detail.abstract: Employee surveys make employees' experiences visible, but organizations routinely ask survey scores to do more than measurement can warrant: identify causes, select interventions, and demonstrate change. Existing research offers important components for these tasks, yet it treats score interpretation, causal diagnosis, intervention design, implementation, and outcome attribution as largely separate problems. This article develops an integrated inferential architecture for survey-informed organizational transformation. First, it distinguishes five validity layers and advances the Validity Non-Transfer Principle: evidence sufficient for one layer does not automatically warrant the next. Second, it theorizes diagnostic equifinality, in which different work-system structures generate the same survey pattern, making causal diagnosis a nonunique inverse problem. Third, it introduces discriminative knowledge integration, through which distributed experiential, institutional, analytic, and contextual knowledge is converted into evidence that can distinguish among competing causal candidates. Fourth, it explains how provisional diagnoses must be translated into intervention mechanisms, realized through implementation, and revised when observed outcomes diverge from predicted causal chains. These arguments are integrated in the Survey-Informed Causal Transformation Cycle (SICTC), a recursive model in which stage transition depends on inferential sufficiency rather than activity completion. The framework generates propositions about diagnosis, knowledge integration, mechanism fit, implementation mediation, outcome discrepancy, and organizational learning. It repositions employee surveys as inputs to a governed causal-learning process rather than as self-sufficient diagnostic devices.

title: The Audition That Never Ends: Civilizational Maskirovka, the Permanent Audition, and the Cognitive War Against Muslim Belonging in India (2014–2026)

detail.title: The Audition That Never Ends: Civilizational Maskirovka, the Permanent Audition, and the Cognitive War Against Muslim Belonging in India (2014–2026)
detail.abstract:
On January 22, 2024, Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of the Republic of India, a republic whose constitution begins with the word secular, performed a Hindu religious consecration ceremony on the site of a mosque demolished by a mob in 1992. The Supreme Court of India had found that demolition a wrongful act, and then awarded the land to those who committed it. The ceremony was broadcast to one billion people. India's 200 million Muslims watched.

What they watched was not a religious event with political implications. It was the culminating performance of a decade-long, institutionally comprehensive cognitive warfare campaign, the most systematic ever conducted by a formally democratic state against a religious minority within its own borders. The campaign operates across five dimensions simultaneously: visible violence, legal architecture, cultural erasure, political exclusion, and the progressive colonization of the Muslim self. Together they constitute what is named here the Permanent Audition, the condition in which a religious minority is required to perform loyalty continuously, on the majority's terms, without the possibility of completing the performance to a standard that removes the requirement to perform again.

Six new analytical concepts are developed across the empirical analysis, civilizational maskirovka, the permanent audition, the model minority cage, the sacred spectacle, historical unwriting, and demographic epistemic warfare, built at the intersection of cognitive warfare doctrine, relational dramaturgy, and political psychology. The analysis descends through five archaeological layers, from the most visible surface of the campaign to its deepest and most consequential work: the partial achievement of civilizational-scale cognitive surrender in a community of 200 million people. The theoretical contribution is the first complete account of the multi-generational cognitive warfare campaign as a distinct strategic form, a form whose ambition is not the defeat of a political movement but the reclassification of a civilization's claim to belong.

detail.abstract: The expectations channel of monetary policy is state dependent because households endogenously adjust attention to macroeconomic conditions. We develop a behavioral framework in which attention trades off forecast accuracy against cognitive cost, so monetary policy operates through an expectations multiplier. Using the Michigan Survey, we proxy attentiveness from whether households’ reading of business conditions matches realized outcomes, measured before identified policy shocks arrive. Policy news moves inflation beliefs primarily among attentive households, especially those with greater economic exposure; others barely respond. In the aggregate, pass-through scales with attentiveness and strengthens in recessions and high-uncertainty periods, making monetary transmission nonlinear.

title: Learning by Doing in the Adjacent Possible: Stepping Stones vs. Sticking Points

detail.title: Learning by Doing in the Adjacent Possible: Stepping Stones vs. Sticking Points
detail.abstract: Students of organizational adaptation have identified two fundamental constraints to attaining desirable configurations. The first is reachability: interdependence among elements of complex systems makes most configurations unattainable in a single move, confining movement to the "adjacent possible". The second is the necessity that learning requires doing: the payoff associated with a configuration can only be learned by enacting it, rather than by inference or observation. The two most commonly used computational models of organizational adaptation have, however, each assumed away one of these constraints. The NK model stresses that search is mostly restricted to the adjacent possible, but it assumes perfect visibility over payoffs in the local neighborhood-one can learn without doing. Conversely, the multi-armed bandit (MAB) model emphasizes that learning requires doing but assumes all alternatives are reachable in a single step-movement is not restricted to the adjacent possible. We develop a unified framework that incorporates both problems, and identify an overlooked regime of adaptation: localized learning-by-doing. In such settings, we show that payoff ruggedness can facilitate rather than hinder adaptation by creating valuable "stepping stones", and also that it makes the two canonical forms of exploration (distant search and non-greedy experimentation) operate as complements for search success but not for cumulative payoffs.

title: Optimal Top-k Identification from Pairwise Comparisons

detail.title: Optimal Top-k Identification from Pairwise Comparisons
detail.abstract: We study the active learning problem of fixed-confidence top-k identification from noisy pairwise comparisons. In this problem, an algorithm sequentially chooses pairs of items to compare, observes the outcomes, and stops when it can return the set of top-k items with error probability at most δ. The objective is to design such a δ-correct procedure that minimizes the expected number of comparisons (the sample complexity). This problem falls within the broader literature on fixed-confidence pure exploration in bandit models, where a common target is asymptotic optimality: the algorithm's expected sample complexity matches the information theoretic lower bound as δ → 0. Asymptotically optimal procedures have been developed for a range of fixed-confidence pure-exploration problems, however to the best of our knowledge, for top-1, or more generally top-k identification from pairwise comparisons under latent utility models an asymptotically optimal algorithm has not been established. In this setting, we develop such an algorithm. We characterize the structure of the lower bound and formulate it as a saddle-point problem. This structure enables a computationally efficient primal-dual procedure that learns the asymptotically optimal comparison allocation online. We then construct an adaptive comparison-allocation algorithm that tracks the allocation learned by the primal-dual procedure and prove it is asymptotically optimal.

title: Long-Run Intergenerational Effects of Social Security
affiliations: , University of Virginia - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Long-Run Intergenerational Effects of Social Security

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Both historically and today, support of aging parents has largely taken the form of in-kind transfers that require physical proximity, such as housing and caregiving. If Social Security substitutes for such support, it can relax constraints on where recipients' children live and work. We investigate the long-run intergenerational effects of the early Social Security program, exploiting within-occupation, cross-industry differences in coverage, and a new dataset linking parents to their children's later-life outcomes. We find that sons whose parents had greater predicted coverage moved farther from their childhood homes, earned more, and lived in better neighborhoods late in life. We find no such effects for daughters, who tended to provide forms of support less easily replaced by Social Security. The gains considerably exceeded the associated Social Security benefits for the average family, with migration to better-matched labor markets a likely key driver. We propose that the early program enabled families to realize gains from migration that were back-loaded, uncertain, and difficult to contract on.

title: The Impact of Central Bank Interest Rate Policy on International Capital Flows in Developing Countries
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Impact of Central Bank Interest Rate Policy on International Capital Flows in Developing Countries
detail.abstract: Using panel data from 25 developing countries from 2015 to 2025, this study aims to look at how central bank interest rate policies impact international capital flows in developing countries. Secondary data comes from each country's central bank, as well as from the World Bank, International Monetary Fund (IMF), Bank for International Settlements (BIS), and the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD). To perform this analysis, descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, panel data regression, and robustness tests were carried out using Fixed Effect Models and Self-Effect Models, as well as the Hausman Test. The results show that economic growth, exchange rate stability, and trade openness increase international capital flows, while inflation and external debt reduce capital flows. These results underscore the importance of strong monetary policy to maintain capital flow stability and strengthen the strength of emerging economies' financial systems.

title: When Fashion Fades: Designing Products Under Dynamic Pricing
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh - Katz Graduate School of Business

detail.title: When Fashion Fades: Designing Products Under Dynamic Pricing
detail.abstract: We study how a firm should choose the fashionability of a seasonal product sold through multiple pricing opportunities. Fashionability raises launch appeal but accelerates obsolescence, so the design choice affects both willingness to pay and how product value evolves over the selling season. We develop a finite-horizon model in which the common valuation state follows a geometric Brownian motion, customers with heterogeneous tastes arrive over time, and the firm dynamically prices the product after choosing fashionability. We show that the realized valuation state multiplicatively scales the revenue-to-go function, allowing the dynamic program to be expressed through normalized cutoffs. The optimal policy has weakly decreasing cutoffs and, when prices are evaluated at a common valuation state, generates a markdown structure. We characterize how pricing flexibility shapes design. Dynamic pricing, despite endogenously generating markdowns, does not uniformly favor more fashion-forward products. When demand arrives mostly early, dynamic pricing increases the value of preserving appeal for later selling opportunities, so static pricing weakly supports more fashionability. When demand arrives more gradually, dynamic pricing can support either more or less fashionability, depending on how later-period value enters the pricing comparison. We also bound the revenue loss from choosing fashionability under a static-pricing approximation and show that this loss can be large when demand arrives late and fashionability sharply shifts value toward launch. The results suggest that firms should coordinate fashionability with both pricing flexibility and the timing of demand-generation activities, such as preorders, drops, launch events, early-access programs, and rolling promotions.

title: Selling with AI Voice Agents: Does Disclosure Still Matter?
affiliations: University of Houston, Independent Researcher  and Independent Researcher

detail.title: Selling with AI Voice Agents: Does Disclosure Still Matter?
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) voice agents are increasingly deployed to sell to customers on the phone, prompting legislation that requires firms to disclose when customers are interacting with AI. Prior research, based on data collected before large language models (LLMs) became widely used, concluded that such disclosure harms sales performance because customers hold prejudices against AI. We revisit this question in the contemporary AI era through three studies. A randomized field experiment (N = 1,337 customers reached) shows that disclosing an AI voice agent no longer reduces conversion rates relative to nondisclosure. A second randomized field experiment (N = 366 customers reached) demonstrates, however, that AI voice agents still substantially underperform human sales agents. This is because contemporary AI voice agents continue to struggle with sales process discipline, including stakeholder qualification, value communication, persistence, and next-step orchestration. Finally, an online experiment (N = 238) reveals that customers largely recognize AI voice agents regardless of disclosure and evaluate disclosed and nondisclosed AI similarly. Customers are less willing to continue a conversation with them because they anticipate that these agents exhibit lower empathy, are less human-like, require greater effort, and signal greater firm insincerity. In summary, our findings suggest that mandatory AI disclosure may no longer be the primary challenge facing sales operations deploying AI voice agents. Instead, managers should focus on improving AI sales-process execution and selectively deploying AI voice agents while recognizing the value of human sales agents.

title: Can Advertising Correct Risk Beliefs? Evidence from U.S. Flood Insurance
affiliations: and University of Rochester - Simon Business School

detail.title: Can Advertising Correct Risk Beliefs? Evidence from U.S. Flood Insurance
detail.abstract: Flood risk is rising in the United States, yet flood insurance take-up remains persistently low, partly because households underestimate their flood risk. This underestimation reflects a broader belief-formation problem: households often have limited personal experience with low-probability, high-impact risks. This paper studies whether public advertising can serve as an information policy lever that corrects flood risk beliefs and increases insurance adoption in this setting. Using administrative records on 7.6 million National Flood Insurance Program policies, and survey measures of disaster beliefs, we estimate the effect of TV advertising on flood insurance enrollment. We find that advertising increases take-up by an economically meaningful margin, with larger responses among objectively riskier properties. Survey evidence shows that advertising raises perceived flood likelihood but does not shift beliefs about unrelated disasters, consistent with a flood-specific belief updating channel. Additional tests suggest that the effect is not driven by awareness or renewal mechanisms. Payout-based return calculations are positive, and we show that returns can be further improved by risk-based targeting. These results show that public advertising can be corrective when it moves underestimated risk beliefs toward objective risk and translates those updates into take-up among households facing greater exposure.

title: Strategic Hedging in a Multipolar Indo-Pacific: The Future of Bangladesh's Relations with China and Russia toward 2035

detail.title: Strategic Hedging in a Multipolar Indo-Pacific: The Future of Bangladesh's Relations with China and Russia toward 2035

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a policy analysis and scenario-based research based entirely on publicly available documents, official statements, and institutional databases. It does not involve human subjects, clinical trials, or animal experiments. Hence, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Bangladesh is entering a period in which its development requirements and geographic position increasingly intersect with great-power competition. China has become central to Bangladesh's import structure, infrastructure cooperation, industrial ambitions, and defence supply relationships, while Russia occupies a narrower but strategically consequential role through nuclear energy and long-term technical cooperation. At the same time, Bangladesh's export exposure to Western markets, geographic interdependence with India, and stated preference for an open and inclusive Indo-Pacific constrain any durable alignment with a single geopolitical bloc. This paper examines how Bangladesh's relations with China and Russia may evolve toward 2035. It uses a structured qualitative evidence synthesis and scenario-analysis framework drawing on official policy documents, bilateral statements, international institutional data, and peer-reviewed or established policy literature. The paper argues that Bangladesh's most plausible trajectory is neither alliance with a China-Russia axis nor geopolitical decoupling from Beijing and Moscow. Rather, Dhaka is likely to pursue a form of issue-based strategic hedging: deepening economic and infrastructure ties with China, preserving high-value energy cooperation with Russia, maintaining security and geographic accommodation with India, and protecting access to Western trade, finance, and technology. The sustainability of this strategy will depend on debt and project governance, sanctions compliance, defence diversification, maritime policy, export diversification, and institutional capacity. Three scenarios-disciplined multialignment, asymmetric China dependence, and bloc-pressure fragmentation-are developed for the period to 2035. The paper concludes that strategic autonomy for Bangladesh will depend less on diplomatic rhetoric than on reducing concentrated dependencies across trade, finance, energy, defence, and critical infrastructure.

title: Adaptive Ad Load Design for Sponsored Search Markets: Evidence, Theory, and Deployment
affiliations: and University of Washington

detail.title: Adaptive Ad Load Design for Sponsored Search Markets: Evidence, Theory, and Deployment
detail.abstract: Ad-load design is a central supply-side decision in sponsored search: more sponsored slots can raise revenue, but may crowd out organic results and degrade user outcomes. We study this trade-off using a large-scale randomized field experiment on an Android app store, where over five million users are exposed to one through six sponsored slots. Increasing ad load raises revenue by up to 43%, but reduces total search conversions by up to 5% and daily engagement by up to 2.2%. These average effects mask substantial heterogeneity: additional slots generate large revenue gains for high-ad-conversion queries, but little or negative marginal revenue for low-conversion queries. The trade-off also shifts within query as advertiser composition changes, such as brand-advertiser presence. Motivated by these findings, we design and deploy a novel adaptive algorithm-exploration-augmented Locally Adaptive Ad Load (e-LAAL). e-LAAL combines LAAL, a model-free query-level decision rule that updates ad-load recommendations using recent outcomes, with static exploration arms that maintain support and provide fixed-policy counterfactual benchmarks. We provide a finite-time dynamic-regret guarantee for the e-LAAL architecture. In a platform-level production deployment serving 22.3 million users and 77.6 million searches, e-LAAL improves the empirical revenue-conversion trade-off relative to deployed static benchmarks and outperforms uniform and historical query-dependent static benchmarks.

title: Algorithmic Impact Assessments as Advocacy Infrastructure: How Civil Society Can Move from Critique to Counter-Proposal

detail.title: Algorithmic Impact Assessments as Advocacy Infrastructure: How Civil Society Can Move from Critique to Counter-Proposal
detail.abstract: Civil society organizations have been effective critics of AI harms-documenting bias, surveillance overreach, discriminatory outcomes, and concentrations of power-but far less effective at proposing concrete alternative system designs that address the same operational problems AI deployers are trying to solve. This asymmetry between critical capacity and constructive capacity undermines civil society's influence in governance processes that increasingly reward actionable proposals over normative objections. This paper argues that Algorithmic Impact Assessments (AIAs)-structured evaluations of AI systems' potential effects on affected communities before deployment-can serve as the institutional mechanism for this transition, transforming advocacy from reactive opposition to proactive governance participation. Drawing on analysis of existing AIA frameworks (Canada's federal Algorithmic Impact Assessment Tool, New York City's Local Law 144 on automated employment decision tools, the EU AI Act's conformity assessment provisions), the paper introduces the Advocacy-Integrated AIA Model (AI-AIA)-an enhanced impact assessment methodology that civil society organizations can use not merely to identify problems but to specify alternative system designs, performance thresholds, monitoring requirements, and community accountability mechanisms. Empirical analysis of 23 civil society interventions across the US, EU, and India reveals that organizations employing counter-proposal strategies achieved measurable policy influence in 61 percent of cases, compared to 17 percent for organizations employing critique-only strategies. The paper argues that AIAs transform civil society's role from external critic to governance co-architect, but that this transformation requires investment in technical capacity, coalition infrastructure, and new organizational competencies that most advocacy organizations currently lack.

title: Brand Loyalty in The Digital Age: Does Brand Loyalty Still Exist?

detail.title: Brand Loyalty in The Digital Age: Does Brand Loyalty Still Exist?
detail.abstract: When consumers are able to compare products and prices online instantly and switch providers with a few clicks on their mobile phones, some researchers might argue that brand loyalty is dying. However, the research conducted by Frederick Reichheld suggests a different conclusion. Brand loyalty remains one of the most important drivers of sustainable business growth, and loyalty might be even more valuable today than it might have been before. “For effective supply chain management, firms should focus on the relationship with their immediate stakeholders in the supply chain, namely, suppliers and customers” (Ahsan et al., 2023). When a company is making a strategy for sustainable business growth, they need to have a focus on the customers and the suppliers. If there are disruptions, delays, or unexpected issues in the supply chain, this can have a negative effect on how the customers have their experience with the brand and can have an effect on their desire to become repeat purchasers or shop elsewhere next time. Reichheld believes that businesses need to prioritize creating loyal customers by building strong relationships with employees that communicate customers. By keeping profitable customers and growing relationships with them, the “loyalty leader” businesses identified by Reichheld performed better than their competitors in the stock market during the 1990s (Finnie, et al., 2002). Reichheld argued that businesses that focused on earning customer loyalty had better results when compared to those that just pursued new customers while not giving enough attention to existing ones. “With greater customer loyalty comes greater repurchase intentions, lower switching intentions, increased strength of preference, positive word-of-mouth, and a willingness to pay a premium price” (Bourdeau, et al., 2024). “Marketing technologies have become an integral part of the modern business, providing new ways to engage with customers. From social media platforms to marketing automation tools, marketing technology has transformed the way businesses approach customer engagement” (Vishnoi et al., 2026).

title: Work (dis)incentives for social benefit recipients in Greece
affiliations: Bank of Greece,  and Athens University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Work (dis)incentives for social benefit recipients in Greece

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Greece Economic Bulletin, Issue 63

detail.abstract: This paper investigates to what extent the strengthening of Greece's social safety net since the recent sovereign debt crisis has weakened work incentives for benefit recipients. Using the taxbenefit microsimulation model EUROMOD and its Hypothetical Household Tool (HHoT), we estimate participation tax rates (PTRs) and marginal effective tax rates (METRs) in 2024 for several stylised household types, accounting for the interaction between income taxes, social insurance contributions and means-tested benefits. Our results suggest that PTRs can reach near-prohibitive levels, particularly when transition into employment is associated with the withdrawal of the unemployment benefit. METRs are similarly distorted, exhibiting sharp kinks where means-tested benefits are abruptly withdrawn rather than gradually tapered. The paper concludes with some policy recommendations to improve work incentives, while preserving the anti-poverty gains achieved over the past decade.

title: Climate change and workers’ health: protecting workers against heat and other climate-related hazards
affiliations: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) and FAME Laboratory

detail.title: Climate change and workers’ health: protecting workers against heat and other climate-related hazards

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In a world of work increasingly shaped and disrupted by climate change, particular attention must be paid to workers who are directly exposed to its impacts. Workplace heat exposure has become one of the most significant — if not the most significant — climate change-related threats to workers' health in Europe. Yet important questions remain: how does heat affect workers? Which workers are the most affected ones? These are some of the central questions that the present report seeks to address.
The primary objective of this report is to identify and analyse the impacts that climate change-related hazards are having on workers' health and safety. Although the report places particular emphasis on workplace heat exposure, this focus does not imply an isolated approach. On the contrary, heat exposure is understood as part of a broader and interconnected climate reality that also includes other increasingly frequent and intense extreme weather events and environmental hazards. Accordingly, the report adopts a comprehensive perspective that seeks not only to identify the impacts of climate change on occupational health, but also to highlight the workers and sectors that are most vulnerable and disproportionately exposed to these physical hazards, as well as the broader consequences that such exposures may have for productivity, working conditions and job security.
At the same time, the report does not merely seek to identify the wide range of impacts that climate change is generating in relation to occupational health. In this context, the report develops a legal narrative demonstrating both the urgency and the necessity of strengthening protection against workplace heat exposure. Finally, the study concludes with a lege ferenda proposal incorporating an EU Directive on workplace heat exposure, aimed at establishing a more coherent, effective and harmonised framework of protection for workers across the European Union

title: The DEALS Framework: A Conceptual Model of Service-Sales Ambidexterity and Strategic Improvisation for B2C Frontline Sales and Service
affiliations: Universitas Prasetiya Mulya

detail.title: The DEALS Framework: A Conceptual Model of Service-Sales Ambidexterity and Strategic Improvisation for B2C Frontline Sales and Service

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a practicing sales trainer, and the DEALS Framework relates to the author's professional training practice. The preliminary field observations referenced in this paper were gathered during a professional engagement with a retail organization. The author received no financial incentive contingent on the paper's findings and declares no other personal or financial relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The preliminary evidence draws on an open-ended questionnaire completed by adult employees as part of an internal organizational training assessment; responses were subsequently anonymized and used illustratively for this conceptual paper. No personally identifying, sensitive, or health-related data were collected. Given the non-clinical, anonymized, and organizational nature of the data, formal institutional ethics-board approval was not required; the data are used illustratively rather than as formal empirical validation.
