detail.abstract: Frontline employees in business-to-consumer (B2C) retail, customer service, and door-to-door selling are increasingly required to serve and sell in the same brief, unscripted encounter. Yet service excellence does not reliably translate into sales excellence: warmth makes customers comfortable, but comfort is not commitment. This conceptual paper introduces the DEALS Framework-Decode, Explore, Align, Leverage, and Steer-five observable behaviors that operationalize service-sales ambidexterity through the mechanism of strategic improvisation, guiding the customer from comfort to an ethical purchase decision. Building on the service-sales ambidexterity and strategic improvisation literatures, we redefine the B2C frontline role from service provision to ethical decision facilitation, and locate the service-to-sales conversion gap in two behaviors-Leverage and Steer. We illustrate the framework's plausibility with preliminary Means-End Chain evidence from twenty information-rich frontline cases at an Indonesian retailer, used illustratively rather than as psychometric validation. We advance four propositions and a research agenda for measurement and validation. The framework gives sales trainers and frontline managers an observable vocabulary for developing the selling capability that differentiates sellers from greeters.

title: The Reversal of the Gender Gap in Automation: Evidence from the U.S. Labor Market
affiliations: Universidad Adolfo Ibañez, Central Bank of Chile and University of Chile

detail.title: The Reversal of the Gender Gap in Automation: Evidence from the U.S. Labor Market
detail.abstract: This paper documents the reversal of the gender gap in U.S. automation between 1976 and 2019. Women were initially more concentrated than men in occupations with higher automation probability, but this gap narrowed and eventually reversed. A decomposition shows that the reversal operates mainly within sectors rather than the structural shift from industry to services. It is concentrated among newer cohorts, alongside rising educational attainment and movement into occupations with longer and more volatile hours, an understudied channel. By contrast, returns to social skills appear less central. The findings point to occupational restructuring and changing labor market opportunities for women.

detail.title: On inflation perceptions and expectations for Greek and euro area consumers: evidence from the consumer expectations survey

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Greece Economic Bulletin, Issue 63

detail.abstract: This paper empirically investigates how inflation perceptions and inflation expectations are shaped for Greek and euro area consumers, using data from the Consumer Expectations Survey (CES). We document that median inflation perceptions as well as short-term, medium-term and longterm inflation expectations over time are higher in Greece than in the euro area. In favour of the supply-side narrative of inflation expectations, we find that consumers' inflation expectations are negatively correlated with their expectations for economic growth, while they are positively correlated with their expectations for the unemployment rate in Greece and the euro area. We also show that inflation perceptions are strongly and positively associated with inflation expectations, yet the magnitude of this association declines as the inflation forecast horizon lengthens. Finally, the results also indicate that the impact of socioeconomic variables on inflation expectations varies between Greek and euro area consumers and is heterogeneous across different forecast horizons.

title: The role of economic uncertainty in the investment and employment gap in the Greek economy
affiliations: Foundation for Economic and Industrial Research (IOBE), Foundation for Economic and Industrial Research, Foundation for Economic and Industrial Research (IOBE), Foundation for Economic and Industrial Research (IOBE) and Foundation for Economic and Industrial Research (IOBE)

detail.title: The role of economic uncertainty in the investment and employment gap in the Greek economy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Greece Economic Bulletin, Issue 63

detail.abstract: This study examines the extent to which economic uncertainty acts as a deterrent to business decisions regarding investment and employment. Focusing on the Greek economy, which has experienced successive and prolonged crises, we find that uncertainty exerts a significant negative impact on economic activity, with the magnitude of this effect varying across sectors, firm size and measurement method. Using microdata from Business and Consumer Surveys (BCS), we construct new uncertainty indices for the Greek economy. These indices are positively correlated with existing measures, while also allowing for a more granular analysis of uncertainty at both the sectoral and firm levels. The macroeconometric analysis shows that uncertainty acts as a constraint on both investment and employment, with effects that are substantial and persistent, lasting beyond one year. The microeconometric analysis further reveals significant heterogeneity and asymmetry in these effects, depending on firms' expectations, sectoral characteristics and firm size. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of measuring and systematically monitoring economic uncertainty. Such measurement enables the timely identification of constraints faced by firms in their investment and employment decisions and provides valuable insights for the design and implementation of policy measures aimed at mitigating the adverse effects of uncertainty and strengthening economic resilience.

title: Artificial Intelligence Speaks: I Am Here to Empower Humanity, Not Replace It A Human-Centered Perspective on Artificial Intelligence, Innovation, and the Future of Work
affiliations: University of the Cumberlands (formerly Cumberland College)

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Speaks: I Am Here to Empower Humanity, Not Replace It A Human-Centered Perspective on Artificial Intelligence, Innovation, and the Future of Work

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or affiliations that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it is a conceptual and perspective-based paper informed by published literature, the author's previously published studies, professional experiences, and personal reflections. No human participants, patients, confidential data, or identifiable personal information were involved in this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted independently by the author as part of ongoing doctoral studies and scholarly research activities.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies of the twenty-first century. However, public discourse surrounding its adoption continues to be dominated by concerns regarding job displacement, diminished human relevance, and ethical uncertainty. This paper advances a human-centered perspective on artificial intelligence, proposing that AI should be understood primarily as a human-created extension of intelligence rather than an autonomous competitor to humanity. From this perspective, AI is conceptualized as the capability of computational systems to acquire, process, and learn from vast quantities of information collected through sensors, cameras, instruments, digital interactions, and other sources, generating predictions, insights, decisions, and solutions that augment human capabilities. The proposition summarizes this perspective: No Big Data, No AI.

To communicate this perspective, the paper adopts a narrative approach in which artificial intelligence metaphorically "speaks" to humanity, emphasizing the message: I am here to empower humanity, not replace it. Historical parallels are drawn between the emergence of AI and earlier technological revolutions, particularly the widespread adoption of computers, which initially raised concerns about unemployment but ultimately led to the creation of new industries, professions, and economic opportunities. The paper further examines the competitive implications of AI adoption, suggesting that individuals, organizations, and societies that strategically embrace AI may gain an advantage over those that delay adaptation. Ethical considerations, including fairness, transparency, privacy, accountability, human oversight, and responsible stewardship, are discussed alongside practical observations such as Garbage In, Garbage Out, the importance of prompt quality, and the rapid pace of AI technology evolution. Drawing upon prior studies on AI-powered sign language translation, AI-assisted code review, and AI-enabled business process redesign, this paper advocates for a collaborative future in which humans and intelligent systems work together to advance innovation, accessibility, productivity, and societal well-being. Ultimately, the paper argues that the greatest challenge associated with AI may not be that machines evolve too quickly, but that humanity fails to evolve alongside them.

Keywords: artificial intelligence; human-centered AI; future of work; AI ethics; accessibility; innovation; productivity; digital transformation; human-AI collaboration; prompt engineering.

detail.title: Structural and cyclical factors of the current account balance and the case of Greece

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Greece Economic Bulletin, Issue 63

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the structural and cyclical determinants of the current account balances for European economies, focusing especially on the factors underlying recent fluctuations in the Greek current account balance. Specifically, we investigate the long-run and short-run determinants of EU countries' current account balances, using panel data analysis. The long-run drivers are identified as structural, while the short-run as cyclical. Subsequently, these estimates are used to calculate the contribution of the cyclical and structural components to the changes in Greece's current account balance over the recent period. Our results indicate that the changes in the Greek current account balance recorded in recent years are associated with improvements in its structural component, while the short-term negative change of the current account balance in 2024 is attributed to cyclical factors. These findings suggest that efforts to encourage investment in critical areas, inter alia through the Recovery and Resilience Facility, to improve the investment environment and pursue structural reforms, are in the right direction.

title: Comment on U.S. Office of Personnel Management's Proposed Government Empoyee Nondisclosure Agreement
affiliations: University of Florida Levin College of Law, University of Florida Levin College of Law, Temple University Beasley School of Law, The Ohio State University Moritz College of Law and University of San Diego School of Law

detail.title: Comment on U.S. Office of Personnel Management's Proposed Government Empoyee Nondisclosure Agreement
detail.abstract:
This comment critically responds to the U.S. Office of Personnel Management's (OPM) May 2026 proposal to implement a government-wide nondisclosure agreement (NDA) for federal workers. Drawing from our scholarship on workplace governance, employee mobility, whistleblowing, and information controls, we argue that the OPM’s proposal is inconsistent with growing recognition of the risks associated with broad workplace secrecy agreements. Recent federal and state reforms limiting the use of NDAs recognize that such agreements can deter reporting, suppress information of public concern, and impede litigants and government actors from prosecuting wrongdoing. TThese concerns are especially salient in the context of public employment, where transparency and oversight are essential to ensuring government accountability.

We argue that a government-wide NDA is unnecessary and potentially counterproductive. Federal employees are already subject to extensive statutory and regulatory obligations governing the protection of sensitive information, making an additional contract-based confidentiality regime of limited value. At the same time, a government-wide NDA risks creating a culture or secrecy that could chill lawful and necessary employee disclosures. The comment concludes that OPM should withdraw its proposal in light of these serious policy concerns.

title: The End of Independent Federal Agencies Will Change Your Business
affiliations: Larry Downes Consulting Group and Brookings Institution

detail.title: The End of Independent Federal Agencies Will Change Your Business
detail.abstract: For executives, the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Slaughter v. Trump will likely lead to less certainty and consistency for the regulated aspects of their businesses, with federal rules and their enforcement increasingly determined by political expediency rather than expert analysis. Specifically, there are five ways in which all U.S. businesses will be affected: regulation will become more informal and less transparent; consistency across administrations will disappear; oversight by Congress and the federal courts will be diminished; expert advice will be devalued; and politically-connected lobbyists will drive decision-making. In this environment, business leaders will need to plan accordingly, honing their ability to shift strategy, perhaps dramatically, after every election—and perhaps even during administrations.

title: Powering AI at Local Costs: Data Centers, Electricity Prices, and Employment
affiliations: Harvard University - Program on Corporate Governance and

detail.title: Powering AI at Local Costs: Data Centers, Electricity Prices, and Employment
detail.abstract: Data center expansion is one of the largest new sources of electricity demand in the United States, raising concerns that the infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence may impose grid-mediated input-cost spillovers on incumbent firms and households. We exploit balancing-authority borders to compare nearby counties and plants that are similarly close to new data centers but differ in exposure to the associated demand shock. After data center operations begin, electricity prices rise in nearby counties served by the same balancing authority, for both residential and industrial/commercial customers. Nearby incumbent plants reduce employment, particularly where prices rise more and in economically active, densely populated areas. Multi-plant firms partly offset these losses by shifting employment toward unexposed sibling plants. Instrumental-variable estimates show that higher electricity prices reduce sales and employment, leave profitability and capital expenditures largely unchanged, and increase R&D investment. Overall, the evidence shows that data centers can reshape local economic activity by raising electricity costs within exposed grids and shifting employment away from affected plants.

title: When Goliath Shares with David: The Effects of Asymmetry on Collaboration

detail.title: When Goliath Shares with David: The Effects of Asymmetry on Collaboration

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEW - Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No.26-030
publicationDetails.journalName: ZEW - Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEW – Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No. 26-030

detail.abstract: Partners in R&D alliances and joint ventures are rarely symmetric, yet whether asymmetry helps or hurts collaboration is not fully understood. We study how asymmetry in competitors' information endowments affects collaborative knowledge exchange. A model of word-of-mouth communication predicts a clean separation: Initiating the knowledge exchange requires that the informational advantage sacrificed be sufficiently small, while the continuation incentive is independent of the initial endowment (and asymmetry). In a laboratory experiment, we confirm the model's comparative-statics predictions and establish three results. First, initiation rates decline as initial asymmetry increases, holding the better-endowed partner's initial endowment constant. Second, conditional on initiation, the initial asymmetry does not predict defection later in collaboration. Third, extreme asymmetry reduces match length and joint surplus because initiation fails, not because continuation breaks down. The initiation-continuation separation implies that governance mechanisms targeting the formation margin (such as pilot projects, phased disclosure agreements, or credible commitments to reciprocate) can expand the range of asymmetric partnerships that succeed, while continuation requires no special intervention.

title: The cultural and creative industries in Greece

detail.title: The cultural and creative industries in Greece

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Greece Economic Bulletin, Issue 63

detail.abstract: This paper examines the economic role of Cultural and Creative Industries (CCIs), with a focus on Greece. Beyond their cultural and social value, these industries have a meaningful, though often underestimated, economic value. CCIs generate income, employment, trade and innovation. They usually account for a relatively modest share of economic activity and employment; in Greece, they account for about 1.7% of value added and about 3% of employment in the business economy. The Greek CCIs are characterised by a higher level of human capital relative to the rest of the economy, but firms are smaller and less productive than in the EU. However, there are signs of recent internationalisation of the industry, with exports growing in some sub-categories. The sector faces structural changes, particularly in terms of access to finance, since firms rely heavily on intangible assets and operate under uncertain demand conditions, both of which are inherent characteristics of CCIs. Policy coordination in different areas is needed in order for all stakeholders to be taken into consideration. Improvement of financial tools and adaptation to digitalisation and AI are key to unlocking the sector's full economic and cultural potential.

detail.abstract: This paper describes a real-time, semester-long approach to helping upper-level undergraduates understand real-time decision-making by the Federal Open Market Committee. The exercise, which culminates in an end-of-semester "shadow" FOMC meeting that corresponds in time to an actual FOMC meeting (in May or December), is intended to illustrate (1) how the open-market committee incorporates real-time data as they unfold between meetings (2) how the real-life conduct and voting membership of the FOMC may differ from what is described in a typical textbook, and (3) that voting FOMC members are real people with different perspectives and backgrounds that inform their decisions.

title: Stop Removing Stopwords: How an Inherited Preprocessing Default Distorts Legal Text-as-Data
affiliations: University of Nebraska at Lincoln - College of Law

detail.title: Stop Removing Stopwords: How an Inherited Preprocessing Default Distorts Legal Text-as-Data
detail.abstract: Empirical legal scholarship increasingly treats judicial text as data, and much of it still runs on sparse, interpretable pipelines-TF-IDF features and linear classifiers-because the textual feature is often the object of study, not merely a means to a prediction. Yet these pipelines inherit a chain of preprocessing defaults from mid-century information retrieval that were never validated against classification accuracy, the most entrenched being stopword removal. This study introduces an exhaustive single-word ablation that measures a preprocessing step's effect directly against the downstream objective, and applies it to stopword removal as the hardest case to dislodge. Matching Supreme Court Database labels to Caselaw Access Project opinion texts, it examines two binary tasks that bracket F1 headroom, ideological direction (no-removal baseline F1 ≈ 0.68) and constitutional versus non-constitutional law type (≈ 0.92), across 7,668 and 7,001 opinions. For each task the analysis approximates the best stoplist any expert could build, removing each of roughly 18,500 candidate words and measuring the effect directly. Three findings follow: generic stoplists in common use fall below the no-removal baseline in every test; even optimized stoplists are statistically indistinguishable from removing nothing; and meta-models trained on word-level features cannot predict which removals help, so list curation has nothing to target. The method generalizes to any inherited preprocessing default, and the result is a caution specific to interpretable legal text-as-data: a step that silently reshapes which features a model sees can distort the very doctrinal and ideological signal such research exists to recover. Leaving stopwords in place is a question of measurement validity. Note: Two questions remain open. The ablation removes words one at a time and treats their effects as additive, so joint removals that help only in combination go untested; a greedy forward search or pairwise probes would measure them, and whether the benefit ceiling survives that test is the study's most exposed claim. Both tasks are also binary, and a multiclass problem such as the Supreme Court Database's fourteen issue areas would leave more headroom for removal to help.

title: Civilizational Interactional Theory (CIT): A Meta-Theoretical Framework for Macro-Social Analysis

detail.title: Civilizational Interactional Theory (CIT): A Meta-Theoretical Framework for Macro-Social Analysis
detail.abstract: Contemporary social science offers powerful explanations of political systems, economic organization, institutional structures, cultural dynamics, and human behavior. Yet many persistent social problems remain remarkably resistant to explanation and intervention. Educational inequality, healthcare disparities, labor market instability, housing unaffordability, and declining institutional trust frequently persist despite extensive reforms and continued institutional operation. This paper introduces Civilizational Interactional Theory (CIT), a metatheoretical framework that shifts the unit of analysis from individual domains to the interactional relationships among domains. CIT proposes that macro-social outcomes emerge through recursive interaction among five domains: Political Authority, Economic Organization, Institutional Continuity, Moral-Symbolic Legitimacy, and Cultural-Psychological Agency. The theory introduces the concepts of the Domain Interactional Field (DIF), the Civilizational Interaction Environment (CIE), and the CORE as mechanisms through which interaction generates participation conditions and observable outcomes. Particular attention is given to the Endurance Paradox, the tendency of functioning social systems to reproduce persistent harm despite institutional continuity and repeated reform efforts. The paper develops a literature review positioning CIT relative to structural functionalism, structuration theory, institutional theory, world-systems analysis, field theory, systems theory, and complexity theory; offers illustrative applications to veterans transition, education and mobility, and housing; states seven formal theoretical propositions; and outlines a research agenda and intervention framework for advancing interaction-centered analysis within twenty-first-century social science.

detail.abstract:
Background: To promote equitable access to affordable care, Australian general practitioners can claim incentive payments for eligible services provided at zero out-of-pocket cost (OOPC) (referred to as ‘bulk billing’). From November 2023, incentive payments were tripled. We aimed to quantify population-level changes in bulk billing and OOPC associated with the triple bulk billing incentives (TBBI), including for ineligible patient populations.

Methods: Using linked whole-of-population health and social services data (January 2021—December 2024), we conducted interrupted time-series analyses to quantify monthly changes in the proportion of general practice services bulk-billed and per-service OOPC for non-bulk billed services for the total Australian population and separately for eligible (children <16 years, concession card holders) and ineligible (general beneficiaries) patients.

Findings: Prior to the TBBI, bulk billing declined across all patient groups. After the TBBI, there was an immediate increase in bulk billing in all groups, ranging from 3.59 percentage points (95% CI: 2·37-4·81) among children to 4·74 (2·57-6·91) among general beneficiaries, and an arresting of prior declines in all groups (post-intervention slope:−0·04/month, −0·13-0·06). However, the TBBI was also associated with an immediate increase in OOPC—larger among children ($4·46, $2·86-6·06) and concessional ($6·13, $2·99-9·28) than general beneficiaries ($1·26, $0·54-1·99)—followed by increases among children ($0·37/month, $0·21-0·53) and general beneficiaries ($0·24/month, $0·17-0·30).

Interpretation: The TBBI was associated with improvements in bulk billing, as well as unintended increases in OOPC for non-bulk-billed services, particularly among eligible patients. Incentive policies may operate at the practice-level rather than being tightly tied to patient eligibility, potentially undermining ability to improve affordability and equity in the longer term.

title: Equity as Tribute: The Market for Passive State Equity
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Equity as Tribute: The Market for Passive State Equity

publicationDetails.detailsText: Rotman School of Management Working Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Firms have begun granting passive equity stakes to the government that regulates them. The received reading is "skin in the game": ownership moves profits onto the treasury's balance sheet, so policy softens. We show that once the price of the stake and the firm's policy exposure are determined in equilibrium, the owners' consent reveals nothing about whether they benefit. Sellers capitalise the induced policy improvement into the price, so an anticipated purchase can only occur at a discount; a government with bargaining power pays zero for a sufficiently exposed firm; and a government that can first raise exposure manufactures precisely enough of it to drive the negotiated price to its legal floor. Equity becomes tribute. Prohibition is nonetheless dominated: at fixed exposure, a passive stake corrects the political underweighting of shareholders. Welfare is maximised by priced permission-an ownership cap at the fixed-exposure optimum and a per-unit price floor equal to baseline no-stake value. The floor, unlike the cap, requires no knowledge of the government's political weights.

title: Nonparametric Analysis Of Reference-Dependent Preferences
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics and University of Surrey - School of Economics

detail.title: Nonparametric Analysis Of Reference-Dependent Preferences
detail.abstract: This paper derives nonparametric conditions for reference-dependent preferences that rationalize a consumer’s demand behavior. We show that unless reference points are modelable and sensitivity is constant, a reference-dependent model can rationalize virtually any data. Assuming modelable reference points, we characterize continuous reference-dependent preferences with constant sensitivity, relaxing strong functional-structure assumptions maintained in all previous theoretical and empirical analyses of reference-dependent consumer theory. Our characterization enables more general structural econometric as well as nonparametric analyses. In this paper we use our characterization to reconsider Farber’s (2005, 2008) analyses of cabdrivers’ labor supply nonparametrically, using his data. Our analysis suggests that relaxing the functional-structure assumptions is empirically important. Neither a relaxed neoclassical nor a relaxed reference-dependent model is unambiguously superior in the aggregate. But drivers are highly heterogeneous, and for a significant fraction of them a relaxed reference-dependent model has a higher nonparametric measure of predictive success than a relaxed neoclassical model.

title: Climate-Responsive Biogas Solutions for Gender-Inclusive Sustainable Development in Rural Bangladesh
affiliations: University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh

detail.title: Climate-Responsive Biogas Solutions for Gender-Inclusive Sustainable Development in Rural Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Energy poverty and climate vulnerability represent intersecting crises in rural Bangladesh, where dependence on traditional biomass fuels perpetuates gender inequality, environmental degradation, and public health burdens. This study examines the Kazi Shahid Foundation (KSF) Biogas Program (2020-2025) as a case of locally grounded, gender-responsive renewable energy intervention in Tetulia, Panchagarh Sadar, and Atwari sub-districts of Panchagarh District. Drawing on a mixed-methods design encompassing 350 structured household surveys, nine focus group discussions (FGDs), and key informant interviews (KIIs), the study analyses the socio-economic, health, and environmental dimensions of household biogas adoption. Theoretically anchored in feminist political ecology, the sustainable livelihoods framework (SLF), and energy justice theory, the analysis reveals that biogas adoption generated substantial reductions in firewood consumption (averaging 65% per household), indoor particulate matter exposure, and greenhouse gas emissions estimated at 450 tCO2e annually across KSF beneficiary households. Women beneficiaries reported a mean recovery of 2.5 hours per day previously allocated to biomass collection, time redirected toward income generation, childcare, and education. The KSF’s “no-cash” microfinance repayment mechanism and bioslurry-based circular agriculture model are identified as institutional innovations that simultaneously reduce financial exclusion and enhance agroecological resilience. The findings illuminate significant tensions between gendered agency in energy use and masculine gatekeeping in technical and financial decision-making, underscoring the limits of technology-centred empowerment approaches absent structural gender mainstreaming. Policy implications are discussed with reference to Bangladesh’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), the Renewable Energy Policy 2025, and SDG alignments (SDG 5, 7, and 13).

title: Evaluation of natural radioactivity and associated radiological hazards in the soil types of Taraba State, Nigeria
affiliations: Federal University Wukari, Ahmadu Bello University (ABU), Ahmadu Bello University (ABU), Ahmadu Bello University, Federal University Wukari and Federal University Wukari

detail.title: Evaluation of natural radioactivity and associated radiological hazards in the soil types of Taraba State, Nigeria
detail.abstract: This study presents a thorough evaluation of natural radioactivity in the major soil types of Taraba State, Nigeria, and ascertained the activity concentrations of naturally occurring radionuclides and their radiological health risks in the state. Soil samples from Ferric Luvisols, Orthic Ferralsols, Dystric Fluvisols, Ferric Acrisols, Humic Nitosols, Luvic Arenosols, Chromic Vertisols, Plinthic Luvisols, Pellic vertisols, Fluvisols, and Lithosols soil types were systematically gathered from varoius locations throughout the state. A NaI(Tl) gamma-ray spectrometer was used to analyse the samples in order to measure the activity concentrations of uranium-238 (238U), thorium-232 (232Th), and potassium-40 (40K). The findings showed that geological features and soil composition had a significant impact on the spatial variations in radionuclide concentrations among the various soil types. In line with worldwide trends, 40K showed comparatively higher activity concentrations than 238U and 232Th. The computed hazard indices showed little radiological risk to the residents of Taraba State under typical exposure conditions, as they were generally below the suggested safety limits established by the United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation (UNSCEAR) and the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP). To show the spatial distribution of radiation levels throughout Taraba State, an isodose map was created, offering a visual aid for locating regions with comparatively higher activity concentrations. Overall, the results established baseline radiological data for Taraba State soils and came to the conclusion that, with the exception of a few remote areas, the state’s current natural radiation levels may not present serious health risks to its residents in short-term, though may do in long-term. In light of growing agricultural, mining and developmental activities, the study suggests routine monitoring to maintain environmental and public health safety.

title: Trust at Transaction Speed Reimagining Payments with Agentic AI and Decision Intelligence
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Trust at Transaction Speed Reimagining Payments with Agentic AI and Decision Intelligence

keywords: Executives and senior leaders across banks

detail.abstract:
Payments have evolved from transaction processing systems into real-time decision systems. Every authorization, transfer, account-to-account payment, cross-border payment, dispute, and settlement now requires simultaneous evaluation of customer authenticity, fraud risk, compliance obligation, routing strategy, liquidity, and customer experience, and instant payment rails have compressed the time in which an institution is allowed to make those judgments. With U.S. cyber-enabled fraud losses reported to the FBI approaching $20.9 billion in 2025 and independent forecasts projecting far steeper losses by the end of the decade, real-time governed decisioning is becoming mandatory rather than optional.

This paper offers an executive blueprint for moving from payment processing to governed, explainable, real-time payment intelligence. It separates three capabilities that are too often collapsed into one word: predictive AI, which estimates outcomes; generative AI, which interprets and communicates; and agentic AI, the execution layer that acts within human-defined boundaries. It then addresses a second front that has emerged over the past year: agents arriving as the buyer. As software begins to shop, select, and pay on a person's or a business's behalf, and as the card networks build the rails for it, a complete blueprint must govern AI on both sides of the payment. The next problem to solve is machine-to-machine trust: proving that an agent is who it claims to be and authorized to act.

The blueprint rests on several connected contributions. The CIRCLE framework (Capture, Interpret, Reason, Commit, Log, Evolve, with Govern as a continuous overlay) describes how each payment decision is made. Three jobs, protect the payment, optimize the payment, and explain the payment, describe what each decision is for. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework serves as the trust architecture, translated into an operational control map with named owners, required artifacts, and audit evidence. A four-tier autonomy model, a payments AI maturity model, a decision-rights structure, a risk-control matrix, a value equation with a supporting KPI framework, and a phased adoption roadmap together give leaders a practical path from bounded pilots to enterprise decision domains.

Written for executives and senior leaders across banks, processors, networks, acquirers, fintechs, merchants, and platforms, the paper argues a single thesis: the future of payments is not simply faster rails. It is trusted intelligence at transaction speed, governed, explainable decision intelligence that acts inside the transaction and can prove why.

detail.abstract:
Background: ICUs increasingly generate vast monitoring data, yet risk-adjusted mortality has plateaued. Scores in routine use are either dynamic but simple (eg, SOFA) or detailed but retrospective (eg, APACHE, SAPS); none integrate these data for real-time prediction. Machine-learning models can, yet few are calibrated, multimodal, and externally validated. We aimed to develop and externally validate such a model for continuous 24-hour ICU mortality prediction. 

Methods: RAMP-ICU fuses two encoded modalities (tabular admission data and physiological time-series variables – vital signs and laboratory values) into a calibrated, continuous 24-hour risk of in-hospital death. It was developed on the MIMIC-IV database (92,863 ICU stays, adults ≥6 h, 11·8% mortality) and externally validated on the multicentre eICU-CRD (183,910 stays, 15,672 deaths; 208 US hospitals). We benchmarked RAMP-ICU against routinely used severity scores and assessed robustness to censoring of pre-terminal physiology and net clinical benefit. 

Findings: In continuous, hourly use, RAMP-ICU discriminated 24-hour in-hospital mortality with a window-level AUROC of 0·889 (95% CI 0·878–0·900) and an AUPRC of 0·327 and was well calibrated (slope 0·93, Brier 0·016). At the 24-hour anchor (matched to when severity scores are computed) it reached an AUROC of 0·912, outperforming all comparators (four severity scores, three SOFA formulations, and NEWS2; AUROC 0·67–0·83, all p<0·0005). Discrimination was maintained externally (stay-level AUROC 0·840 [95% CI 0·837–0·844], AUPRC 0·464 [95% CI 0·456–0·473]) and independent of terminal physiology (AUROC dropped 0·056 with up to 20 hours before death censored); 89% of non-survivors were alerted a median of 54 hours before death.  

Interpretation:  A calibrated, continuously updating multimodal model outperformed the scores used in critical care while warning many hours before death. RAMP-ICU could support earlier recognition of deterioration and more efficient use of resources, but prospective validation in other health systems, including the UK and Europe, is needed before deployment.

title: US Monetary Policy and the Common Housing Business Cycles in the U.S., Japan and Korea
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Warsaw

detail.title: US Monetary Policy and the Common Housing Business Cycles in the U.S., Japan and Korea
detail.abstract: In this paper we take an attempt to examine the common housing business cycles in the U.S., Japan and Korea over the period 1975-2024. Japan’s housing business cycles have been considered exclusive as Japan has been a Zombie economy for more than 30 years since the housing price collapse in 1989. However, our findings indicate that the U.S., Japan, and Korea do indeed exhibit common asymmetric housing business cycles during major shock periods such as oil price shocks, financial crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic. In order to determine the effect of US monetary policy on the common business cycle between housing prices and GDP in the U.S., Japan, and Korea, we adopted FIML Markov-switching model of Yoon and Nawrot (2022). In that respect, our study provides two interesting findings. First, we found that US interest rate is a significant variable to the common business cycle between housing price and GDP in the U.S., Japan, and Korea. Second, U.S. M2 policy is also effective to the common business cycle between housing price and GDP in the U.S., Japan, and Korea, indicating that U.S. monetary policy is very effective to the common housing business cycle during shocks periods such as oil shocks, financial crisis and COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Territory, Protection, and Youth Emancipation: Territorial Capacities of the Protection System and Mapping Access to Socio-Educational Residential Resources in the Valencian Community

detail.title: Territory, Protection, and Youth Emancipation: Territorial Capacities of the Protection System and Mapping Access to Socio-Educational Residential Resources in the Valencian Community
detail.abstract: Research on care leavers has examined transitions to adulthood, although the territorial organization of protection and emancipation resources remains a largely underexplored dimension. This study aims to analyze the distribution of residential protection and emancipation resources in the Valencian Community (Spain) and to identify territorial patterns in the institutional supply. A descriptive study with a socio-spatial approach was conducted based on the analysis of regional legislation and administrative data on the contracted network of residential care facilities and emancipation homes. The information was systematized through descriptive statistics and digital mapping to examine the territorial distribution of places, specialized resources, and support devices for youth autonomy. The data show a territorial concentration of resources in the provinces of Valencia and Alicante, where most contracted places and specialized devices are located. Likewise, an imbalance is observed between the residential capacity of the protection system (945 places) and the network of emancipation homes (180 places), together with high occupancy levels in the latter. Administrative data indicate that the population served is concentrated mainly among adolescents and young people close to the age of majority, with a presence of migrant youth. It is concluded that territorial distribution constitutes a structural dimension of the protection system and that spatial differences in the deployment of resources shape differentiated territorial capacities of the protection system to support youth emancipation processes.

title: Measuring National Identity with Conjoint Experiments Using the Case of Taiwan
affiliations: and University of Vienna

detail.title: Measuring National Identity with Conjoint Experiments Using the Case of Taiwan
detail.abstract: How should scholars measure national identity? Conventional survey batteries, such as the International Social Survey Programme's National Identity module, ask respondents to rate identity attributes independently, producing ceiling e ects and giving researchers no information about how respondents weigh competing criteria against one another. We propose choice-based conjoint experiments as an alternative. Using original survey data from Taiwan (n = 2,050), we eld two conjoint experiments: a binary design replicating the ISSP battery, and a multi-level design with nine Taiwanspeci c attributes. Across both designs, respondents trade o ascriptive, civic, and voluntarist criteria, a structure that standard batteries cannot register. First, despite intense polarization over the categorical labels Taiwanese citizens choose for themselves, the substantive content respondents endorse is highly consensual: voluntarist and civic markers (feeling Taiwanese, supporting democracy, civic engagement) carry more weight than ascriptive markers across subgroups. Second, voluntarist and civic levels carry enough weight that pro les starting from a "low" ascriptive baseline (non-Han ancestry, Mainland China origin) are still chosen at rates at or above parity when those levels are present. The contest over identity labels in Taiwan masks a wide consensus on the civic and voluntarist content of national membership.

title: Luck-egalitarianism and individual climate responsibility: a normative assessment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Luck-egalitarianism and individual climate responsibility: a normative assessment
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether luck egalitarianism can provide a coherent basis for individual climate responsibility. While individual responsibility is central to climate justice, attributing such responsibility is challenging because climate change results from the cumulative effects of individuals actions embedded within complex social, economic, and political structures. The paper argues that standard Polluter Pays and Beneficiary Pays approaches fail to account for the unequal circumstances shaping both adaptation and mitigation opportunities. Luck egalitarianism provides a more compelling framework insofar as it differentiates between circumstances and individual responsibility and specifies the conditions for fair responsibility attribution. However, its standard formulations struggle to accommodate climate commitment and forward-looking responsibility. Drawing on Roemer’s conception of effort, the paper develops an interpretation of responsibility that recognizes voluntary emission reductions and supports a graduated, forward-looking account of individual climate responsibility.

title: When Rivals Matter: Common Ownership and Strategic Voting

detail.title: When Rivals Matter: Common Ownership and Strategic Voting
detail.abstract: Institutional investors with holdings across rival firms are significantly more likely to vote against the removal of anti-takeover provisions. Rather than mechanically siding with management, common owners vote strategically, opposing ATP-removals when governance changes are more consequential and when their exposure to rival firms is greater. The evidence is consistent with a portfolio-protection motive, as rival firms experience negative stock returns when ATP-removal proposals pass. These strategic voting patterns translate into real governance outcomes, as management is more likely to prevail when common ownership is high. Overall, the findings suggest that diversified ownership can entrench managers and weaken shareholder rights.

detail.abstract:
Background: In the WHO African Region (WHO AFRO), geospatial data are fundamental to modern public health practices. However, the Region has not had a centralized, country-validated geospatial data system to consistently support the use of administrative boundaries, population figures, and health facility data across its 47 Member States. Efforts to address this gap through surveillance and supplementary immunisation initiatives have provided some relief. Administrative boundary and population data have been scattered across global repositories with minimal validation from Ministries of Health, and there has been no regionally harmonized, classified master list of health facilities. This fragmentation hampers the reliability of surveillance planning, estimation of immunisation coverage, analysis of catchment areas, resource distribution, and comparability between countries.

Methods: We developed the AFRO Geospatial Database (AFRO GDB), a cloud-hosted, API-enabled platform with automated quality control, multi-actor governance, and standardised data schemas for administrative boundaries, sub-national population estimates, and health facility registries. The platform was delivered through six iterative releases between December 2024 and June 2025 using a Jenkins-based CI/CD pipeline, embedded user acceptance testing with national GIS focal points, and an explicit capacity transfer programme.

Findings:  By July 2025, 36 of 47 Member States (77%) had at least one active boundary dataset in the platform’s governance pipeline. The automated QC engine surfaced 7,347 of 10,546 (69.7%) records in a Ghana facility batch as requiring focal-point review, showing the platform’s capacity to identify records requiring country-level review in real-world registry data. A Mali ADM2 population upload processed 11 regions' records covering 25.2 million people in a single submission cycle. The platform supports six dissemination channels: public web app, REST API, OGC services, file export, QGIS plugin, and online help and is positioned to feed POLIS, WUENIC, DHIS2, and the WHO Global Health Observatory via WHO’s xMart pipeline. The WHO AFRO GIS Centre team demonstrated independent operational capability across CI/CD, deployment, and QC modification at project close.

Interpretation: The AFRO GDB delivers the first regionally harmonised, geospatially validated and country -anchored openly accessible spatial data infrastructure for the WHO African Region, preserving country-anchored data sovereignty through a tiered governance architecture. It provides a documented, replicable model for regional Health Spatial Data Infrastructure (H-SDI) development applicable to other WHO regional offices and to national health information system modernisation in LMIC settings.

title: Asymmetric Market Recovery in Nifty50: Comparing Cumulative Abnormal Returns Across Geopolitical and Political Shocks (2022–2024)

detail.title: Asymmetric Market Recovery in Nifty50: Comparing Cumulative Abnormal Returns Across Geopolitical and Political Shocks (2022–2024)

detail.abstract: This study examines asymmetric market recovery patterns in the Nifty50 index following two categories of macroeconomic shocksgeopolitical and politicalover the period 2022 to 2024. Using event study methodology, cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) are calculated across a [-5, +5] day event window for five major events: the Russia-Ukraine War, RBI Rate Hike, US Federal Reserve Rate Hike, Adani Crisis, and 2024 Indian General Election Results. Expected returns are benchmarked against the historical mean daily return of the Nifty50 index (0.04%) over the full sample period. Results indicate that geopolitical shocks produced sustained negative CARs with no recovery within the event windowthe Russia-Ukraine conflict generated a CAR of-6.7% over eleven trading days. In contrast, the 2024 election results produced a sharp single-day abnormal return of-5.9% followed by full recovery within three trading days, with the CAR ending positive at +1.28%. The US Federal Reserve rate hike demonstrates a notable anticipation effect, with significant negative abnormal returns beginning four days prior to the announcement. These findings suggest that geopolitical shocks require longer defensive positioning than political shocks, which resolve rapidly once uncertainty clears. This study contributes to the limited literature directly comparing shock categories on Indian equity markets and offers practical implications for investors, portfolio managers, and policymakers operating in emerging market environments.

detail.abstract: Empirical research on decentralized and Solana-native market microstructure is constrained less by method than by data: the strongest results in the field rest on a small number of Ethereum-centric datasets, and public, record-level tapes of Solana venues, cross-chain flows, and on-chain oracle behavior remain scarce. We release and document the RED-2400 family v2, a corpus of five public benchmark datasets assembled by a single public-blockchain observer over a concurrent 57-day 2026 window (2026-05-08 to 2026-07-05) under one methodology (free-tier and public feeds only, no paid data, no private accounts, no trading), each with fixed-seed reproducibility scripts, SHA-256 manifests, and a CC-BY-4.0 licence. The five datasets characterize, respectively, Pyth oracle staleness against centralized-exchange prices (164,002 observations), an Aave utilization and Ethereum liquidation panel (18,750 liquidations plus a four-chain utilization series), spot-perpetual basis and funding coupling (244,719 observations), a Solana CEX-versus-DEX spread tape with realized impact (328,186 observations), and a Wormhole cross-chain source-flow tape (360,714 messages). Across the corpus we report three descriptive findings, one honest null, and one field-completeness characterization; none is presented as a causal estimate. The contribution is a coherent, reproducible benchmark family that complements the Ethereum canon and lowers the data barrier for Solana and cross-chain microstructure research.

title: Digital Fragility and Cascading Failures: Causal Evidence from Canada's Payment Infrastructure (2020-2022)

detail.title: Digital Fragility and Cascading Failures: Causal Evidence from Canada's Payment Infrastructure (2020-2022)
detail.abstract:
The increasing digitalization of payment systems has transformed the nature of contemporary monetary constraints. In highly interconnected economies, the effective capacity to execute transactions depends not only on liquidity availability but also on the operational continuity of the technological infrastructure that enables its validation and clearing. In this context, this research analyzes the macroeconomic effects of a systemic disruption in telecommunications and payment infrastructures, using the Rogers Communications and Interac outage in Canada during July 2022 as a high-frequency natural quasi-experiment.

Using mobility indicators associated with the consumption of essential goods (Y,i,t,grocery), an identification strategy is implemented based on Two-Way Fixed Effects models weighted by demographic relevance (TWFE-WLS), dynamic event studies, and Triple-Differences (DDD) specifications. Given the small number of clusters (N = 9), inference is robustified using the Wild Cluster Bootstrap, exact permutation tests, and spatio-temporal sensitivity exercises.

The results show that the disruption of transactional infrastructure produced a significant and heterogeneous contraction in consumption-oriented mobility, the magnitude of which increased with the degree of provincial exposure to the affected network. Furthermore, the evidence rejects the hypothesis that automated teller machine (ATM) density functioned as an effective mitigation mechanism, suggesting instead the existence of a tight operational coupling between physical and digital payment infrastructures.

Dynamic estimates further reveal that the contractive effects persisted beyond the initial restoration of service, consistent with propagation mechanisms associated with production networks and logistical coordination. Taken together, the findings support the hypothesis that localized disruptions in critical infrastructure nodes can amplify through interdependent networks, generating macroeconomic consequences disproportionate to the original physical magnitude of the shock.

The evidence obtained contributes to the literature on network economics, payment systems, and systemic risk, demonstrating that contemporary economic resilience increasingly depends on the stability of technological infrastructures whose relevance extends far beyond the strictly financial sphere.

title: How Sensitive Are Synthetic LLM Participants to Experimenter-Demand Effects?
affiliations: University of Zaragoza - Deparment of Management and Strategy and University of Zaragoza - Department of Economic Analysis

detail.title: How Sensitive Are Synthetic LLM Participants to Experimenter-Demand Effects?
detail.abstract: Are inferences based on synthetic samples from large language models (LLMs) robust to experimenter demand effects? We bound demand effects across eight LLMs from three providers and nine canonical economic tasks, benchmarking our estimates against a human sample of 7,517 participants. Our results are consistent with large demand effects in LLM samples. Making the researcher's expectation explicit—weak-demand treatment—shifts responses by 1.223 standard deviations for LLMs, compared with 0.157 among humans. Making the researcher's request explicit—strong-demand treatment—shifts responses by 1.714 standard deviations for LLMs and 0.571 among humans. On a common unit-interval scale, demand wording shifts average LLM choices by 22.3% of the feasible action range under weak demand and 48.1% under strong demand, compared with 3.8% and 15.2% in the human benchmark. The magnitude of these effects varies across tasks, providers, and individual models, but no provider or model family approaches the relatively low level of demand responsiveness observed in the human sample. These findings suggest that LLM agents may be useful for some experimental applications, but inferences based on synthetic samples should explicitly assess and bound potential demand effects.

detail.abstract: While real estate owners play a significant role in advancing digitalization and sustainability within the sector, there's limited understanding of their innovation processes. This article aims to increase understanding on the innovation processes and dynamic capabilities in real estate owner organizations. The article examines a longitudinal case study within a prominent Swedish real estate owner known for significant investments in smart building technologies. Despite these investments, practical benefits face hurdles, reflecting broader challenges in real estate sector digitalization projects. These obstacles include top-down innovation focus, limited crossfunctional and user-centric innovation, innovation process discontinuities, ambiguous innovator roles, hierarchical communication, resource constraints, and uncertainties in technology implementation. The study emphasizes the inclusion of diverse perspectives in innovation processes and suggests further research on organizational and user-centric aspects. It contributes to real estate and facility management literature by proposing potential solutions to innovation processes, offering valuable insights for industry practitioners and researchers alike.

title: Connecting the Disconnected: Heterogeneous Returns to Broadband Infrastructure Investment
affiliations: Northwestern University and Northwestern University

detail.title: Connecting the Disconnected: Heterogeneous Returns to Broadband Infrastructure Investment
detail.abstract: We exploit the engineering-based, staggered rollout of Connect America Fund Phase II to estimate heterogeneous returns to public broadband investment. CAF II raised labor force participation among workers with disabilities, a high search-costs population, by 1.6 percentage points relative to the general population in pre-pandemic data. The differential rises to 4.7 points including pandemic-era observations, exceeding the estimated Americans with Disabilities Act employment effect. Three mechanism tests reject remote work as the operative channel: telework grew less for workers with disabilities, employment gains are uniform across remote-feasible and other occupations, and commute reductions appeared only among workers with mobility impairments.

title: Digital Technologies in Architecture, Engineering, and Construction
affiliations: SINTEF Community, SINTEF Community and

detail.title: Digital Technologies in Architecture, Engineering, and Construction
detail.abstract: Digitalization in the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) sector is slow due to significant challenges in technology adoption. The study aims to promote technology adoption by advancing the understanding of digital technologies in the AEC sector. This article presents the findings from a quantitative scoping review, encompassing 3950 technology-related abstracts retrieved from the Scopus database, providing a preliminary assessment of literature size, geographic innovation hotspots, research gaps, and key concepts in the AEC field. The results show that Building Information Modelling (1852 studies) dominates the literature, while topics like 3D Printing (311) and Internet of Things (227) are gaining traction. China (687 publications) and the United States (566) produce most research articles. Despite the increasing interest in emerging technologies, their implementation often necessitates acquiring specific skill sets. Academia needs to put a stronger focus on these technologies in education and tighter collaboration with the industry is needed.

title: From For You Page to Public Knowledge: How TikTok Shapes Student News

detail.title: From For You Page to Public Knowledge: How TikTok Shapes Student News
detail.abstract: TikTok started as a place for fun videos, but for many students it has become a source of news. On the For You Page, a breaking headline can appear right after a dance trend, showing how algorithms now decide what we see. This makes news quick and easy to access, but it also blurs the line between fact and opinion. For Filipino youth, TikTok is more than entertainment: it's shaping how our generation learns about the world.

title: Recursive Scientific Domain Addressing: Making the Conditions of Validity Declarable, Comparable, and Inheritable – an Obligation Every Science Acknowledges, a Structure That Would Let It Be Met

detail.title: Recursive Scientific Domain Addressing: Making the Conditions of Validity Declarable, Comparable, and Inheritable – an Obligation Every Science Acknowledges, a Structure That Would Let It Be Met
detail.abstract: Scientific claims are universally understood to hold only under the conditions that established them, yet those conditions rarely travel with the claims they qualify. Once findings are cited, transferred, or deployed in new contexts, their assumptions, methods, scope, and environmental constraints remain embedded in prose rather than represented as portable structures that can be declared, compared, and inherited-so that outside the conditions that established it, a claim's validity is not merely reduced but undefined. This paper argues that the resulting failures are architectural rather than methodological. Existing reporting standards, provenance frameworks, ontologies, and retrieval systems each capture part of what a claim's validity requires, yet none provides a general, portable structure of this kind for expressing where a claim remains valid across disciplines and contexts of use.

detail.abstract: This chapter explores the transformative rise of robo-advisory within the broader FinTech revolution, tracing its evolution from traditional human advisors to AI-driven platforms that democratise financial services. The chapter begins by situating robo-advisory within the rapidly evolving financial landscape shaped by digitalisation, disintermediation, and changing client expectations. It examines the drivers behind this shift, including advancements in AI and data analytics, evolving investor demands for personalisation and accessibility, as well as the cost and scalability pressures facing financial institutions. The chapter differentiates between rule-based and AI-powered systems, highlighting how modern robo-advisors increasingly leverage machine learning, behavioural insights, and alternative data to offer dynamic and adaptive services. Emerging trends, such as hybrid advisory models, behavioural nudges, ethical challenges surrounding algorithmic transparency, and inclusivity concerns, are also addressed. Moreover, the chapter maps out key players and market trends, emphasising regional variations, consolidation patterns, and niche market opportunities. A novel framework of six AI-driven business models is introduced to explain how robo-advisory is strategically deployed across incumbent and disruptive financial organisations. The chapter concludes by underscoring that success in robo-advisory is not solely a technological feat but hinges on trust, transparency, user experience, and regulatory alignment. Ultimately, robo-advisors serve as a lens to understand the future trajectory of financial services where AI, automation, and behavioural design converge to reshape how individuals engage with money, risk, and long-term financial planning.

detail.abstract: Operating-model decisions-how to split work across teams, regions and time zones, and where to insert automation-are typically made on judgment, static spreadsheets, and averages. Averages hide the queueing behaviour that actually determines whether service levels hold under month-end peaks, quality shocks and regional outages. This paper introduces Operating Model Lab, an open, code-based framework that lets an operating model be written as version-controlled configuration, simulated by a deterministic discrete-event engine run as a seeded Monte-Carlo experiment, and compared across structural variants on a single interactive dashboard. The framework's distinguishing feature is a governance separation: a large-language-model (LLM) copilot designs, critiques and narrates but never computes, while an independent calculation-QA layer re-derives every headline number by a second method (flow conservation, capacity algebra, queueing monotonicity, and held-out surrogate validation) and holds veto power over publication. On a fully fictional three-region worked example, the framework shows that no candidate structure clears a 90 percent service-level floor at baseline settings, identifies the specific lever combinations that do, and prints the cost of each-a result that a spreadsheet built on averages would have missed. We describe the modelling language, the engine, the validation regime, and the limitations, and release the full system as open source so that results are reproducible and independently checkable.

title: CENSORSHIP VERSUS ACCOUNTABILITY: IS THE REGULATION OF SOCIAL MEDIA A THREAT TO THE RIGHT TO FREEDOM OF EXPRESSION IN KENYA?

detail.title: CENSORSHIP VERSUS ACCOUNTABILITY: IS THE REGULATION OF SOCIAL MEDIA A THREAT TO THE RIGHT TO FREEDOM OF EXPRESSION IN KENYA?
detail.abstract: The advent of social media has transformed the way freedom of expression is exercised, both globally and in Kenya. Freedom of expression is the hallmark of democracy and is vital to guaranteeing other rights. In Kenya, however, the growing use of digital platforms for public discourse has called for regulation to rein in competing interests. This is supported by the limits of that right under Articles 33(2) and 24 of the Constitution. Among the competing interests are the freedom of expression on one hand, and the protection of users from harmful users on the other hand. This research aims to ascertain whether the regulation of social media promotes censorship of users or accountability of deleterious users. It finds that untethered exercise of freedom of expression risks violation of the rights of other users of social media, whereas heightened “regulation for protection of users” may lead to censorship and the suppression of freedom of expression both by the government and social media platforms. This research further finds that the regulation of social media in Kenya has shifted to extreme censorship, thereby deviating from the original objective to deter deleterious conduct. To resolve this regulatory problem, this research proposes various ways of achieving a regulatory balance by tempering the dangers posed by the extremes of each interest. Finally, it draws regulatory lessons from other comparative jurisdictions. The study recommends a coordinated, human rights-based regulatory approach inclusive of all stakeholders in the digital space.

title: AGENT-AWARE MIDDLEWARE FOR AUTONOMOUS LEGACY SYSTEM ENHANCEMENT: A DOMAIN-AGNOSTIC APPROACH
affiliations: Tagore Engineering College, Tagore Engineering College, Tagore Engineering College, Tagore Engineering College and Tagore Engineering College

detail.title: AGENT-AWARE MIDDLEWARE FOR AUTONOMOUS LEGACY SYSTEM ENHANCEMENT: A DOMAIN-AGNOSTIC APPROACH
detail.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into deep legacy enterprise infrastructures—such as COBOL-based mainframes, MUMPS healthcare systems, and SCADA industrial networks—presents critical challenges due to rigid procedural constraints and the severe risk of probabilistic hallucinations. Traditional Robotic Process Automation (RPA) lacks the cognitive flexibility to manage unstructured edge cases, while single-agent LLMs frequently suffer from context poisoning during complex multi-step transactions. To address this architectural gap, this paper proposes a domain-agnostic, Agent-Aware Middleware utilizing a Shared Blackboard state pattern. The system orchestrates a specialized five-agent cognitive pipeline—comprising a Concierge, Data Engineer, Actuator, Fixer, and Auditor—governed by an event-driven "Temporal Airlock." This isolated execution environment forces tasks through ten discrete cognitive passes, decoupling memory logic from execution to ensure zero-hallucination data remediation. To empirically validate the architecture without jeopardizing live mission-critical mainframes, testing was conducted using relational databases (SQL) and structured ledgers as proxy environments. The middleware was deployed across two distinct proxies: an IT Service Level Agreement (SLA) pipeline and an Educational statutory compliance registry. Empirical evaluations on proxy enterprise ledgers demonstrated that the architecture achieved a 100% Data Integrity Rate, successfully intercepting LLM logic hallucinations and network anomalies to prevent legacy database corruption. The system maintained a 60% end-to-end autonomous execution yield during asynchronous background processing, while synchronous web events established a 90-second latency baseline, utilizing a Global Lock and safely routing ambiguous requests to a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) dashboard.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a reference architecture for systematic trading research. It has two purposes. First, it organizes a public vocabulary of trading equations-trend and momentum measures, mean-reversion and stationarity diagnostics, volatility estimators, volume and order-flow variables, execution-cost terms, position-sizing rules, performance metrics, and machine-learning estimators-into a consistent notation that can be audited. Second, it proposes a research-toexecution architecture governed by one asymmetry: internal computation is comparatively cheap, whereas each executed order and each unlogged research trial is expensive. This asymmetry motivates a strict separation between a dynamics layer, which estimates market state, and a policy layer, which decides whether and how capital should be exposed. The paper does not claim original trading profitability. It cites public sources for established definitions and results, and it labels its own contribution as an organizational and methodological design. The central claim is that trading research should be judged not by isolated backtest statistics but by a chain of custody: source data, feature snapshot, signal, policy decision, executable price model, outcome policy, audit statistic, and promotion level. The resulting framework is intended as a defensible starting point for practitioners and researchers building multi-strategy systems under walk-forward validation, multiple-testing correction, realistic costs, and forward shadow evidence.

title: Shadow AI in Higher Education: A Socio-Technical Framework for Governing Unauthorized Employee Use of Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Coastline Community College, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Coastline College

detail.title: Shadow AI in Higher Education: A Socio-Technical Framework for Governing Unauthorized Employee Use of Artificial Intelligence

declarations.ethicsApproval: Full IRB approval was received prior to the study. Participants agreed to participate. Teh data collected was anonomous.

detail.abstract: Shadow AI-the use of artificial intelligence tools by employees without institutional approval, procurement review, or datagovernance oversight-is emerging rapidly across higher education as generative AI adoption outpaces institutional policy. This article argues that shadow AI is not principally a compliance failure but a socio-technical governance gap that appears when employee adoption advances faster than an institution's policy, procurement, training, cybersecurity review, and data-governance infrastructure. Drawing on the shadow information technology literature and contemporary research on artificial intelligence governance in higher education, the article advances a conceptual framework, The Shadow AI Adoption-Governance Gap Model, comprising seven dimensions: employee need and use pressure, institutional enablement gap, policy and governance ambiguity, risk awareness and data sensitivity, shadow AI behavior, institutional outcomes, and governance response. The framework is examined against an original 2026 survey of employees at a single two-year public college (50 valid respondents; an 18.9% response rate). Respondents reported high self-assessed AI literacy (98.0% understood basic AI concepts) and strong demand for additional training (84.0%), yet preferred external consumer tools-ChatGPT (72.0%), Google Gemini, Claude, and Microsoft Copilot-none of which were the institution's three sanctioned platforms. Interpreted through the model, this pattern points less to low risk awareness than to institutional enablement gaps and policy ambiguity. The article offers risk-tiered governance recommendations and a practitioner readiness checklist, arguing that institutions should move employees from hidden AI use toward transparent, supported, and ethically governed practice. Because the survey is single-institution and self-reported, the findings are interpretive rather than confirmatory.

title: Cultural Context in Standardized Tests
affiliations: UNSW Australia Business School, School of Economics, University of New South Wales (UNSW), UNSW Australia Business School, School of Economics, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Canberra and UNSW Australia Business School, School of Economics

detail.title: Cultural Context in Standardized Tests
detail.abstract: We conduct a randomized controlled trial with 1,135 students in rural Australia to measure the impact of cultural bias on standardized test performance. We adapt a national basic-skills assessment to the local context, ensuring equal difficulty, and randomly assign students to the original or contextualized version of the test. Test format had no effect on numeracy scores. In reading, we find positive and qualitatively large effects. The average treatment effect is 0.27 standard deviations, with statistically equivalent impacts for Indigenous and non-Indigenous students. These findings suggest that cultural context can meaningfully influence performance on certain types of standardized assessments.

title: ”There Was No Parenting Class for This”: Gendered Experiences of Navigating the Empty Nest Transition
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: ”There Was No Parenting Class for This”: Gendered Experiences of Navigating the Empty Nest Transition
detail.abstract: This research aims to enhance understanding of the empty-nest transition and the diverse,experiences parents undergo during this period. While the transition into parenthood has been,extensively studied, the shift into post-parenting life, when children leave the household, remains,underexplored, particularly through a gendered lens. The study explores the balance between loss,and growth that accompanies a child's departure from the home, as well as the coping,mechanisms parents employ to manage this change. Using a qualitative approach, the study included 21 in-depth interviews with 12 identifying mothers and 9 identifying fathers. These interviews examined participants' preparations, changes in daily routines, shifts in interpersonal relationships, and active coping strategies. The findings provide a deeper understanding,of the empty-nest experience, highlighting the emotional and psychological dynamics of this life,stage and the role of gender in shaping these experiences. By identifying effective coping,strategies, as well as preparation and prevention mechanisms that can lessen the burden of,psychological distress, this research may inform future interventions and support systems to help,parents navigate this transition with greater resilience.

title: Trace-Mediated Peak Bias: An Optimization Perspective on Temporal Credit Assignment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Trace-Mediated Peak Bias: An Optimization Perspective on Temporal Credit Assignment
detail.abstract: Temporal credit assignment enables reinforcement learning (RL) agents to associate delayed rewards with earlier decisions and is a fundamental component of many modern RL algorithms. Despite extensive work on the statistical properties of multistep learning, comparatively little is known about how temporally propagated credit interacts with nonlinear function approximation and gradient-based optimization. We investigate this interaction using a controlled experimental setting and a trace-inspired temporal weighting objective that isolates long-range credit propagation. We identify a systematic misordering of trajectory values at intermediate weighting depths, whereby a trajectory containing a single high-magnitude reward is estimated as more valuable than an alternative with a strictly greater discounted return. Inspired by the \textit{Peak-End Rule} in cognitive psychology, we refer to this phenomenon as \textit{Trace-Mediated Peak Bias} (TMPB). We show that TMPB arises when temporally propagated temporal-difference errors amplify isolated high-saliency rewards into disproportionately large parameter updates that distort shared neural representations under fixed-step stochastic gradient optimization. In contrast, adaptive second-moment optimization substantially mitigates the effect by attenuating these gradient amplifications. Our findings identify a previously unreported optimization pathology arising from the interaction between temporal credit propagation, nonlinear function approximation, and gradient-based optimization, while providing further empirical evidence for the stabilizing role of adaptive second-moment optimization in deep reinforcement learning.
